s: Welcome to the southern tip of Manhattan, the oldest part of New York City and, for most of its history, the whole of it.
Before any Europeans arrived, this was Lenape country.
The Lenape called the island something close to Manahatta, often translated as the island of many hills.
The hills are mostly gone now, shaved down and dumped into the rivers, but the street plan you are walking on still remembers the people who came next.
In 1624 and 1625 the Dutch West India Company established a trading post here called New Amsterdam.
It was a company town in the most literal sense: a commercial venture built to ship beaver pelts back to Europe.
In that respect, almost nothing has changed.
Lower Manhattan was founded as a business, and it has been a business ever since.
Notice how the streets down here twist and wander.
North of about Houston Street, Manhattan is famous for its rigid grid, laid down by the Commissioners' Plan of 1811.
But down here, the streets predate the grid.
They follow old cow paths, property lines, a canal, and the original shoreline.
Pearl Street was once literally the edge of the East River.
Water Street, Front Street, and South Street were each added, one after another, as merchants dumped fill into the river to create more valuable waterfront land.
If you are standing anywhere east of Pearl Street, you are standing on what used to be river.
The same is true on the west side, where the entire neighborhood of Battery Park City was built on fill excavated from the original World Trade Center site.

Wall Street itself takes its name from a wooden palisade the Dutch built in 1653 to protect against attack from the north, by the English or by the Lenape, depending on which year's anxieties you consult.
The English took the colony in 1664 without a fight and renamed it New York, after the Duke of York.
The wall came down in 1699.
The name stayed.
In the nineteenth century, this district became the counting house of the nation.
The Erie Canal opened in 1825 and made New York the gateway between the Atlantic and the interior of the continent.
Grain, cotton, and capital flowed through these blocks.
Banks, insurers, and shipping lines crowded together, because in an age before telephones, physical proximity was information.
The Great Fire of 1835 burned hundreds of buildings in the area, which is one reason so little of colonial New York survives, and much of what replaced it was rebuilt bigger, in stone.
By the early twentieth century, the district had become the birthplace of the skyscraper race.
Land was so expensive and so scarce that the only direction left was up.
Walk these streets and you will notice that they feel like canyons.
Many are barely wider than they were in the 1600s, but the buildings lining them are forty, fifty, sixty stories tall.
That tension, a medieval street plan with modern towers stacked on top, is the signature experience of the Financial District.
Here is something to look for as you walk.
Along lower Broadway, near Bowling Green, stood what was called Steamship Row.
In the early 1900s, the great transatlantic shipping lines kept their ticket offices and headquarters here, close to the harbor and the customs house.
The Cunard Line, the White Star Line's parent company, and others sold passage to Europe from grand halls along this stretch.
Some of those buildings survive, with nautical carvings of ships, shells, and sea creatures still on their facades.

On this tour we will start at the Battery, where the harbor opens up, and work our way north past Bowling Green, the old Dutch streets, Wall Street, Trinity Church, the Federal Reserve, and finally the World Trade Center site.
Along the way, keep looking up.
The best details in this neighborhood are often thirty feet above your head.
You are in Battery Park, named for the artillery batteries that once defended the harbor.
The round sandstone fort in front of you is Castle Clinton, and it may be the most reinvented building in New York.
It was built between 1808 and 1811, when tensions with Britain were rising toward what became the War of 1812.
When it was built, it did not sit in a park.
It stood on a small artificial island about two hundred feet offshore, connected to Manhattan by a wooden bridge.
Everything between here and the old shoreline is fill.
The fort was armed with heavy cannon, but it never fired a shot in anger.
In 1815 it was renamed for DeWitt Clinton, the mayor and later governor who would go on to champion the Erie Canal.
The army gave the fort to the city in the 1820s, and it became Castle Garden, an entertainment venue with a roof added over the open center.
This was one of the most fashionable places in New York.

In 1850, the showman P. T. Barnum brought the Swedish soprano Jenny Lind here for her American debut, and the publicity frenzy he built around her is often described as one of the first modern celebrity marketing campaigns.
Tickets were auctioned off.
The demand was extraordinary.
Then the building changed purpose entirely.
From 1855 to 1890, Castle Garden served as New York State's immigrant landing depot.
Roughly eight million people entered America through this building, before Ellis Island existed.
If your ancestors arrived in New York in the mid-nineteenth century, many of them from Ireland and Germany, there is a good chance they walked through here.
The operation was meant to protect new arrivals from the swindlers, fake boarding house agents, and con artists who worked the docks.

After Ellis Island took over federal immigration processing, the building was reinvented again, this time as the New York Aquarium, which opened in 1896 and became one of the most popular attractions in the city.
In the 1940s, the parks commissioner Robert Moses moved the aquarium to Coney Island and wanted to tear the fort down entirely, partly to make way for his plans for a bridge to Brooklyn.
Preservationists fought him, and the fort was eventually designated a national monument.
Today it is where you buy tickets for the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island ferries.
Look out across the harbor.
The Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island, a gift from France dedicated in 1886.
To its right, Ellis Island.
Farther left, you can see Governors Island, a former army and Coast Guard base that is now a public park, and beyond it, Brooklyn.
Somewhere in this park you will also find The Sphere, a large, damaged bronze sculpture by the German artist Fritz Koenig.
It originally stood in the plaza between the Twin Towers.
It survived the collapse on September eleventh, battered and torn, and was moved here, and later to Liberty Park near the World Trade Center site.
Its scars were deliberately left in place.
This small oval is Bowling Green, the oldest public park in New York City.
In 1733, the city leased it to three neighbors for the token rent of one peppercorn a year, on the condition that they turn it into a bowling green for the recreation of the inhabitants.
The Dutch had used this spot earlier as a cattle market and parade ground.
Look at the iron fence surrounding the green.
It dates to 1771, which makes it one of the oldest surviving fences in the city.
It once had small crowns ornamenting its posts.
In 1770, the city had installed a gilded lead equestrian statue of King George the Third in the center of the green.

On July ninth, 1776, after the Declaration of Independence was read to George Washington's troops in New York, a crowd marched here, pulled the statue down, and sawed off the crowns from the fence posts.
Much of the lead from the statue was reportedly shipped to Connecticut and melted into musket balls for the Continental Army.
Pieces of it still turn up in museum collections.
At the north tip of the green is the Charging Bull, the bronze sculpture by Arturo Di Modica.
He installed it without permission in December 1989, dropping it overnight in front of the New York Stock Exchange as a gift to the city after the 1987 market crash.
The police removed it, public outcry followed, and the city found it a new home here.
Now turn and look at the buildings around you.
This stretch of lower Broadway was Steamship Row.
In the age of the great ocean liners, a trip to Europe began with a visit to one of these offices.
Look for 25 Broadway, the Cunard Building, completed in 1921.
Cunard was the British line that operated famous ships like the Lusitania and, later, the Queen Mary.
Its ground floor booking hall was one of the most lavish interiors in the city, with a vaulted, painted ceiling meant to evoke the great domed halls of the Renaissance.
The building's ornament is full of maritime references.
Across the way, at One Broadway, stood the offices of the International Mercantile Marine Company, J. P. Morgan's shipping trust, which controlled the White Star Line, owner of the Titanic.
Look at the entrances: one door is marked First Class and another Cabin Class, a leftover from when you bought your ticket according to your station in life.
Now look at 26 Broadway, the long, curved building that follows the bend of the street.
This was the headquarters of John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil Company, which at its peak controlled the overwhelming majority of oil refining in the United States.
The company was broken up by the Supreme Court in 1911, and its pieces became, among others, the ancestors of ExxonMobil and Chevron.
The top of the tower is designed to suggest an oil lamp, a quiet reminder that Standard Oil's first fortune came from kerosene for lighting, not gasoline for cars.
Finally, the massive building facing the south end of the green is the Alexander Hamilton United States Custom House, designed by Cass Gilbert and completed in 1907.
Before the federal income tax arrived in 1913, customs duties were a principal source of federal revenue, and the Port of New York collected a large share of them.
The building looks like a temple to commerce because it was one.
The four large sculptures in front, by Daniel Chester French, represent four continents, and the twelve figures along the cornice represent great seafaring powers of history.
Today it houses a branch of the Smithsonian's National Museum of the American Indian, which is free, and its oval rotunda, with murals of ships entering the harbor, is worth a look if it's open.
You are now in the oldest surviving fabric of the street plan.

Stone Street, the narrow lane lined with nineteenth century buildings and outdoor tables, takes its name from the fact that it was reportedly one of the first paved streets in New Amsterdam, cobbled in the 1650s.
The Dutch knew it as Brouwer Straat, Brewers Street, because breweries lined it.
The buildings you see today mostly went up right after the Great Fire of 1835 destroyed the neighborhood.
They were warehouses and counting rooms for merchants.
Today it is one of the few places downtown where you can feel the scale of the old city.
A short walk away, at the corner of Pearl and Broad Streets, is Fraunces Tavern, the brick building with the hipped roof.
In 1762, Samuel Fraunces bought the building and opened a tavern called the Queen's Head.
It became a meeting place for the Sons of Liberty before the Revolution.
Its most famous moment came on December fourth, 1783.
The British had just evacuated New York, the war was over, and George Washington gathered his officers in the tavern's Long Room to say goodbye.
Accounts describe an emotional scene, with Washington asking each officer to come and take him by the hand.
He then walked to the waterfront and left the city, expecting to retire to private life.
A fair caution: the building you see is substantially a 1907 reconstruction, based on careful guesswork about what the colonial original looked like.
But it occupies the same spot, and it houses a small museum upstairs.
Notice Pearl Street itself.
It probably takes its name from the oyster shells that littered the original shoreline.
When New Amsterdam was founded, Pearl Street was the waterfront.
Everything to the east of it was water.
Now walk toward the triangle where Beaver Street and South William Street meet.
That building, with the columns at its rounded corner entrance, is Delmonico's.

The Delmonico brothers, immigrants from the Italian speaking part of Switzerland, opened a small café downtown in 1827, and their family went on to create what is often called the first fine dining restaurant in America: a place where you sat at your own table and ordered from a printed menu, rather than eating whatever the tavern served at a common table.
The current building dates from 1837.
Delmonico's is credited, with varying degrees of certainty, with popularizing or inventing Lobster Newberg, Eggs Benedict, Baked Alaska, and of course the Delmonico steak.
It was the place where Wall Street celebrated its deals.
A block away is Hanover Square, a little triangular park.
The handsome brownstone Italianate building on its south side is India House, built in the early 1850s for Hanover Bank.
It later housed the New York Cotton Exchange, a reminder that the profits of the slave economy of the American South flowed directly through these streets.
New York's banks financed cotton crops, its insurers insured them, and its ships carried them to England.
Today it is a private club.
You are at the intersection of Wall and Broad, arguably the most symbolically loaded street corner in the world.
Start with the building with the Greek temple front and the large bronze statue of George Washington on its steps.
This is Federal Hall National Memorial.
The building itself dates from 1842 and was built as the United States Custom House, later becoming a branch of the Treasury.
But the site is what matters.
An earlier building here served as New York's City Hall, and in 1735, it hosted the trial of the printer John Peter Zenger, who was charged with seditious libel for criticizing the colonial governor.
His acquittal became an early landmark in the idea of a free press.
After the Revolution, New York was briefly the capital of the United States, and the old City Hall was remodeled as Federal Hall to house the new Congress.
On April thirtieth, 1789, George Washington stood on a balcony here and took the oath of office as the first president.
The statue, by John Quincy Adams Ward, marks roughly the spot.
The first Congress met here, and it was here that it drafted the amendments that became the Bill of Rights.
Now face the building with the six giant Corinthian columns across Broad Street.
That's the New York Stock Exchange, completed in 1903 to a design by George B. Post.
Look at the sculpture in the pediment above the columns.
It is called Integrity Protecting the Works of Man, and it shows a central figure of Integrity with figures representing agriculture, mining, industry, and science.

The exchange traces its origins to the Buttonwood Agreement of 1792, when twenty four brokers agreed to trade with each other under fixed commissions, supposedly beneath a buttonwood tree that stood a short distance from here on Wall Street.
Now look at the low, plain, marble building on the southeast corner of Wall and Broad, at 23 Wall Street.
It has no name on it.
It didn't need one.
This was the headquarters of J. P. Morgan and Company, the most powerful private bank in the country, known on the street simply as The Corner.
In the Panic of 1907, J. Pierpont Morgan personally organized the rescue of the banking system, a crisis that led directly to the creation of the Federal Reserve a few years later.
Walk up to the Wall Street side of the building and look closely at the stone.
You will see pockmarks and gouges.
On September sixteenth, 1920, just after noon, a horse-drawn wagon packed with dynamite and iron weights exploded right here.
Thirty eight people were killed and hundreds were injured.
No one was ever convicted, though anarchists were widely suspected.
Morgan's firm chose not to repair the damage.
It is still there, a century later.
One more building to notice.
Look up along Wall Street for a tower topped by a stepped pyramid.
That is 14 Wall Street, built for Bankers Trust, and its pyramid was modeled on the ancient Mausoleum at Halicarnassus.
Bankers Trust later made the pyramid its corporate logo.
And farther down, at 40 Wall Street, is the tower with the green pyramidal roof and spire, built in 1930 for the Bank of Manhattan Company.
It briefly raced the Chrysler Building to be the world's tallest, and lost when the Chrysler's builders secretly assembled a spire inside their dome and raised it into place.
The Bank of Manhattan has an interesting origin of its own: it began as the Manhattan Company, chartered in 1799 supposedly to supply the city with clean water.
Its real purpose, engineered by Aaron Burr, was to slip a bank charter past Alexander Hamilton's Federalists.
Through a long chain of mergers, it is an ancestor of today's JPMorgan Chase.
At the head of Wall Street, framed perfectly by the canyon of buildings, stands Trinity Church.
Its location is no accident.
Wall Street was laid out as the church's front walk, in effect.
Stand on Wall Street looking west and the church closes the view, like an altar at the end of a nave.
The congregation dates to 1697, chartered by King William the Third, which makes it one of the oldest Anglican, now Episcopal, parishes in the country.
The current building is the third on the site.
The first burned in the Great Fire of 1776, during the British occupation.
The second was weakened by heavy snow.
The building you see now was designed by Richard Upjohn and completed in 1846.
It's one of the most important early Gothic Revival churches in America, and its brownstone was meant to look like a church from medieval England.
For decades, its spire, about two hundred eighty feet tall, was the tallest structure in New York.
Sailors approaching the harbor used it as a landmark.
Imagine that: a whole skyline dominated by a church steeple, until the commercial towers overtook it at the end of the nineteenth century.
Today it looks small, but in its time, it was the skyline.
Trinity also has one of the great fortunes in New York real estate history.
In 1705, Queen Anne granted the church a large tract of farmland on the west side of lower Manhattan.

Over three centuries, the church sold much of it, and gave away parcels to found other institutions, but it still owns substantial property, especially in the Hudson Square neighborhood to the north, and its real estate operation remains a major landlord.
Step into the churchyard, which is open most days.
Here you'll find some notable graves.
Alexander Hamilton is buried here, under a white marble pyramid-topped monument near the south side, with his wife Eliza nearby.
Hamilton founded the Bank of New York, which still exists today as part of BNY, and as first Treasury Secretary he designed much of the financial architecture of the young country.
He was killed in 1804 in a duel with Aaron Burr, the same Aaron Burr behind the Manhattan Company you just heard about.
The two men are, in a sense, still competing on Wall Street.
Also here: Robert Fulton, the inventor and engineer whose steamboat, the Clermont, made its famous run up the Hudson to Albany in 1807 and launched commercial steam navigation in America.
Albert Gallatin, Treasury secretary under Jefferson and Madison, is also buried here.
So is William Bradford, the colonial printer.
As you stand here, notice how the old gravestones, some dating from the late 1600s, sit in the shadow of glass towers.
Trinity's churchyard is one of the only pieces of open ground in this part of the city that has stayed open continuously since the seventeenth century.
You are now on Liberty Street, in front of a building that looks like a fortified Italian Renaissance palace, which is exactly the effect its architects intended.
This is the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, completed in 1924 and designed by the firm York and Sawyer.
They modeled it on the palazzos of fifteenth century Florence, like the Strozzi Palace, built for banking families who wanted their wealth to look secure, imposing, and untouchable.
Look at the ironwork on the windows and lanterns.
It was made by Samuel Yellin, a Philadelphia metalsmith considered the greatest American ironworker of his era.
It is functional security disguised as craft.
The New York Fed is the most important of the twelve regional Federal Reserve banks.
It carries out the Fed's open market operations, the buying and selling of securities that steers interest rates.
And underneath your feet, roughly eighty feet below street level, sitting directly on Manhattan's bedrock, is a vault holding one of the largest stores of gold in the world.
Most of it doesn't belong to the United States.
It belongs to foreign governments and central banks, which keep it here for safekeeping.
When one country pays another in gold, sometimes the bars are simply moved from one locked compartment to another inside this vault.
The New York Fed offers public tours, booked in advance, if you want to see it for yourself.
Now look across the street at the plain, glass-and-aluminum tower set back on a broad open plaza.
That's 28 Liberty Street, originally One Chase Manhattan Plaza, finished in 1961 and designed by Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings and Merrill.
Its story is about confidence.
In the 1950s, many companies were fleeing lower Manhattan for Midtown.

David Rockefeller, then a rising executive at Chase Manhattan Bank, pushed for the bank to build a giant new headquarters here instead, and his commitment is often credited with helping keep the Financial District alive.
He and his brother Nelson later pushed the plans that led to the World Trade Center.
Two pieces of art on the plaza are worth finding.
The tall, black-and-white sculpture that looks like a cluster of cartoon trees is Group of Four Trees by Jean Dubuffet, installed in 1972.
And set into the plaza is a sunken circular garden by Isamu Noguchi, with stones and patterns meant to evoke a Japanese dry garden.
You can look down into it from the plaza level.

This combination, a Renaissance fortress for the nation's money on one side and a sleek modernist tower for private banking on the other, captures the two eras of the Financial District in a single glance.
You are now at the World Trade Center site.
The original World Trade Center was conceived in the late 1950s and 1960s, championed by David and Nelson Rockefeller and built by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey.
To make room, the city cleared an entire neighborhood of small streets, including Radio Row, a cluster of electronics shops where New Yorkers once bought radios, parts, and gadgets.
The architect Minoru Yamasaki designed the two towers, which opened in the early 1970s and were, briefly, the tallest buildings in the world.
The soil and rock excavated to build them were dumped into the Hudson River, creating the landfill on which Battery Park City now stands.
In August 1974, a French high-wire artist named Philippe Petit strung a cable between the two towers and walked across it, more than thirteen hundred feet above the street, for nearly an hour.
He was arrested, and then celebrated.
On the morning of September eleventh, 2001, terrorists hijacked four airliners.
Two were flown into the towers, which collapsed within two hours.
In all, two thousand nine hundred seventy seven people were killed in the attacks in New York, at the Pentagon, and in Pennsylvania, the large majority of them here.
The memorial, called Reflecting Absence, was designed by Michael Arad with the landscape architect Peter Walker, and opened in 2011.
The two pools sit in the footprints of the original towers.
Water falls thirty feet down all four sides and then disappears into a smaller square void in the center whose bottom you cannot see.
Around the edges, the names of the victims, including those killed in the 1993 bombing here, are cut into bronze panels.
The names are not alphabetical.
They are arranged according to what the designers called meaningful adjacencies: coworkers next to coworkers, friends next to friends, family members together, based on requests from the families.
At night, light shines up through the cut letters.
On victims' birthdays, staff place a single white rose in their names.
Look for the Survivor Tree, a Callery pear found in the rubble badly burned, with snapped roots and just one living branch.
It was nursed back to health in a Bronx nursery and replanted here.
It flowers every spring.
The tallest tower on the site is One World Trade Center, opened in 2014.
Its height to the tip of its spire is one thousand seven hundred seventy six feet, a deliberate reference to the year of the Declaration of Independence.

Finally, the white, ribbed structure that looks like a bird with outstretched wings, or a skeleton, depending on whom you ask, is the Oculus, the transit hub designed by the Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava.
It opened in 2016 and became one of the most expensive train stations ever built.
Its central skylight is aligned so that each year on the morning of September eleventh, the sun shines down the length of the opening, at the time the second tower fell.
Step inside if you can.
The interior, all white ribs and open space, is one of the great rooms of modern New York.
End your walk at St. Paul's Chapel, the stone church with the tall steeple facing Broadway.
Completed in 1766, it is the oldest surviving church building in Manhattan, and one of the few buildings in the city that predates the American Revolution.
The chapel was built as an outpost of Trinity Church, for the growing population moving north of Wall Street.
Its design was inspired by St. Martin-in-the-Fields in London.

Notice that the church seems to face the wrong way: its grand portico, with the columns, faces Broadway, but the main entrance was originally on the other side, facing the Hudson River, which back then came up close to the churchyard.
The steeple was added in the 1790s.
During the Great Fire of 1776, when much of the city burned during the British occupation, St. Paul's survived, reportedly thanks to a bucket brigade on its roof.
On April thirtieth, 1789, after taking the oath of office at Federal Hall, George Washington walked here with members of Congress for a service of prayer.
His pew is preserved inside, along with a painting of the Great Seal of the United States.
The chapel had a second historic moment in 2001.
Even though it stood just across the street from the World Trade Center, it was not seriously damaged.
Not even a window broke, according to the parish.
A large sycamore tree in the churchyard is often credited with shielding it from debris.
In the months after the attacks, St. Paul's became a relief center for rescue and recovery workers.
Volunteers served meals, provided cots, offered massages and counseling, and kept the doors open around the clock.
Firefighters and police slept in the pews.
Their boots scuffed the pews, and some of those marks were deliberately preserved.
Inside you will find a small exhibit about that period.
Behind the chapel, look for a bronze sculpture made from the root system of that sycamore tree, a reminder of how the old and the new are fused together in this neighborhood.

As you leave, consider the arc of this walk: from a Dutch trading post on the edge of the water, to the steamship lines and Standard Oil, to Morgan's bank and the Stock Exchange, to the towers that defined the modern skyline, and the memorial that stands in their place.
Lower Manhattan has been destroyed and rebuilt many times, by fire, by speculation, and by attack.
Each time, it has rebuilt itself in the same place, along the same crooked streets.

This walk covers a compact stretch of lower Manhattan where the city's government, its press, its poorest slums, and one of its most vibrant immigrant communities all grew up within a few blocks of each other.
In the colonial era, this area sat just north of the settled town.
The open land known as the Commons, now City Hall Park, was the town's pasture, gallows ground, and gathering place.
Just to the northeast was a deep, spring-fed lake called the Collect Pond, the main source of fresh water for the early city.
In the 1700s it was a picnic spot.
By the 1800s, tanneries, breweries, and slaughterhouses had turned it into an open sewer, and the city filled it in.
The fill was poorly done.
The ground settled, became damp and foul, and the people who could afford to leave did.
What grew on top of the old pond was Five Points, the most notorious slum in nineteenth century America.
Meanwhile, the area around City Hall became the hub of civic power, and Park Row, facing the park, became Newspaper Row.
In the late 1800s, the city's great papers, the Times, the Tribune, the Sun, Joseph Pulitzer's World, all had their headquarters here, competing to build the tallest tower.
Their reporters walked to City Hall, the courts, and the police headquarters, and they walked into Five Points to find the stories that sold papers.
The proximity of power and poverty in this neighborhood is the key to understanding it.
Just to the east, Chinatown took root in the late nineteenth century, on Mott, Pell, and Doyers Streets.
The community grew under severe pressure: the federal Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 barred most Chinese immigration for six decades.
For a long time, Chinatown was a small enclave of mostly men, organized around family associations, merchant guilds, and rival societies called tongs.
After immigration law changed in 1965, the neighborhood expanded dramatically, absorbing much of what had been Little Italy and parts of the Lower East Side.
Today it is one of the largest Chinese communities outside Asia.

On this walk you'll see City Hall, the Woolworth Building, the gateway to the Brooklyn Bridge, the African Burial Ground, the site of Five Points, and the twisting streets of old Chinatown, ending beneath the grand arch of the Manhattan Bridge.
You're in City Hall Park, the old Commons.
In the colonial era, this was the open field at the edge of town where people grazed cattle, drilled militia, protested, and hanged criminals.
On July ninth, 1776, George Washington's troops assembled near here to hear the Declaration of Independence read aloud.
The crowd then went down Broadway and tore down the king's statue at Bowling Green.
Look at City Hall itself, the elegant white building with the cupola.
It was completed in 1812, designed by Joseph François Mangin, a French émigré, and John McComb Junior.
It blends French Renaissance and American Federal styles, and it is still the working seat of city government, among the oldest city halls in the country still used for its original purpose.

A popular story says that the front and sides were clad in fine marble, but the back was faced in cheaper brownstone, because the city fathers couldn't imagine anyone important ever living north of it.
The story may be partly myth, but it captures how small New York still was in 1812.
In April 1865, Abraham Lincoln's body lay in state in the rotunda here, and tens of thousands of New Yorkers filed past.
Behind City Hall is the Tweed Courthouse.
It is a monument to corruption.
Construction began in 1861 under the control of William Magear Tweed, known as Boss Tweed, the leader of the Tammany Hall political machine.
The project took about twenty years, and its cost ballooned to many times the original budget, as contractors billed the city for absurd amounts.
One plasterer was paid a fortune for supposedly repairing the work he had just installed.
The scandal, exposed by the New York Times and by Thomas Nast's cartoons in Harper's Weekly, eventually sent Tweed to prison, where he died.
Now look east, across the park, toward Park Row.
That street was Newspaper Row.
The New York Times, the Tribune, the Sun, and the World all stood along here.
The competition between Joseph Pulitzer's World and William Randolph Hearst's Journal in the 1890s gave birth to the term yellow journalism.
Pulitzer's World Building had a gilded dome that, for a while, made it one of the tallest buildings in the city.
It was demolished in the 1950s to make way for Brooklyn Bridge ramps.
A statue of Benjamin Franklin, holding a copy of his Pennsylvania Gazette, stands in the small plaza called Printing House Square as a reminder of the area's past.
One surviving tower from that era is 41 Park Row, the old New York Times building from the 1880s, now part of Pace University.
And the tall, slender building with the two small cupolas, the Park Row Building at 15 Park Row, was the tallest office building in the world when it opened in 1899.
Look up at the white terracotta tower on Broadway across from City Hall Park.
This is the Woolworth Building, completed in 1913 and designed by Cass Gilbert, the same architect behind the Custom House at Bowling Green.
At about seven hundred ninety two feet, it was the tallest building in the world until 1930.
Its owner, Frank Winfield Woolworth, built his fortune on a simple idea: the five-and-dime store.
In 1879 he opened a store where everything cost five cents, and later ten cents.
Prices were fixed and clearly marked, goods were displayed openly so customers could handle them, and volume made up for thin margins.
By the time this building went up, F. W. Woolworth and Company had hundreds of stores.
Woolworth reportedly paid for the tower in cash, around thirteen and a half million dollars.
He liked to say it was built with nickels and dimes.
The Gothic detail was deliberate.
Gilbert wrapped a modern steel skeleton in the language of medieval cathedrals: pointed arches, gargoyles, pinnacles, and tracery.
At the opening ceremony, a clergyman called it the Cathedral of Commerce, and the nickname stuck.
On the night of April twenty fourth, 1913, President Woodrow Wilson pressed a button in Washington, and the building's eighty thousand light bulbs switched on at once.
If you can get a look at the lobby, which is sometimes accessible by guided tour, it's one of the most lavish in the world, with a vaulted ceiling covered in glass mosaics.
Hidden in the corners are small carved caricatures: one shows Frank Woolworth counting coins, another shows Cass Gilbert holding a model of the building, and another shows the building's banker.
Gothic cathedrals often included small portraits of their builders, and Gilbert was playing on that tradition.
The Woolworth company itself is a lesson in corporate evolution.
The five-and-dime stores faded in the late twentieth century, and the last American Woolworth stores closed in 1997.
But one of the company's side ventures, a chain of athletic shoe stores, thrived.
The corporation eventually renamed itself after it: Foot Locker.
The company sold this building in 1998.
Today, the upper floors have been turned into luxury apartments, including a penthouse in the pinnacle itself.
In front of you, straddling Chambers Street, is the Manhattan Municipal Building, now named for David N. Dinkins, the city's first Black mayor.

Completed in 1914 and designed by the firm McKim, Mead and White, it was one of the first skyscrapers built by the city for its own offices, created after the five boroughs were consolidated into Greater New York in 1898 and the city's bureaucracy exploded in size.
Notice that a street literally runs through the bottom of the building, under a grand vaulted arch, and that a subway station is built into its base.
This was a new idea: a skyscraper designed as part of the city's transit infrastructure.
At the very top stands a gilded copper statue called Civic Fame, holding a crown with five turrets, representing the five boroughs.
It is one of the largest statues in the city.
The building was influential.
Its tiered, wedding-cake silhouette is often said to have inspired the so-called Seven Sisters skyscrapers built in Moscow under Stalin, as well as other civic towers in the United States.
This is also where many New Yorkers come to get married.
The City Clerk's office, where civil ceremonies happen, has been in a nearby building on Worth Street since 2009, but for decades the weddings happened here.
To your right is the pedestrian entrance to the Brooklyn Bridge.
When it opened in 1883, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world, and the first to use steel wire for its cables.
It joined two separate cities, New York and Brooklyn, fifteen years before they merged.
We'll cover the bridge's story in detail on the Brooklyn Bridge and DUMBO tour, but if you have time, walking even halfway across is one of the essential New York experiences.
The best view of the Manhattan skyline, arguably, is from the bridge's first tower.
Look also for the Surrogate's Court building nearby, on Chambers Street, a Beaux-Arts building with sculptures representing the history of New York along its roofline.
Inside, its lobby is modeled on the grand Paris Opera house.
It holds the city's records of wills, adoptions, and estates.
You are standing at one of the most significant archaeological sites in the United States.
In 1991, the federal government began construction on a new office tower at 290 Broadway.
Historic maps had shown that a burial ground for Africans had existed in this area in the colonial period, but most people assumed it had been destroyed long ago by two centuries of building.
It hadn't.
Construction workers began finding human remains, and archaeologists ultimately uncovered the remains of about four hundred nineteen people, buried here roughly between the 1690s and 1794.
Scholars estimate the full burial ground, which covered several city blocks, may have held as many as fifteen thousand people.
To understand why this place exists, you need to know something that surprises many visitors: colonial New York was a slave city.
The Dutch West India Company brought enslaved Africans to New Amsterdam as early as the 1620s, and under English rule slavery expanded.
By the mid-1700s, enslaved people made up a significant share of the city's population, larger than in many Southern cities of the time.
They built roads, fortifications, docks, and the original wall that gave Wall Street its name.
Africans were barred from being buried in churchyards inside the city, so they buried their dead here, outside the settlement, beyond the Collect Pond.
Tensions ran high.
In 1712, a group of enslaved people set fire to a building and attacked whites who came to put it out.
In 1741, a series of fires led to hysteria over an alleged conspiracy, and dozens of people, mostly enslaved Africans, were executed, some burned at the stake.
New York State passed gradual emancipation laws starting in 1799, and slavery wasn't fully abolished in New York until 1827.

The excavated remains were studied by researchers at Howard University, revealing much about the lives of the people buried here: evidence of hard labor, malnutrition, and early death, but also burial customs that connected them to West and Central Africa.
Some coffins bore symbols, and one was decorated with a heart-shaped design that has been interpreted as an Akan symbol called Sankofa, meaning roughly to go back and retrieve what was lost.
The remains were reinterred here in 2003, and the site was designated a national monument in 2006.
The outdoor memorial, designed by the architect Rodney Leon, includes a spiral ramp, a map of the Atlantic world, and an ancestral chamber.
There's also a visitor center inside the federal building, free to the public.
You are now at Foley Square, surrounded by courthouses.
Look around: the hexagonal granite building with the massive Corinthian portico is the New York County Supreme Court, completed in 1927.
It's been the backdrop for countless film and television scenes, especially courtroom dramas.
Next to it, the tall tower with the gilded pyramid top is the Thurgood Marshall United States Courthouse, designed by Cass Gilbert and completed in 1936.
These are monuments to order and law.
The irony is where they stand.
Right around here, roughly to your northeast, was the Collect Pond, and once the pond was filled, a few blocks from here was Five Points, the most notorious slum in America.
The name came from the five corners created by the intersection of three streets, Anthony, Orange, and Cross.
Those streets have since been renamed or erased, but the intersection was roughly where Worth and Baxter Streets meet, near what is now Columbus Park, just a short walk east of here.
By the 1830s and 40s, Five Points was packed with the poorest immigrants in the city, mostly Irish refugees fleeing famine, along with free Black New Yorkers, Germans, and later Italians and Jews.
Crowding was extreme.
Tenements and rear buildings were stuffed into every lot.
Disease, especially cholera, swept through regularly.
The neighborhood also became a magnet for slumming tourists and moralizing reformers.
Charles Dickens visited in 1842 and described it in his book American Notes, with horror and fascination.
But Five Points wasn't only misery.
It was a place where cultures mixed in ways unthinkable elsewhere.
In dance halls like Almack's, Irish jigs and African American dance traditions collided.
The great Black dancer William Henry Lane, known as Master Juba, competed against Irish dancers here, and historians often trace the roots of tap dance to that cultural collision.

Five Points was also the territory of political gangs, groups with names like the Dead Rabbits, the Bowery Boys, and the Plug Uglies, whose rivalries were romanticized in Herbert Asbury's 1928 book The Gangs of New York.
A few blocks north, along Mulberry Street, was a stretch called Mulberry Bend, one of the worst blocks of all.

The photographer and reporter Jacob Riis documented it in his 1890 book How the Other Half Lives, among the first works of photojournalism to use flash photography to reveal the interiors of tenements.
Riis's images shocked middle class readers and helped push housing reform.
The city eventually demolished Mulberry Bend, and in its place created a park, now Columbus Park, which opened in the 1890s.
Today, Columbus Park is one of the most lively spaces in Chinatown, filled with people playing cards, mahjong, and Chinese chess, practicing tai chi, and making music.
You're now in the heart of old Chinatown, the triangle formed by Mott, Pell, and Doyers Streets.

Chinese immigrants began settling here in significant numbers in the 1870s and 1880s, many coming east after working on the railroads and in the mines of the American West, where violent anti-Chinese movements had made life dangerous.
Then, in 1882, Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act, the first major federal law to bar immigration by a specific national group.
It wasn't repealed until 1943.
Because of exclusion and related laws, the community remained small and overwhelmingly male for decades.
Most men worked in laundries, restaurants, and small shops, often sending money home to families in southern China, especially from the Guangdong province region around Taishan.
To navigate a hostile country, residents relied on family associations, district associations, and merchant organizations.
The most prominent umbrella group was the Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association, which acted almost like a local government.

There were also tongs, secret fraternal societies like the On Leong and Hip Sing, which could function as mutual aid societies but also controlled gambling and other rackets, and fought violent wars with each other in the early twentieth century.
Walk down Doyers Street, the short street with the sharp bend in it.
That curve gave it the nickname the Bloody Angle.
During the tong wars of the early 1900s, the curve made it a notorious ambush spot, because you couldn't see who was waiting around the corner.
Today it's quiet, lined with restaurants and barbershops.
One of them, Nom Wah Tea Parlor, has been serving dim sum and pastries on this street since 1920, making it one of the oldest restaurants in Chinatown.
On Mott Street, look for the Church of the Transfiguration, at the corner of Mott and Mosco Streets.
The building dates to 1801 and was originally built as an Episcopal church.
It later became a Catholic church that served, in succession, Irish immigrants, then Italians, then Chinese.
In that sense, this one building tells the whole immigrant history of the neighborhood.
After the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 eliminated national-origin quotas, Chinatown grew rapidly, with newcomers from Hong Kong, Taiwan, Guangdong, and later Fujian province.
The garment industry became the neighborhood's economic engine through the 1980s and 1990s, with hundreds of small factories employing tens of thousands of women.
That industry has largely faded, but the neighborhood's restaurants, groceries, and markets remain.

At Chatham Square, where many streets converge, look for the Kimlau Memorial Arch, honoring Chinese Americans who died in World War Two, and the statue of Lin Zexu, the Qing dynasty official famous for trying to stop the British opium trade in the 1830s.
End your walk at the corner of Canal Street and the Bowery, at the entrance to the Manhattan Bridge.
Canal Street really was a canal, or at least a drainage ditch.
Around 1805, the city dug a channel to drain the polluted Collect Pond westward to the Hudson River.
It quickly became a stinking, stagnant mess, and by the 1820s it was covered over and turned into a broad street.

Today, Canal Street is one of Manhattan's busiest and most chaotic commercial streets, long famous for its street vendors, jewelry shops, and, notoriously, counterfeit handbags and watches sold out of storefront back rooms.
The Bowery, the street running north from here, is one of the oldest roads in Manhattan, following the path of a Lenape trail.
Its name comes from the Dutch word bouwerij, meaning farm.
Peter Stuyvesant, the last Dutch director of New Amsterdam, had his farm along this road.
We'll talk more about the Bowery on the Lower East Side and East Village tours.
Now look at the monumental arch and the curving colonnades in front of you.
This is the Manhattan entrance to the Manhattan Bridge, which opened in 1909.
The arch and colonnade were designed by the firm Carrère and Hastings, which also designed the New York Public Library.
They were completed in 1915 as part of the City Beautiful movement, which held that grand public architecture could ennoble a city and its citizens.
The arch was modeled on the Porte Saint-Denis in Paris, and the curving colonnades were inspired by Bernini's colonnade at St. Peter's Square in Rome.
The sculptures on the arch, by Carl Augustus Heber, depict Native American and pioneer themes.
The point was to give working-class commuters crossing to Brooklyn a gateway as grand as anything in Europe.
The Manhattan Bridge itself was a technical milestone.
It was among the first suspension bridges designed using deflection theory, a mathematical method that allowed for a lighter, more flexible deck.
That theory later influenced bridges like the Golden Gate.
It also carries subway trains, which is why you may hear a rumble overhead.
If you have energy left, you can walk across the bridge's pedestrian path, which offers great views of the Brooklyn Bridge, and lands in DUMBO, where another tour in this app begins.
If you want to understand how America absorbed the great waves of immigration of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, there is no better place to walk than the Lower East Side.
For about a century, from the 1840s to the 1920s, these streets were among the most densely populated places on Earth.

At its peak, around 1900, parts of the Lower East Side packed in several hundred thousand people per square mile, a density that rivaled or exceeded the most crowded parts of Bombay or London at the time.
They lived in tenements, five and six story walk-up buildings built to squeeze as many families as possible onto a standard twenty five by one hundred foot city lot.
The first great wave was German.
By the 1850s, the area east of the Bowery and north of Division Street was known as Kleindeutschland, Little Germany.
It was one of the largest German speaking cities in the world, with its own beer halls, newspapers, theaters, and gymnastic clubs.
Over time, prosperous Germans moved uptown, to Yorkville and elsewhere, a migration accelerated by a terrible tragedy in 1904 that we'll talk about on the East Village tour.
Then came the Eastern European Jews.
Between about 1880 and 1924, around two and a half million Jews came to America, fleeing poverty and pogroms in the Russian Empire, Austria-Hungary, and Romania.
A large share of them came first to these streets.
They brought Yiddish, a garment industry built on small workshops, a passionate radical politics, and a culture of newspapers, theater, and debate.
At the same time, Italians, mostly from southern Italy and Sicily, settled just to the west, around Mulberry Street, in what became Little Italy.
This was where the garment industry was born, in crowded sweatshops in tenement apartments.
It was where the labor movement found some of its fiercest organizers.
It was also where urban reformers, horrified by conditions, pushed the laws that shaped how cities everywhere build housing, requiring windows, air shafts, toilets, and fire escapes.
After immigration restrictions in 1924, the neighborhood slowly emptied.
Puerto Rican families arrived after World War Two, giving the area east of Avenue A the name Loisaida, a Spanglish rendering of Lower East Side.
Chinatown expanded from the south.
And in the last few decades, the neighborhood has become a destination for bars, galleries, and restaurants, with new towers rising alongside the old tenements.

As you walk, look for the fire escapes zigzagging down the fronts of buildings, the decorative cornices at the tops of tenements, which landlords used to make cheap buildings look respectable, and the old Jewish delis and appetizing shops that have survived a century of change.
You're on Mulberry Street, the main artery of what remains of Little Italy.
In the late nineteenth century, Italian immigrants, overwhelmingly from the poor rural south, from Campania, Calabria, Basilicata, and Sicily, settled in the blocks around here.
Many came as young men intending to work for a few years and return home, and many did.
Others brought their families and stayed.
Streets in Little Italy were often organized by region and even by village.
Neapolitans clustered on one block, Sicilians on another, Genoese on a third, each with its own dialect, saints, and festivals.
The most famous of those festivals still happens right here.
The Feast of San Gennaro, honoring the patron saint of Naples, has been held every September since 1926.
For eleven days, Mulberry Street fills with sausage and pepper stands, zeppole, cannoli, games, and a procession carrying the saint's statue through the streets.
At its height in the early twentieth century, Little Italy stretched over dozens of blocks.
Today it's a few blocks of restaurants, mostly along Mulberry between Broome and Canal.
After World War Two, the children and grandchildren of the original immigrants moved to Brooklyn, Staten Island, Queens, and New Jersey.
Chinatown expanded north into the space.
Today, very few Italian Americans actually live here.
A few institutions remain.
On Grand Street, a short walk east, Ferrara Bakery has been selling Italian pastries since 1892, and claims to be among the first espresso bars in the country.

The Italian American Museum, at the corner of Mulberry and Grand, occupies the former Banca Stabile, a bank founded in the 1880s that served as a lifeline for immigrants: it held their savings, wrote letters home for those who couldn't write, sold steamship tickets, and wired money back to Italy.
Banks like this, informal and family run, were the backbone of immigrant financial life.
That history connects to a much bigger story.
In San Francisco, an Italian immigrant named Amadeo Giannini founded the Bank of Italy in 1904 to serve immigrants who were ignored by established banks.
It grew into the Bank of America.
The idea that ordinary working people deserved bank accounts and small loans was, in part, an immigrant innovation.
Little Italy is also tied to the history of organized crime, and the neighborhood is not shy about that legend.
The restaurant Umberto's Clam House, for example, became infamous in 1972 when the gangster Joey Gallo was shot dead while celebrating his birthday there.
It has since moved to a new location on Mulberry Street.
At the corner of Mott and Prince Streets, behind a high brick wall, is the Basilica of St. Patrick's Old Cathedral.
Before the famous St. Patrick's Cathedral on Fifth Avenue was built, this was the cathedral of the Catholic Archdiocese of New York.
It was completed in 1815, designed by Joseph François Mangin, one of the two architects of City Hall.
It was among the earliest Gothic Revival buildings in the country.
It was built at a time when Catholics were a small and distrusted minority in Protestant New York.
As Irish immigration surged in the 1830s and 40s, anti-Catholic feeling grew violent, and the nativist movement held marches and riots against immigrants.
According to tradition, the high brick wall around the churchyard, which you can still see, served as a fortification, and parishioners at times stood guard to protect the church from nativist mobs.
The church later became the spiritual home of the Italians of Little Italy as the neighborhood changed around it.
In 1866, it was badly damaged by fire and rebuilt.
When the new cathedral on Fifth Avenue opened in 1879, this one was demoted to a parish church.
In 2010, Pope Benedict the Sixteenth elevated it to the rank of a minor basilica.
Beneath the church are catacombs, rare in New York, where prominent early Catholic families are buried.

One notable figure who was once buried in the cemetery here is Pierre Toussaint, a formerly enslaved Haitian who became a wealthy hairdresser to New York's elite in the early nineteenth century, and used his fortune to support orphans, the poor, and the building of churches, including this one.
He is now a candidate for sainthood, and his remains were moved to the crypt of the Fifth Avenue cathedral, a remarkable honor.
The cathedral and its grounds have appeared in many films.
The baptism scene in The Godfather, in which Michael Corleone renounces Satan while his men carry out killings across the city, was filmed inside.
Walk around the outside of the wall along Mulberry and Mott Streets.
This little patch of graves and old trees is one of the most peaceful and atmospheric corners in downtown Manhattan.
You're on the Bowery, one of the oldest roads in New York.
Its path follows a Lenape trail, and the Dutch named it after the word bouwerij, meaning farm, because it led to the farms north of town, including Governor Peter Stuyvesant's.
In the early nineteenth century, the Bowery was a lively, working class entertainment strip, a rival to the more genteel Broadway.
It had theaters, beer gardens, oyster bars, and dime museums.
The Bowery Theatre, which opened in 1826, was famous for raucous crowds and melodramas.
The Bowery Boys, a working class gang and youth subculture, swaggered up and down the street in high hats and slicked hair, and became stock characters in plays and later movies.
In 1878, the Third Avenue elevated railway was built above the Bowery.
The El cast the street into permanent shadow and noise, and the neighborhood declined.

By the early twentieth century, the Bowery had become the most famous skid row in America, lined with flophouses, cheap lodging houses where men rented cages or cots by the night, along with missions and saloons.
The Bowery Mission, which opened in 1879 and still operates at 227 Bowery, is one of the oldest rescue missions in the country.
For much of the twentieth century, saying someone ended up on the Bowery meant they had hit bottom.
Look at the grand building with the classical columns and arched entrance at 130 Bowery, near Grand Street.
This was the Bowery Savings Bank, designed by McKim, Mead and White and completed in 1894.
It was a savings bank for working people, built in a monumental style meant to reassure depositors that their small savings were safe.
Today it's an event space.
Also notable is the building that looks like a stack of offset white boxes, at 235 Bowery.
That's the New Museum, a contemporary art museum designed by the Japanese firm SANAA and completed in 2007.
Its arrival marked the transformation of the Bowery from skid row to an art and luxury corridor.
The Bowery is also famous today for its restaurant supply district, a stretch of shops selling commercial kitchen equipment, from industrial mixers to stacks of plates.
If you're a serious home cook, it's worth a browse.
And farther north is where the punk club CBGB once stood, which you can visit on the East Village tour.
You're now on Orchard Street, standing near 97 Orchard Street, the building that houses the Lower East Side Tenement Museum.
The building was constructed in 1863 by a German immigrant named Lucas Glockner.
It's a typical tenement: five stories plus a basement, with four apartments per floor, each about three hundred twenty five square feet, divided into three small rooms.
Only one of those rooms had windows to the outside.
At first, there was no indoor plumbing at all: residents used outhouses in the backyard, and water came from a pump.
Over about seventy years, from 1863 to 1935, an estimated seven thousand people from more than twenty countries lived in this one building.
In 1935, rather than comply with new housing laws, the landlord evicted the residents and sealed the upper floors.
The apartments stayed closed for over fifty years.

In 1988, the historian Ruth Abram and her colleague Anita Jacobson found the building and discovered the sealed floors almost like a time capsule, with layers of wallpaper, linoleum, and objects left behind.

They founded the museum, which has restored individual apartments to tell the stories of specific families who actually lived there: a German Jewish dressmaker abandoned by her husband during the Panic of 1873, Italian Catholic immigrants, Sicilians, Eastern European Jews, Irish, and later families.
The building's history is also the history of housing law.
Reformers horrified by tenement conditions pushed a series of laws.
The Tenement House Act of 1879 required that every bedroom have a window, which led landlords to build the so-called dumbbell tenement, with narrow air shafts pinched into the middle of the building.
The shafts were dark, foul, and often filled with garbage.
Then the Tenement House Act of 1901 required much larger courtyards, indoor toilets for each apartment, and better fire safety.
That 1901 law is considered one of the founding pieces of American housing regulation.
Orchard Street itself was the center of a famous pushcart market.
By the early 1900s, hundreds of peddlers lined the streets selling everything from pickles and herring to hats, fabric, and pots.
In the mid-twentieth century, Orchard Street became known as a bargain shopping district, especially on Sundays, since many Jewish merchants closed on Saturdays for the Sabbath.
The museum offers guided tours of the apartments, and if you have the chance, they're one of the most moving and intimate history experiences in the city.

In front of you, on Eldridge Street, is a building that seems almost out of place among the tenements around it: a tall facade with a great rose window, horseshoe arches, and Moorish and Gothic details.
This is the Eldridge Street Synagogue, completed in 1887.
It was the first great synagogue built in America by Eastern European Jews.
Before this, most synagogues for the new immigrants were tiny congregations meeting in rented rooms or converted churches.
This building was a statement.
Its builders, mostly working class immigrants who had prospered a little, wanted to show that they had arrived and that Judaism had a permanent place in America.
On the High Holidays at the turn of the century, the sanctuary was reportedly packed with worshippers, with crowds spilling into the street.
The Moorish Revival style, with its horseshoe arches and geometric patterns, was popular for synagogues across Europe and America in the nineteenth century.
It evoked the era of Muslim Spain, sometimes remembered as a golden age for Jewish culture, and set synagogues apart from the Gothic style of Christian churches.
As the Jewish population moved away to Brooklyn, the Bronx, and the suburbs, the congregation shrank dramatically.
By the 1950s, the main sanctuary was closed off, and the remaining worshippers met in the smaller basement chapel.
Pigeons lived in the sanctuary, and the building deteriorated badly.
In the 1980s, preservationists launched a long effort to save it, and after a restoration of about twenty years, it reopened in 2007 as the Museum at Eldridge Street.
Look at the great round window on the facade.

The original window had been lost, and in 2010 it was replaced with a new stained glass window designed by the artist Kiki Smith with the architect Deborah Gans, featuring a field of stars on a blue background.
The synagogue now sits at the edge of Chinatown.

On the surrounding blocks you'll see Chinese signs, groceries, and businesses, mixed with traces of the old Jewish neighborhood: an old building cornerstone with Hebrew lettering, a former matzo bakery, a sign over a doorway.
It's a compact lesson in how New York neighborhoods layer one community atop another.
You're at Seward Park, at the corner of Essex Street and East Broadway.
Opened in 1903, it's often cited as the first permanent, municipally built public playground in the United States.
Reformers argued that children of the tenements had nowhere to play but the street, and that parks with organized play would make them healthier and keep them out of trouble.
On opening day, crowds of children reportedly swarmed the playground.
Now look at the tall building across the street at 175 East Broadway, with ornate carvings and the name FORWARD across the top.
This was the headquarters of the Jewish Daily Forward, known in Yiddish as the Forverts.
It was founded in 1897, and under its legendary editor, Abraham Cahan, it became the most widely read Yiddish newspaper in the world.
At its peak in the 1920s, it had a circulation of around a quarter million copies.
The Forward was socialist, pro-union, and passionately engaged in teaching immigrants how to become Americans.
It ran English lessons, advice on etiquette and hygiene, and serialized fiction by writers including Isaac Bashevis Singer, who later won the Nobel Prize.

Its most famous feature was the Bintel Brief, meaning a bundle of letters, an advice column where readers wrote in with their problems: husbands who had abandoned them, children who refused to keep kosher, dilemmas of love, work, and faith in a new country.
It's one of the great primary sources of immigrant life.
Look closely at the facade.
Above the entrance, there are relief portraits of socialist figures, including Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels.
Today the building has been converted into luxury condominiums, which says something about how far the neighborhood has traveled.
Nearby on East Broadway stood the Educational Alliance, a settlement house founded by established German Jews to help the newer Eastern European arrivals assimilate.
It offered classes, libraries, art lessons, and a gym.
Among the young people who passed through it were artists and performers who went on to shape American culture.
The garment unions also had deep roots here.
The International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union, founded in 1900, drew much of its strength from Jewish and Italian women working in shops on these streets.
In 1909, tens of thousands of shirtwaist makers went on strike in what became known as the Uprising of the Twenty Thousand.
Two years later, the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire, which you'll hear about on the Greenwich Village tour, killed one hundred forty six workers, many of them young women from this neighborhood.
You're now on East Houston Street, which, a New Yorker will tell you, is pronounced HOW-ston, not like the city in Texas.
It is named after William Houstoun, a Georgia delegate to the Continental Congress.
On the corner of Houston and Ludlow is Katz's Delicatessen, founded in 1888.
It's one of the last of the great Jewish delis that once filled these streets.
You take a ticket at the door, order from a counterman who slices your pastrami by hand, and the counterman will usually give you a sample while he works.
A tip, traditionally, earns you a thicker sandwich.
During World War Two, when the owners' sons were serving overseas, Katz's coined the slogan Send a salami to your boy in the army, and shipped salamis to soldiers.
And yes, the famous scene in the 1989 movie When Harry Met Sally was filmed here.
A sign hangs over the table where it happened.
A few doors west is Russ and Daughters, an appetizing shop, opened in 1914 by Joel Russ, a Polish immigrant who began by selling herring from a pushcart.

Note the distinction: in New York Jewish food culture, a delicatessen sells meat, and an appetizing store sells fish and dairy, things you eat with bagels, like smoked salmon, herring, whitefish, and cream cheese.
The separation comes from kosher dietary law, which prohibits mixing meat and dairy.
Russ and Daughters was also notable as one of the first businesses in the country to have Daughters in its name.
Joel Russ had no sons, and he made his daughters partners in the 1930s.
Also on Houston Street is Yonah Schimmel Knish Bakery, which has been baking knishes, dough pockets stuffed with potato, kasha, or other fillings, since 1910.
It looks like it hasn't changed much since then.
These three businesses are survivors.
In 1920, the Lower East Side had dozens of delis, appetizing stores, bakeries, and dairy restaurants.
Most closed as the Jewish population left.
The ones that remain survived by becoming destinations, drawing visitors from all over the world.
End your walk at Delancey and Essex Streets, near the Manhattan entrance of the Williamsburg Bridge.
Essex Market, now in a modern building at the Essex Crossing development, has its roots in a reform by Mayor Fiorello La Guardia.
In the 1930s, the streets of the Lower East Side were still clogged with thousands of pushcart vendors.
La Guardia, the son of an Italian father and a Jewish mother from Trieste, wanted to modernize the city and clear the streets.
He created a system of enclosed public markets, where vendors could rent stalls with refrigeration and running water.
The original Essex Market opened in 1940, across the street.
In 2019, it moved into the new building here.
Essex Crossing itself has an unusual history.

In 1967, the city demolished tenements on several blocks here for an urban renewal project, displacing hundreds of mostly Puerto Rican and Jewish families, with a promise that they could return to new housing.
But politics stalled the project, and for nearly fifty years the land sat empty, mostly as parking lots.
It was one of the largest undeveloped city-owned sites in Manhattan.
Construction finally began in the 2010s, with a mix of market rate and affordable housing, a park, offices, and the market.
Now look up at the Williamsburg Bridge, rising above Delancey Street.
When it opened in 1903, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world, surpassing the Brooklyn Bridge.
It was also the first major suspension bridge with towers made entirely of steel rather than stone.
Its builders went for strength over beauty, and critics at the time considered it ugly.
But the bridge transformed both sides of the river.
It gave the crowded Lower East Side an escape route.
Tens of thousands of Jewish families moved across it to the Williamsburg section of Brooklyn, so many that the bridge was sometimes nicknamed the Jews' highway.
Today, Williamsburg is home to a large Hasidic community, as well as the young, artsy population that made it famous in the 2000s.
You can walk across the bridge on its pedestrian path, and pick up the Williamsburg and Greenpoint tour on the other side.
Look back at Delancey Street as you go.
It was widened for the bridge approach, and it became a busy commercial strip of bargain stores.
The 1988 movie Crossing Delancey took its title from the idea that crossing this street, from the old neighborhood to the uptown world, was the defining journey for the children of immigrants.
It still is, in a way.
The story of the Lower East Side is the story of people arriving, working, saving, and eventually crossing over to somewhere else.
This walk covers three neighborhoods that share one big story: how industrial Manhattan became residential Manhattan.
For most of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the area west of Broadway and south of Houston Street was a working landscape.
Along the Hudson River were piers, freight rail yards, and warehouses.
Tribeca was the center of the city's wholesale food trade, with butter, eggs, cheese, and produce moving through enormous markets.
SoHo was a district of textile and dry goods warehouses and small factories, housed in some of the most beautiful commercial buildings ever built in America, with facades made of cast iron.
Hudson Square, just to the north and west, was the city's printing district, filled with presses that produced everything from magazines to phone books.
After World War Two, that economy faded.
Container shipping moved the port to New Jersey.
Manufacturing left the city.
Trucks replaced freight trains.
Buildings emptied out.

City planners in the 1950s and 60s viewed much of SoHo as a slum of decaying industrial buildings, and Robert Moses planned to run an elevated expressway right through it, along Broome Street, connecting the Holland Tunnel with the Manhattan and Williamsburg Bridges.
Artists saved it.
They had discovered that these empty factory floors, with high ceilings, big windows, and cheap rents, made ideal studios.
They moved in, often illegally, since the buildings weren't zoned for residential use.
Together with preservationists and activists like Jane Jacobs, they helped defeat the Lower Manhattan Expressway in the 1960s.
In 1971, the city legalized artists living in lofts, and in 1973, SoHo's cast iron buildings were protected as a historic district.
Galleries followed the artists.
Then boutiques followed the galleries.
Then the bankers, celebrities, and luxury brands followed the boutiques.
The artists who saved SoHo were mostly priced out of it, a cycle so familiar that urbanists sometimes call it the SoHo effect.
Tribeca went through a similar transformation a little later, and the name itself, short for Triangle Below Canal Street, was coined in the 1970s.
Hudson Square is in the middle of its own reinvention, as media and tech companies, including Google and Disney, have built major offices in its old industrial buildings.

As you walk, look for things that reveal the old industrial life: loading docks raised to the height of a truck bed, metal canopies over sidewalks where goods were unloaded, old painted signs on brick walls, and the glass-studded vault lights set into the sidewalks, which let daylight into basements below.
You're near the corner of West Houston Street and West Street, beside the long, massive building that stretches south along the river.
This is St. John's Terminal, and if you work at Google New York, you may know it well from the inside.
The name goes back to St. John's Park, which once existed a few blocks south of here.
In the early 1800s, Trinity Church built a grand chapel, St. John's Chapel, and laid out a private, fenced square around it, modeled on London's elegant residential squares.
It became one of the most fashionable addresses in the city.
But in 1867, Trinity sold the park to Commodore Cornelius Vanderbilt, who paved it over and built a giant freight terminal for his Hudson River Railroad.
The chapel was demolished in 1918.
The fashionable families had already fled uptown.
Trains used to run down the middle of the West Side streets, at street level.
Tenth Avenue, in Chelsea, was nicknamed Death Avenue because of the number of people killed by freight trains.
In the 1930s, the New York Central Railroad built the West Side Improvement Project, which lifted the trains onto an elevated viaduct.
That viaduct is what we now know as the High Line.
Its southern end was right here: freight trains rolled directly into the third floor of this building, which opened in 1934, so that goods could be unloaded straight into storage.
As trucking took over, the rail line was cut back.
The southern portion, including the connection to this building, was demolished in the early 1990s.
If you look at the building's north end, you may notice where the old rail tracks once entered.
In recent years, Google acquired and rebuilt the terminal as a major office, adding new floors above the old freight structure.
It's part of a broader reinvention of Hudson Square.
The neighborhood, much of which is still owned by Trinity Church's real estate arm, was the printing district for most of the twentieth century.
The big industrial buildings with heavy floors, built to hold the weight of printing presses, now hold offices for media and tech companies.
The Walt Disney Company has also built its New York headquarters a few blocks south.
As you head south, you'll pass the entrance to the Holland Tunnel, which opened in 1927 under the Hudson River to Jersey City.
It was the first mechanically ventilated underwater vehicle tunnel in the world.
Its chief engineer, Clifford Holland, died during construction, possibly from the stress and exhaustion of the job, and the tunnel was named after him.
Huge ventilation buildings on both sides of the river exchange the air inside the tunnel every ninety seconds.
At the corner of North Moore Street and Varick Street stands a small, ornate Beaux-Arts firehouse.
This is the home of Hook and Ladder Company 8, completed in 1903.
With its red doors, rusticated stone, and elaborate cornice, it shows how seriously the city took its civic architecture at the turn of the century.
Even a firehouse was meant to look like a small palace.
The building became internationally famous as the headquarters of the paranormal exterminators in the 1984 film Ghostbusters.
Fans still come here to take pictures, and the firefighters inside have embraced the connection; there's often a Ghostbusters sign displayed inside.
But this firehouse also has a quieter history.
The firefighters of Ladder 8 responded to the World Trade Center on September eleventh, 2001.
Fire stations throughout lower Manhattan lost members that day.
Tribeca itself, as a name, is a recent invention.
In the 1970s, artists began moving into the abandoned warehouses south of Canal Street, following the same path as in SoHo.
Real estate brokers and residents called the area the Triangle Below Canal, and shortened it to Tribeca.
Today it is one of the most expensive neighborhoods in the United States, home to celebrities and finance executives who live in converted warehouses with eighteen-foot ceilings.
After September eleventh, the neighborhood, just north of the World Trade Center, was deeply affected.
To help bring people back downtown, the actor Robert De Niro, the producer Jane Rosenthal, and the investor Craig Hatkoff founded the Tribeca Film Festival in 2002.
De Niro had long been invested in the neighborhood: his company, Tribeca Productions, was based in a former coffee warehouse nearby, in what's now called the Tribeca Film Center.
As you walk the streets around here, North Moore, Franklin, White, and Walker, notice the dense collection of handsome nineteenth century warehouses, many with their loading docks still intact.
These buildings once held dry goods, textiles, and groceries on their way to stores across the city and the country.
You're on Harrison Street, near Greenwich Street.
Look at the row of small brick houses with peaked roofs and dormer windows.
These are Federal-style townhouses, built in the late 1700s and early 1800s, when this was a residential neighborhood for merchants and artisans.

Several of them weren't originally here: in the 1970s, as urban renewal swept through the area, a few of these historic houses were moved from nearby Washington Street to save them from demolition and reassembled here.
That urban renewal was aimed at what was once the largest wholesale food market in the city: the Washington Market.
Founded in the early 1800s, it spread over many blocks along the Hudson waterfront.

By the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, it was the place where much of New York's fresh food, fruits, vegetables, meat, poultry, came into the city by boat and rail and was sold to grocers, restaurants, and pushcart peddlers.
The area was chaotic, crowded, and notoriously congested, with trucks jammed in the streets day and night.
In the 1950s and 60s, city planners decided the market was obsolete and should move to a modern facility.
The wholesale produce trade moved to Hunts Point in the Bronx in the 1960s, where it still operates as one of the largest food distribution centers in the world.
Most of the Washington Market area was demolished.
Part of it became the site of the original World Trade Center.
Part became Independence Plaza, the large apartment towers you see nearby, and part became Manhattan Community College.
Just to the south and east, the area around Duane Park, a small triangular park, was the city's butter and egg district.
Dairy wholesalers clustered around here, and the old warehouses still bear names of food businesses on their facades.
Duane Park itself has a curious origin: the city bought the land from Trinity Church in 1797 for the price of five dollars.
It was originally part of a farm owned by a Dutch woman named Annetje Jans in the 1600s.

One survivor of the food trade was the Bazzini nut company, which roasted and sold nuts in Tribeca from the late 1800s until the 2000s, when it, too, moved out to the Bronx, and its building became apartments.
Today, the only market in Washington Market Park is the playground.
But walk around and you'll see the old names, still carved into stone.

At the corner of Thomas Street and Church Street, look up at the strangest building in Tribeca: a massive, windowless tower of concrete and granite, with no windows at all, just a few vents near the top.
This is 33 Thomas Street, completed in 1974 for AT&T, and originally known as the Long Lines Building.
It was designed to house telephone switching equipment, not people.
Its architects designed it to withstand a nuclear blast and to be self-sufficient for up to two weeks in a disaster, with its own fuel and water supplies.
Its floors are unusually tall, to accommodate large equipment.

In 2016, an investigation by The Intercept and a documentary drew on leaked documents to report that the building was likely a site where the National Security Agency monitored international communications.
Whatever happens inside, it remains one of the city's great architectural enigmas, a building designed for machines.
A short walk away, at 60 Hudson Street, stands another telecom landmark: the Western Union Building, completed in 1930.
Look at its brickwork.
The bricks shift gradually in color from dark at the bottom to light at the top, in a subtle gradient, an Art Deco flourish.
