Western Union was the telegraph monopoly of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the company that wired news, stock prices, and money across the country.
This building was its headquarters and its nerve center.
Today 60 Hudson is one of the most important internet hubs in the world, a so-called carrier hotel.
Dozens of telecommunications companies and data networks connect their equipment inside, because the building sits at the junction of major fiber optic routes.
The same reasons that made it valuable for telegraph lines a century ago, being a central point where cables converge, make it valuable for internet traffic today.
When you send data from New York to London, there's a decent chance it passes through this building.
There's a nice continuity here.
Western Union's telegraph, AT&T's telephones, and today's fiber optic networks have all occupied the same few blocks of Tribeca.
The infrastructure of communication is sticky: once the cables are in the ground, the buildings keep their importance, even when the technology inside changes completely.
Welcome to SoHo, and to Greene Street, one of the most beautiful streets in New York.
Look at the facades on both sides: rows of columns, arches, and ornate details, stacked five or six stories high.
Most of this is not stone.
It's cast iron.
Here's a test: if you carry a small magnet, put it against one of the columns.
It'll stick.
Cast iron architecture flourished in New York from the 1850s to the 1880s.
It was an early form of mass production in building.
Foundries cast facade pieces, columns, capitals, window frames, cornices, from molds, and those parts could be ordered from a catalog, shipped to the site, and bolted together.
This allowed builders to imitate the look of expensive carved stone palaces, Venetian, French, or Italian Renaissance, at a fraction of the cost.
It also allowed for large windows, since the iron was strong enough to carry loads with thin supports.
In an era before electric light, big windows meant more daylight for workers.

Two names to know are James Bogardus, an inventor who promoted cast iron construction in the 1840s and 50s, and Daniel Badger, whose Architectural Iron Works produced facades for buildings across the country.
The buildings were usually painted to look like stone, often in cream, gray, or white.

Look for 28 to 30 Greene Street, a grand building with a mansard roof, known as the Queen of Greene Street, and farther north, 72 to 76 Greene Street, known as the King of Greene Street, with its tall columns and projecting central bay.
These buildings mostly housed textile and dry goods businesses: wholesalers of fabric, clothing, and household goods.
Ground floors held showrooms.
Upper floors held stock or light manufacturing.
Despite the iron, fires were common, since the contents were flammable and the iron could buckle under heat.
Firefighters called the district Hell's Hundred Acres.
By the 1960s, the buildings were nearly empty.
That's when artists came.
They found the open loft floors perfect for large canvases and sculpture.
Look for small signs reading A.I.R. near the doorways of some buildings, short for Artist in Residence.
They told firefighters that people, not just goods, lived in the building, which was important in buildings never designed for residential use.
At the corner of Broadway and Broome Street stands one of the most important commercial buildings in American history: the Haughwout Building, completed in 1857.
Look at the facade.
It's a cast iron recreation of a Venetian palace, inspired by the Sansovino Library in Venice, with rows of arched windows framed by columns, repeated over five stories.
The rhythm is hypnotic, and it's one of the purest expressions of the cast iron style.
The building was built for E. V. Haughwout and Company, a retailer of fine china, glassware, silver, and chandeliers.
It was a luxury store, comparable to Tiffany and Company, which was located nearby on Broadway at the time.
Haughwout's customers reportedly included the White House: the company is said to have supplied china for Mary Todd Lincoln.
But the building's real claim to fame is inside.
In 1857, it became the first commercial building in the world to install a passenger elevator, built by Elisha Graves Otis.
A few years earlier, at the 1854 Crystal Palace exhibition in New York, Otis had staged a dramatic demonstration.
He rode a platform high into the air and then had the rope holding it cut.
Instead of plunging, the platform stopped, held by his safety brake, a spring-loaded mechanism that locked into the guide rails if the cable failed.
All safe, gentlemen, he reportedly announced.
The problem with early elevators wasn't lifting; it was falling.
Otis solved the problem of trust.

Without the safety elevator, the skyscraper would have been impossible, because no one would rent an office on the twentieth floor if they had to climb twenty flights of stairs, or if they feared riding up a rope.
The Haughwout elevator, powered by a steam engine in the basement, was the first step toward the vertical city.
The company Otis founded, the Otis Elevator Company, became the largest elevator maker in the world, and still is one of the leaders.
You've probably ridden in one of its elevators today.
Look for the name on the inspection plate the next time you step into an elevator in an office building.
Broadway itself, through SoHo, was once a premier shopping street of the city, before the retail center migrated north to Ladies' Mile and later to Fifth Avenue.
In a way, the boutiques here now have returned the street to what it was in the 1850s.

On Broadway, just north of Prince Street, look for the building at 561 Broadway with an unusual facade: a delicate lattice of green-painted iron, terracotta, and huge sheets of glass, with ornamental balconies.
This is the Little Singer Building, completed in 1904 and designed by Ernest Flagg.
It was built for the Singer Manufacturing Company, the maker of the famous sewing machine.
Singer is one of the great stories in American business history.
Isaac Merritt Singer, a colorful inventor and actor with a complicated personal life, patented improvements to the sewing machine in the 1850s.

But his business partner, Edward Clark, a lawyer, came up with the innovations that made the company a giant: installment payments, which allowed families to buy an expensive machine a little at a time, and a direct sales force.
Singer became one of the first truly multinational American companies, with factories and salesmen around the world.
It also helped transform the garment industry, making mass production of clothing possible, including in the sweatshops of the Lower East Side.
Flagg's design here was strikingly modern: the facade is mostly glass, with a thin metal framework, anticipating the glass curtain walls of twentieth century skyscrapers.
A few years later, Flagg designed the much taller Singer Tower downtown, which in 1908 was briefly the tallest building in the world.
Tragically, that tower was demolished in 1968, among the tallest buildings ever deliberately demolished at the time.
Look around you now at SoHo's streets: Prince, Spring, Mercer, Wooster, West Broadway.
In the 1970s and 80s, this was the center of the art world.

The dealer Leo Castelli, who championed artists like Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg, Roy Lichtenstein, and Andy Warhol, opened a gallery at 420 West Broadway in 1971, and dozens of galleries followed.
Artists like Donald Judd bought entire buildings here.
Judd's home and studio, at 101 Spring Street, a cast iron building he bought in 1968, is preserved as a museum.
In 1977, a gourmet food store called Dean and DeLuca opened on Prince Street, introducing many Americans to imported cheeses, olive oils, and specialty foods.
The store became an emblem of the neighborhood's transformation.
By the 1990s and 2000s, most of the galleries had moved to Chelsea, driven out by rising rents, and SoHo became a high end shopping district.
Apple opened its first New York store in a former post office on Prince Street in 2002.
Before you leave, look up at the cornices, columns, and window frames above the shop signs.
The ground floors have changed many times, but the iron facades above have watched over all of it: textile merchants, firefighters, artists, collectors, and shoppers.
Greenwich Village has been, for more than a century, the place where America's rebels, bohemians, and dissenters came to live.
Before that, it was literally a village.
In the eighteenth century, Greenwich was a separate rural hamlet, a couple of miles north of the city, with country estates and farms.
Its growth was driven by fear.
In the early 1800s, yellow fever and cholera epidemics repeatedly swept through crowded lower Manhattan, and residents fled north to the healthier air of Greenwich.
During the epidemic of 1822, banks and businesses relocated here temporarily; Bank Street is said to take its name from banks that set up offices there.
Many people who came during the epidemics stayed.
Because the Village developed before the 1811 street grid, its streets follow old property lines, country lanes, and a buried stream called Minetta Brook.
That's why the West Village is a maze of angled streets, and why, famously, West 4th Street crosses West 10th, 11th, and 12th Streets, something that should be geometrically impossible on a grid.
The maze kept out through traffic and kept rents low, and that, in turn, attracted artists.
By the early twentieth century, the Village was America's bohemia.
Writers, painters, radicals, feminists, and free-love advocates crowded its cheap rooming houses and cafés.
Eugene O'Neill's early plays were staged here.
The radical magazine The Masses was published here.
In the 1950s, the Beat poets gathered in its coffeehouses, and in the 1960s, the folk revival was born on MacDougal Street, launching Bob Dylan and many others.
The Village was also home to one of the earliest and most visible gay communities in America, and in 1969, it became the birthplace of the modern gay rights movement at the Stonewall Inn.

The Village is also where the modern historic preservation movement and modern urbanism found one of their greatest voices: Jane Jacobs, who lived on Hudson Street and who defeated Robert Moses's plans to remake the neighborhood.
Today, the Village is one of the most expensive places to live in the country, and the bohemians largely can't afford it.
But its street life, its historic buildings, and its sense of being a small town inside a big city have been carefully preserved, in large part thanks to the fights you'll hear about on this walk.
You're in Washington Square Park, the heart of Greenwich Village.
This land has a grim past.
From 1797 to 1825, it served as a potter's field, a burial ground for the poor, the unknown, and victims of yellow fever.
Archaeologists estimate that thousands of people may still be buried beneath the park, and bones are occasionally unearthed during construction work.
Public executions were also held in the area, and a large old English elm in the northwest corner is called the Hangman's Elm, though historians doubt anyone was actually hanged from it.
In 1826, the city converted the field into a parade ground and later a public park, and wealthy families built elegant homes around it.
Look at the north side of the park, along Washington Square North.
The row of red brick Greek Revival townhouses, built in the 1830s, is known as The Row.
This was old money New York.
The novelist Henry James was born nearby, and his 1880 novel Washington Square captured the world of these houses.
Now look at the marble arch at the foot of Fifth Avenue.
In 1889, for the centennial of George Washington's inauguration, a temporary wooden arch was built here.
It was so popular that the city commissioned a permanent version, designed by Stanford White, of the firm McKim, Mead and White, and completed in 1892.
It's modeled on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.
Two statues of Washington, as general and as president, were added to the north face in the following decades.

In 1917, a group of artists, including Marcel Duchamp, climbed to the top of the arch through an internal stairway and declared the Free and Independent Republic of Washington Square, a classic Village prank.
The park was also the site of a major battle over the future of cities.
For years, Fifth Avenue traffic ran right through the park, under the arch.
In the 1950s, Robert Moses proposed extending Fifth Avenue as a sunken highway through the center of the park.
Local mothers, led by Shirley Hayes and joined by Jane Jacobs, organized a campaign against it.
Not only did they win, but by the early 1960s, traffic was banned from the park entirely.
It was one of the first major defeats of Moses's highway plans.
The park has long been a stage for music and protest.
In 1961, when the city tried to ban folk singing in the park, hundreds of musicians and fans gathered in defiance, a confrontation sometimes called the Beatnik Riot.
The city backed down.
Today, the fountain area is still filled with musicians, performers, chess players, and students from New York University, which surrounds the park and owns many of the buildings around it.
At the corner of Washington Place and Greene Street, look at the ten-story building, now owned by New York University and known as the Brown Building.
On the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors of this building was the Triangle Waist Company, a factory that made women's blouses, called shirtwaists.
On the afternoon of Saturday, March twenty-fifth, 1911, near closing time, a fire broke out on the eighth floor, probably from a discarded cigarette or match in a bin of fabric scraps.
The fire spread with terrifying speed through piles of cotton and tissue paper.
Workers on the eighth floor escaped.
Workers on the tenth floor, including the owners, escaped to the roof.
But on the ninth floor, the workers were trapped.
One exit door was locked, reportedly to prevent theft and unauthorized breaks.
The single flimsy fire escape collapsed under the weight of people trying to flee.
The fire department's ladders only reached the sixth or seventh floor.
Crowds on the street watched as workers, many of them young Jewish and Italian immigrant women, some in their teens, jumped from the windows to escape the flames.
In less than half an hour, one hundred forty six people died.
The owners, Max Blanck and Isaac Harris, were tried for manslaughter and acquitted.
But the fire galvanized the city.
Huge crowds marched in a funeral procession through the streets.

The state created a Factory Investigating Commission, led by state legislators Robert Wagner and Al Smith, which pushed through dozens of new laws on fire safety, sprinklers, working hours, and factory conditions.
One eyewitness was a young social reformer named Frances Perkins, who happened to be having tea nearby and ran to the scene.
She later said the New Deal began on that day.

Perkins went on to become Franklin Roosevelt's Secretary of Labor, the first woman to serve in a presidential cabinet, and was a driving force behind Social Security, the minimum wage, and limits on working hours.
Look at the building's corner.
You may see a series of small plaques, and on the anniversary each year, people gather here and chalk the names of the victims on the sidewalk.
A permanent memorial was installed on the building in 2023, with ribbons of steel bearing the victims' names.
You're on MacDougal Street, just south of Washington Square, the center of Village bohemia for over a century.
In 1916, a group of writers and artists moved their small theater company from Cape Cod to MacDougal Street and became the Provincetown Players.
Their most important discovery was a young playwright named Eugene O'Neill, whose early plays were first performed here.
The Provincetown Playhouse building still stands on MacDougal, south of the park, though it's been rebuilt by NYU.

On the corner of MacDougal and Minetta Lane, look for Minetta Tavern, which opened in 1937 and was a hangout for writers like Ernest Hemingway, E. E. Cummings, and Ezra Pound, at least according to legend.
Nearby, Caffe Reggio, open since 1927, claims to have introduced the cappuccino to America, and its antique espresso machine is on display.
Minetta Lane follows the curve of the buried Minetta Brook, which still flows underground.
In the 1950s and 60s, the coffeehouses of MacDougal and Bleecker Streets became the stage for the folk revival.
Places like the Gaslight Cafe, the Café Wha?, and, a few blocks away on West Fourth Street, Gerde's Folk City, hosted open mic nights where young musicians performed for tips, often passing a basket.
A nineteen-year-old from Minnesota named Bob Dylan arrived in the winter of 1961 and began playing at Café Wha?.
Within a year, after a glowing review in the New York Times of a show at Gerde's, he had a record contract.
Others who played these clubs included Joan Baez, Dave Van Ronk, Phil Ochs, Peter, Paul and Mary, and Simon and Garfunkel.
The Café Wha? also gave an early stage to a guitarist then calling himself Jimmy James, who soon became known as Jimi Hendrix.
The Beat writers were here too, in the 1950s.
Jack Kerouac, Allen Ginsberg, and Gregory Corso read poetry at coffeehouses and drank at bars like the San Remo, which stood at the corner of MacDougal and Bleecker.
Comedy has its own history on these blocks.

Comedians like Woody Allen, Bill Cosby, and Richard Pryor performed in Village clubs in the 1960s, and the Comedy Cellar, on MacDougal, opened in 1982 and is still among the most famous comedy clubs in the country.
Big name comedians often drop in unannounced late at night.
At the corner of Sixth Avenue and West 10th Street, look up at the fairy tale building with a tall clock tower, pointed arches, and colorful bands of brick and stone.
This is the Jefferson Market Library, a branch of the New York Public Library.
But it wasn't built as a library.
Completed in 1877, it was a courthouse, the Third Judicial District Courthouse, designed by Frederick Clarke Withers and Calvert Vaux, who also co-designed Central Park.
Its style is Victorian Gothic, inspired by the writings of the English critic John Ruskin, who championed colorful, richly decorated medieval architecture.
In an 1880s poll of architects, it was voted one of the most beautiful buildings in America.
The tower housed a fire lookout and bell.
The court handled the petty crimes of the neighborhood: drunkenness, prostitution, and street disputes.
After the courts moved out in the 1940s, the building sat empty and was slated for demolition.
In the late 1950s and early 60s, neighborhood residents, including the poet E. E. Cummings, campaigned to save it, and it was converted into a library, opening in 1967.
It was one of the early victories of the preservation movement in New York.
Next door, where the lovely Jefferson Market Garden is now, stood the Women's House of Detention, a massive Art Deco jail that operated from 1932 to 1974.
Inmates would shout down to friends and family on the sidewalk, and passersby would shout back.
Among the women held there were the political activist Angela Davis and the writer Dorothy Day.
It was demolished in 1974, and the community turned the site into a garden.
Across Sixth Avenue, on West 10th Street, look for a small iron gate leading to a little dead-end street of brick houses.
That's Patchin Place, built in the 1840s.
Its tiny houses became home to an astonishing number of writers.
E. E. Cummings lived at number four for about forty years.
The novelist Djuna Barnes lived at number five for decades.
The journalist John Reed, who wrote Ten Days That Shook the World about the Russian Revolution, also lived here.
Around the corner is a similar alley called Milligan Place.
Notice also the old gas lamp at the end of Patchin Place, one of the last gas street lamps in the city, now converted to electricity.
You're on Christopher Street, at Christopher Park, a small triangle of green.
Across the street is the Stonewall Inn.
In the 1960s, gay life in New York was largely hidden and heavily policed.

It was illegal for bars to serve alcohol to people believed to be gay, and police regularly raided gay bars, arresting patrons, especially those who wore clothing that didn't match their perceived gender.
Because legitimate businesses avoided serving gay customers, many gay bars were run by the Mafia, which paid off the police.

The Stonewall Inn was one of them: a dingy, unlicensed bar with watered-down drinks, but one of the few places where gay men, lesbians, drag queens, and transgender people, many of them young and poor, could dance together.
In the early morning hours of June twenty-eighth, 1969, police raided the Stonewall.
This time, the patrons didn't scatter.
A crowd gathered outside and began to resist, throwing coins, bottles, and bricks.
The police barricaded themselves inside the bar.
The confrontations continued for several nights, with crowds of hundreds and then thousands.

Among those involved, according to many accounts, were activists including Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera, who became prominent figures in the movement that followed, though the details of who did what on which night are still debated.
The uprising didn't begin the gay rights movement, which had existed in quieter forms for years, but it transformed it into a more militant, visible, mass movement.
Within months, new organizations formed.
On the first anniversary, in June 1970, activists organized the Christopher Street Liberation Day march, from here to Central Park.
That march is considered the first gay pride parade, and pride marches held every June around the world commemorate Stonewall.
In 2016, President Barack Obama designated the Stonewall National Monument, the first national monument dedicated to LGBTQ history.
It includes Christopher Park and the surrounding streets.
In the park, look for the white statues by the sculptor George Segal, called Gay Liberation: two standing men and two seated women, cast in bronze and painted white.
They were commissioned in 1979 and installed here in 1992 after years of controversy.
Christopher Street itself is one of the Village's oldest streets, named for Charles Christopher Amos, an heir to an eighteenth-century estate.
Walk west along it toward the Hudson, and you'll see the shops and bars that made it the main street of gay New York for decades.
You're now in the quiet, winding heart of the West Village, around Bedford and Commerce Streets.
At 86 Bedford Street, look for a door with no sign.
This is Chumley's, a former speakeasy.
Opened by Leland Stanford Chumley in 1922, during Prohibition, it had hidden entrances, trapdoors, and escape routes so patrons could vanish if the police arrived.

The bar became a literary hangout: writers including John Steinbeck, William Faulkner, Willa Cather, and John Dos Passos are said to have drunk here, and the walls were lined with book jackets of authors who'd been regulars.
Chumley's is also connected to a well-known piece of slang.
To eighty-six something means to get rid of it, or to throw someone out.
One popular story claims it comes from this address: when the police were coming, the bartender would shout eighty-six it, telling customers to leave through the Bedford Street door.
Etymologists are skeptical, and there are many competing explanations, but it's a good story.
Down the street, at 75 and a half Bedford Street, is a building you might walk right past: a red brick house only about nine and a half feet wide, among the narrowest houses in New York.
It was built in 1873 in what had been a carriage alleyway between two houses.
The poet Edna St. Vincent Millay, who won the Pulitzer Prize in 1923, lived here in the 1920s.
The actor John Barrymore and, according to some accounts, the cartoonist William Steig and the anthropologist Margaret Mead also lived here at various times.
Around the corner, at 38 Commerce Street, the Cherry Lane Theatre, founded in 1924 in a former brewery and box factory, is among the oldest continuously operating Off-Broadway theaters in New York.
It has premiered works by playwrights including Samuel Beckett, Edward Albee, and Sam Shepard.
Look around at the old houses, the angled streets, and the trees.
This part of the Village feels like it was built for walking, and it was.
The street pattern predates the city grid, and it's the reason this neighborhood has stayed so intimate.
Walk toward the Hudson, to the block bounded by West, Bethune, Washington, and Bank Streets, and you'll find a massive complex of connected industrial buildings.
Today it's called Westbeth, the largest artists' housing complex in the world.
But for most of the twentieth century, this was the headquarters of the most important industrial research laboratory in history: Bell Telephone Laboratories.
The buildings were originally built for Western Electric, the manufacturing arm of AT&T.
Beginning in 1925, when Bell Labs was formally established as AT&T and Western Electric's research division, this complex served as its headquarters.
Engineers and scientists here worked on just about everything related to communications, and a remarkable list of breakthroughs came out of this site.
In 1927, AT&T engineers demonstrated long-distance television transmission, sending live images of Herbert Hoover, then Commerce Secretary, from Washington to an audience in New York.
Bell Labs and Western Electric developed sound systems for motion pictures, and the technology helped launch the talkies, including the 1927 film The Jazz Singer.
Engineers here developed high-fidelity sound recording and improved vacuum tubes.

In 1937, a Bell Labs mathematician, George Stibitz, built an early binary adding circuit on his kitchen table, a precursor to digital computing; his later relay computers were built in this era of Bell Labs.
And during World War Two, the labs worked on radar and other military technology.
Look closely at the building on the West Street side.
An elevated freight railway, what is now the High Line, used to run right through the building.
Trains passed through a tunnel in the building's structure.

After World War Two, Bell Labs moved most of its operations to a campus in Murray Hill, New Jersey, where scientists would invent the transistor in 1947, a device that made modern electronics possible.
Later came the laser, the solar cell, the UNIX operating system, and the C programming language, along with work that earned several Nobel Prizes.
If you work in tech, this is your ancestral home.
In 1970, the buildings were converted into Westbeth, subsidized housing and studios for artists, with support from the J. M. Kaplan Fund and the National Endowment for the Arts.
The architect Richard Meier, then early in his career, designed the conversion.
Generations of painters, dancers, musicians, and writers have lived here.
The choreographer Merce Cunningham's dance company had its studio on the top floor for decades.
It's a very Village kind of story: a building where engineers once invented the future of communication, now filled with people imagining the future of art.
Walk east to Hudson Street, near West 11th Street.
At 555 Hudson Street, look for a modest three-story building.
In the 1950s and 60s, this was the home of Jane Jacobs, the writer and activist whose 1961 book, The Death and Life of Great American Cities, changed how the world thinks about cities.
Jacobs wasn't an architect or a planner.
She was a journalist with an extraordinary eye.
Sitting at her window and walking her neighborhood, she observed how city streets actually worked.
She described what she called the sidewalk ballet of Hudson Street: shopkeepers opening their stores, children walking to school, workers on lunch break, bar patrons late at night.
She argued that busy streets with mixed uses, short blocks, old buildings, and density created what she called eyes on the street, a natural, informal safety and vitality.
This directly contradicted the planning orthodoxy of the time, which favored tearing down old neighborhoods, separating uses, and building towers in parks surrounded by highways.
Jacobs also put her ideas into action.

She helped lead the fights against Robert Moses's projects: the road through Washington Square Park, the designation of the West Village for urban renewal, and the Lower Manhattan Expressway through SoHo.
She won all three.
She later moved to Toronto, where she lived until her death in 2006.
Her ideas are now the foundation of modern urbanism, and if you've ever heard a planner talk about walkability or mixed-use neighborhoods, you're hearing Jane Jacobs.
A few steps away, at the corner of Hudson and West 11th Street, is the White Horse Tavern, which dates to 1880.
In the 1950s, it became a haunt of writers.
The Welsh poet Dylan Thomas was a regular, and according to legend, in November 1953, after drinking at the White Horse, he returned to the Chelsea Hotel and fell ill.
He died a few days later.
The extent to which drinking at the White Horse was responsible is debated, but the bar has embraced the legend.
Jack Kerouac, James Baldwin, Norman Mailer, and Bob Dylan were also among its patrons.
Stand here for a moment and watch the street.
People walking dogs, neighbors chatting at the corner, delivery workers, people sitting at sidewalk tables.
That's the sidewalk ballet Jane Jacobs described, still going on more than sixty years later, on the same street, in the neighborhood she fought to save.
The far west side of lower Manhattan, from the Meatpacking District up through Chelsea to Hudson Yards, was for most of its history the city's back of house.
This was where the goods came in.
Along the Hudson River, a continuous wall of piers handled ocean liners and freighters.
Behind them ran the freight railroad tracks of the New York Central, which carried meat, milk, produce, and manufactured goods into the city.

At first, the trains ran at street level down Tenth and Eleventh Avenues, so dangerous to pedestrians that Tenth Avenue was nicknamed Death Avenue, and the railroad employed men on horseback called West Side Cowboys to ride ahead of the trains waving red flags.
In the 1930s the tracks were lifted onto an elevated viaduct that ran directly into the warehouses and factories.
Today that viaduct is the High Line.
The warehouses and factories along the line included some of the great names in American industry.
The National Biscuit Company, Nabisco, baked crackers and cookies here, including the first Oreo.
Massive freight terminals were built so trucks and trains could deliver directly to upper floors.
In the Meatpacking District, hundreds of slaughterhouses and packing plants processed meat for the city.
Inland, Chelsea itself has a gentler history.
The name comes from an estate owned in the 1700s by Captain Thomas Clarke, who named it after the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London.
His grandson, Clement Clarke Moore, developed the estate into a neighborhood of elegant rowhouses in the 1830s and 40s.
In the late nineteenth century, West 23rd Street was the center of the American theater, and later an early center of the film industry.
After World War Two, shipping moved to container ports in New Jersey, trucks replaced trains, and industry left Manhattan.
The piers rotted.
The High Line was abandoned.
The Meatpacking District became a mix of the remaining meat businesses and late night clubs.
Then, starting in the 1990s, art galleries began moving to West Chelsea from SoHo, followed by restaurants, boutiques, and luxury condos.
The High Line reopened as a park in 2009 and became one of the most influential urban design projects of the century, copied in cities around the world.
And at the north end, Hudson Yards rose on a platform built over an active rail yard.
This is also, as it happens, one of the main centers of the tech industry in New York.
Google has a cluster of buildings here, and much of the neighborhood's transformation has been driven by companies that wanted big, open, industrial floors for their offices.
As you walk, you'll see how buildings designed for freight trains and meat hooks became homes for software engineers.
You're on the cobblestone streets of the Meatpacking District, near Gansevoort Street and Washington Street.
Look up at the metal canopies sticking out over the sidewalks from many of the buildings.
These were built to shelter meat as it was unloaded and hung on hooks.
If you look closely, you might still spot the steel rails and hooks that carried carcasses into the buildings.
The district's name comes from its role as a center of meat processing.
By 1900, there were reportedly around two hundred fifty slaughterhouses and packing plants in the area, serving the hotels, restaurants, and butcher shops of the city.
Animals arrived by train and boat, and meat went out by truck and cart.
The area's oldest name is Gansevoort, after Fort Gansevoort, a small fort that stood near the river in the early nineteenth century.
The fort was named after Peter Gansevoort, a Revolutionary War hero.
His grandson was the novelist Herman Melville, who, after his literary career faded and Moby-Dick failed to find an audience, took a job as a customs inspector on the New York docks.
For nearly twenty years, the man who wrote one of the greatest American novels inspected cargo on the waterfront, including at a pier on Gansevoort Street, the street named for his own grandfather.
Gansevoort Market, an earlier market building, was a major wholesale center.
In the mid-twentieth century, the meat trade began to decline, as refrigerated trucks and national meatpacking companies made the old local system obsolete.
By the 1980s, the neighborhood was gritty and partly abandoned at night, known for underground gay clubs, sex clubs, and late night street activity.
Then the neighborhood flipped.
In 1999, the French bistro Pastis opened here, and it became a celebrity hangout.
Shows like Sex and the City featured the neighborhood.
Fashion designers and boutiques arrived, including Diane von Furstenberg and Stella McCartney.
Hotels and restaurants followed.
A handful of meat businesses still operate here, in a cooperative building, but they're a small presence compared to the luxury stores.
As you walk the streets, notice the contrast between the cobblestones and old brick warehouses and the sleek glass buildings now rising among them.
You're at the southern entrance to the High Line, at Gansevoort Street, next to the Whitney Museum of American Art.
The museum, the large, asymmetrical building with steel cladding and outdoor terraces stepping down toward the river, was designed by Renzo Piano and opened here in 2015.
The Whitney's story begins with Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney, a sculptor and heiress who collected the work of living American artists.
In 1929, she offered her collection to the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
The Met declined.
So in 1931, she founded her own museum, in Greenwich Village.
The Whitney later moved to Midtown and then to a famous building on Madison Avenue, before coming here.
Its Biennial exhibition is one of the most important surveys of contemporary American art.
Now look at the elevated structure above you, the High Line.
As you heard in the overview, the railroad tracks were lifted off the street in the 1930s as part of the West Side Improvement Project, which removed over a hundred street-level crossings.
The new elevated line, completed in 1934, ran from St. John's Terminal in Hudson Square up to the rail yards at 34th Street.
It ran through the middle of blocks rather than over the avenues, and it passed directly into factories and warehouses, so trains could unload right inside buildings.
As trucking took over, rail traffic dwindled.
The last train, reportedly carrying a load of frozen turkeys, ran in 1980.
The southern section was demolished.
The rest sat abandoned for nearly twenty years, and wild grasses, flowers, and small trees took root on the old tracks.
Property owners wanted it torn down.
In 1999, two neighborhood residents, Joshua David and Robert Hammond, met at a community meeting and founded Friends of the High Line to save it.
Initially, the idea seemed absurd.
But photographs by Joel Sternfeld of the wild meadow growing on the tracks helped capture the public imagination.
The city, under Mayor Michael Bloomberg, embraced the project.
The first section opened as a park in 2009.

The design, by the landscape architecture firm James Corner Field Operations with the architects Diller Scofidio and Renfro, kept the old rails in places and used planting by the Dutch designer Piet Oudolf, who chose grasses and perennials inspired by the self-seeded landscape that grew there during the abandoned years.
The High Line became an instant hit, and a catalyst for development.
Billions of dollars in new buildings went up alongside it.
It also became a symbol of a broader debate about how public improvements can drive gentrification.
Even its founders have acknowledged that the park benefited wealthy newcomers more than longtime residents of nearby public housing.
Walk to the river, along the Hudson River Park, to the park built on what look like giant concrete tulips rising out of the water.
This is Little Island, which opened in 2021.
It was designed by the British designer Thomas Heatherwick and funded largely by the media mogul Barry Diller and his wife, the fashion designer Diane von Furstenberg.
Its undulating surface is held up by about one hundred thirty two concrete pots on piles, and it contains lawns, gardens, and an amphitheater.
But look just south of it, at the remains of an old pier and a steel archway.
That arch is the last remnant of Pier 54, and it carries one of the great stories of the steamship era.

In the early twentieth century, this stretch of the Hudson, from about 12th to 23rd Streets, was home to the Chelsea Piers, a set of grand ocean liner terminals designed by the architects Warren and Wetmore, who also designed Grand Central Terminal.
They opened in 1910 and were used by the great transatlantic lines, including Cunard and White Star.
In April 1912, the White Star Line's new ship, the Titanic, was headed for these piers on its maiden voyage.
It never arrived.
After it struck an iceberg and sank, the Cunard ship Carpathia rescued about seven hundred survivors and brought them here to Pier 54 on the night of April eighteenth.
Thousands of people crowded the waterfront in the rain, waiting for news of their loved ones.
Three years later, in May 1915, another famous ship left from Pier 54: the Cunard liner Lusitania, bound for Liverpool.
Off the coast of Ireland, it was torpedoed by a German submarine and sank, killing nearly twelve hundred people, including over one hundred Americans.
The sinking helped turn American public opinion against Germany and toward entry into World War One.
Look for the word Cunard still faintly visible on the steel arch.
The great piers declined after ocean liners moved to larger terminals farther north in the 1930s, and air travel eventually ended the transatlantic liner era.
A few blocks north, the Chelsea Piers complex has been converted into a giant sports and entertainment center.
Also nearby is Pier 57, a former marine terminal that has been redeveloped and now includes offices for Google, a food hall, and a rooftop park.
It's another example of how the old maritime infrastructure of the west side has been transformed.
You're at Chelsea Market, the block-long complex of brick buildings between Ninth and Tenth Avenues and 15th and 16th Streets.
Walk inside and look at the exposed brick, iron beams, and old pipes.
This was a factory, and a historic one.
In 1898, several large baking companies merged to form the National Biscuit Company, later known as Nabisco.
Its headquarters and main bakery were here, in a complex of about eighteen buildings that eventually spread over several blocks.
The company pioneered mass-market packaged foods.

Its first major national brand, launched in 1898, was the Uneeda Biscuit, a soda cracker sold in an innovative package lined with waxed paper to keep it fresh, at a time when crackers were usually sold loose from barrels.
Nabisco's advertising campaign for Uneeda was one of the first large-scale national ad campaigns in American history.
And in 1912, the bakers here created a new cookie: two chocolate wafers with a cream filling, called the Oreo.
Nobody knows for sure where the name came from.
The Oreo went on to become the best-selling cookie in the world.
Animal Crackers and Fig Newtons were also produced by Nabisco in this era.
A plaque on the Ninth Avenue side commemorates the Oreo's birth on this block, and the street outside has at times been nicknamed Oreo Way.
Nabisco moved its manufacturing to a modern plant in New Jersey in 1958, and the buildings were used by other businesses.
In the 1990s, a developer, Irwin Cohen, converted the ground floor into a food hall and market, which opened in 1997 as Chelsea Market.
He kept many industrial details, including a waterfall made from a pipe.
The upper floors became offices for media companies and tech firms.
In 2018, Google bought Chelsea Market, for a reported price of about two point four billion dollars, one of the most expensive real estate deals for a single building in New York at the time.
It's now part of Google's Chelsea campus.
Note that the High Line passes right through the building's western side.
When the rail viaduct was built, Nabisco had loading docks connected directly to the tracks, so flour and sugar could come in and finished products could go out without ever touching the street.
Across Ninth Avenue, filling the entire block from Eighth to Ninth Avenues and 15th to 16th Streets, is a massive Art Deco building: 111 Eighth Avenue.
If you work at Google, you may know this building very well.
It was completed in 1932 as the Port Authority Commerce Building, also called the Union Inland Terminal Number One.
The Port Authority of New York, which built bridges and tunnels, wanted a freight distribution hub where trucks coming through the new Holland Tunnel could drop off goods.
The building was designed so trucks could drive right inside and ride oversized elevators up to the upper floors, delivering goods directly to warehouses on each floor.
Its floors are enormous and built to carry very heavy loads.
At about three million square feet, it was one of the largest buildings in the city by floor area.
In fact, at the time it was built, it was among the largest buildings in the world by floor space.
It covers an entire city block.
Later, the building became a hub for a different kind of freight: data.
In the internet age, its central location, huge floors, strong structure, and electrical capacity made it a major hub for telecommunications and data centers, like 60 Hudson Street downtown.
In 2010, Google bought the building for about one point nine billion dollars, at the time one of the largest single-building sales in the country.
Google had been leasing space here since 2006, and the building became the core of its New York operations.
It's now joined by other Google buildings in the neighborhood: Chelsea Market, Pier 57, and St. John's Terminal in Hudson Square.
There's something poetic about this.
The building was designed to make the movement of physical goods more efficient, and it now houses engineers building the software that moves information around the world.
And it's not unique.

Up and down the west side, buildings designed for freight have found new life as offices for tech companies, because the same things that made them good for freight, big floors, high ceilings, strong structures, and lots of power, make them good for modern offices too.
On West 23rd Street, between Seventh and Eighth Avenues, look for the red brick building with ornate iron balconies and a vertical sign reading Hotel Chelsea.
It was built in 1884 as one of the city's first cooperative apartment buildings, and for a time it was among the tallest buildings in the city.
In the 1880s, West 23rd Street was the heart of New York's theater district, with theaters and music halls lining the street.
Within a couple of decades, the cooperative had failed, and the building became a hotel.
Over the twentieth century, the Chelsea became legendary as a residence for artists, writers, and musicians, many of them on long-term stays.
Its manager for many years, Stanley Bard, was known for letting struggling artists pay their rent late, or even with artwork, which covered the walls of the lobby.
The list of residents is remarkable.
Mark Twain and O. Henry are said to have stayed here.
The poet Dylan Thomas was living here when he fell ill in 1953.
Arthur C. Clarke worked on 2001: A Space Odyssey while staying here.
Andy Warhol filmed parts of his 1966 film Chelsea Girls here.
Leonard Cohen wrote a song about an encounter at the hotel with Janis Joplin.
Patti Smith and Robert Mapplethorpe lived here in the late 1960s, as she describes in her memoir Just Kids.
Bob Dylan, Jimi Hendrix, Madonna, and many others passed through.
The hotel's history also has darker chapters.
In October 1978, Nancy Spungen, the girlfriend of the Sex Pistols bassist Sid Vicious, was found stabbed to death in their room.
Vicious was charged with her murder but died of a heroin overdose before trial.
The hotel closed to new guests in 2011 for a long and contentious renovation, during which some long-term residents remained.
It reopened in 2022 as a luxury hotel.

Also on this street, look for the Chelsea's neighbor, the old YMCA building, and the site of the Grand Opera House, which once stood on Eighth Avenue and was owned by the notorious financier Jim Fisk, who ran the Erie Railroad from offices there.
In 1872, Fisk was shot dead by a rival in love and business at a hotel on lower Broadway.
Chelsea has always been full of drama.
You're now in the Chelsea Historic District, near Ninth Avenue and West 21st Street.
Look at the full block of green lawn and Gothic buildings, the campus of the General Theological Seminary, the oldest seminary of the Episcopal Church.
The land was donated to the seminary in 1827 by Clement Clarke Moore, who owned the Chelsea estate.
Moore was a scholar of Hebrew and Greek who taught at the seminary.
He's best known, though, for something else: he's generally credited with writing, in 1822, the poem A Visit from St. Nicholas, which begins, Twas the night before Christmas.
The poem helped create the modern American image of Santa Claus, with his sleigh, eight reindeer, and trip down the chimney.
Some scholars have argued that another writer, Henry Livingston Junior, actually wrote it, but Moore's authorship is the traditional view.
Moore had good reason to develop his land.
When the city's street grid was imposed in 1811, Ninth Avenue was cut through the middle of his estate.

He was furious, but he made the best of it, dividing the land into lots and selling them with strict covenants about what could be built: residential houses only, with setbacks from the street, and no stables or factories.
That's why this area has such elegant, consistent rows of townhouses.
Walk along West 20th Street, between Ninth and Tenth Avenues, to see Cushman Row, a row of Greek Revival houses built in the 1840s by a merchant named Don Alonzo Cushman, a friend of Moore's.
Look for the small, square attic windows with iron wreaths around them, and the iron pineapples, a symbol of hospitality, on the newel posts of some stoops.

On Tenth Avenue, look also for the Empire Diner, an Art Deco diner car, and to the north, the massive London Terrace complex, built in 1930 and once one of the largest apartment buildings in the world, with its own swimming pool and doormen dressed as London bobbies.

It's a remarkable contrast: just a block or two from the freight terminals, the slaughterhouses, and the piers, Moore's carefully planned neighborhood of churches and townhouses has survived nearly two centuries.
You're in West Chelsea, near Eleventh Avenue and West 26th Street.

The blocks around you, roughly between Tenth and Eleventh Avenues from 18th to 28th Streets, contain one of the densest concentrations of art galleries in the world, hundreds of them, many in former garages and warehouses.
Galleries began moving here from SoHo in the late 1980s and 1990s, as SoHo's rents rose.
The Dia Art Foundation opened an exhibition space on West 22nd Street in 1987, and big dealers followed.
Garages, with their high ceilings, large open spaces, and freight doors, were perfect for showing large contemporary works.
Today, galleries like Gagosian, David Zwirner, and Pace operate huge spaces here, and Thursday evenings, when many shows open, the sidewalks fill with art lovers.
Now look at the massive building that fills the block between 26th and 27th Streets, along Eleventh Avenue, with continuous horizontal bands of windows wrapping around its rounded corners.
This is the Starrett-Lehigh Building, completed in 1931, and it's one of the great industrial buildings of the twentieth century.
It was built as a joint venture between the Starrett construction family and the Lehigh Valley Railroad.
The railroad had a freight yard here, and the building was designed so freight trains could enter the ground floor on tracks.
Even more remarkable, trucks could drive into enormous elevators and be lifted directly to any of the upper floors, then drive right up to the tenants' doors.
It was essentially a vertical freight yard.
Its architecture is equally striking.
Instead of a traditional facade with vertical columns, the building has cantilevered concrete floors with ribbons of steel windows running continuously around it.
It was celebrated by the Museum of Modern Art in an early exhibition on modern architecture as an example of the new International Style.
Like 111 Eighth Avenue, it later found new life with creative companies.
Martha Stewart's media company had offices here, as have photographers, fashion companies, and tech startups.
The interior's huge windows offer some of the best Hudson River views in the city.
End your walk at Hudson Yards, the cluster of glass towers rising at the northern end of the High Line, around West 33rd Street.
The towers you see are built on a platform over an active rail yard.
Beneath your feet, the Long Island Rail Road stores commuter trains between rush hours.
For decades, the yard was an enormous hole on the far west side of Manhattan.
Plans to cover it went back to the 1950s.
In the 2000s, the city tried to build a football stadium here for the New York Jets, as part of a bid for the 2012 Olympics.
That plan collapsed.
Instead, the city rezoned the area, and the developers Related Companies and Oxford Properties built Hudson Yards, which opened its first phase in 2019.
To build it, engineers drilled hundreds of caissons down to bedrock between the rail tracks and built a giant platform over the yard while trains continued to run.
It is often described as the largest private real estate development in American history.
The city also extended the 7 subway line to a new station here, which opened in 2015.
The towers house offices for companies including financial firms, media companies, and tech companies, as well as a shopping mall, apartments, and a hotel.
Look up at 30 Hudson Yards, the tallest tower, which has an outdoor observation deck called Edge, jutting out from the building in a triangular point at about eleven hundred feet.
It's one of the highest outdoor observation decks in the Western Hemisphere.
In the central plaza, you'll see the Vessel, a honeycomb-like structure of interlocking staircases, designed by Thomas Heatherwick, the designer of Little Island.
It has about one hundred fifty four flights of stairs and was meant to be climbed.
Access has been restricted at times for safety reasons, with added barriers on the upper levels.
Next to it, the building with the giant movable outer shell, on rails, is The Shed, a cultural center that can expand its size by rolling its shell outward over the adjacent plaza.
Hudson Yards has been controversial.
Critics have called it a playground for the rich, and debated the tax incentives the city provided to support it.
Admirers point to the engineering achievement and the economic activity it brought to a former rail yard.
Either way, it represents the latest chapter of the west side's transformation, from freight trains and piers to the most expensive real estate in America, all in about a century.
For a long time, the East Village wasn't called the East Village at all.
It was simply the northern part of the Lower East Side.
The name was invented in the 1960s, partly by real estate agents hoping to attach some of Greenwich Village's bohemian glamour to cheaper tenement apartments to the east.
The marketing worked, perhaps too well: within a few years, the neighborhood had become the center of the hippie counterculture, and later of punk rock.
But the history goes much deeper.
In the seventeenth century, this was the farm, or bouwerij, of Peter Stuyvesant, the last Dutch director-general of New Amsterdam.
His family held the land for generations, and a few traces of their estate survive in diagonal streets and an old church.
In the nineteenth century, the area became the heart of Kleindeutschland, Little Germany, one of the largest German-speaking communities in the world outside of Berlin and Vienna.
It was a neighborhood of beer halls, bakeries, singing societies, gymnastics clubs called Turnvereine, and Lutheran and Catholic churches.
It was also a hotbed of labor organizing and socialist politics.
As the Germans moved out in the early twentieth century, Eastern European Jews, Ukrainians, Poles, and Italians moved in.
Second Avenue became the Yiddish Rialto, the center of a thriving Yiddish theater scene.
After World War Two, Ukrainian refugees built a community around Seventh Street, and Puerto Rican families settled in the area east of Avenue A, known as Alphabet City, or in Spanglish, Loisaida.
Then came the artists and the counterculture.
In the 1950s and 60s, Beat poets, jazz musicians, and abstract painters moved into cheap apartments here.
In the 1960s, St. Mark's Place became the East Coast counterpart to San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury.
In the 1970s, the CBGB club on the Bowery launched punk rock.
In the 1980s, the neighborhood was the center of a vibrant art and music scene, but it also suffered from drugs, abandoned buildings, arson, and the AIDS crisis.
In the 1990s and 2000s, it gentrified rapidly.

As you walk, notice the layers: German names carved on old buildings, Ukrainian churches, Yiddish theater history, Puerto Rican murals and community gardens, punk landmarks, and new luxury buildings, all mixed together.
You're at Astor Place, the busy intersection where Lafayette Street, Fourth Avenue, the Bowery, and Eighth Street converge.
Start with the large brownstone building on the triangular block to the south.
This is the Foundation Building of the Cooper Union, completed in 1859.
It was founded by Peter Cooper, one of the most remarkable figures in American industrial history.
Cooper had very little formal schooling, but he became a successful inventor and industrialist.
He built the Tom Thumb, one of the first American-built steam locomotives, in 1830.
He ran glue factories and ironworks, made rolled iron beams used in early fireproof buildings, and was a major backer of the first transatlantic telegraph cable.
He even patented a gelatin dessert, decades before Jell-O.
Cooper wanted to give working people the education he never had.
He founded Cooper Union to provide free education in science, engineering, and art, open to men and women, regardless of race or religion, which was radical for the time.
For most of its history, tuition was free for all students.
Fun detail: Cooper was so convinced that the passenger elevator would soon be practical that he had a round shaft built into the Foundation Building, before a working elevator design existed.
He assumed elevators would be cylindrical.
Today, an elevator runs in that shaft.
The building's Great Hall, in the basement, is one of the most historically important rooms in America.
On February twenty-seventh, 1860, a little-known Illinois lawyer named Abraham Lincoln gave a speech there arguing against the expansion of slavery into the western territories.
The speech was carefully reasoned and widely reprinted, and it helped make Lincoln a serious contender for the Republican nomination for president.
A photograph taken by Mathew Brady the same day became one of his most famous portraits.
Lincoln later reportedly said that Brady and the Cooper Union speech made him president.
The Great Hall has hosted presidents, suffragists, and civil rights leaders ever since.
Now look at the big black cube balanced on one corner in the middle of the plaza.
That's Alamo, a sculpture by Tony Rosenthal, installed in 1967.
If you push it, it spins.
The plaza's name honors John Jacob Astor, a German immigrant who made a fortune in the fur trade and then invested it in Manhattan real estate, becoming the richest man in America.
Near here stood the Astor Opera House, site of the Astor Place Riot of 1849.

The riot began as a rivalry between two actors, the American Edwin Forrest and the Englishman William Charles Macready, but it became a violent clash between working-class nativists and the upper-class patrons of the opera house.
Militia troops fired into the crowd, killing over twenty people.
Across Lafayette Street, the large Italianate brownstone building is the Public Theater.
It was originally the Astor Library, founded with a bequest from John Jacob Astor and one of the first free public libraries in the city.
Its collection later became part of the New York Public Library.
In the 1960s, the producer Joseph Papp saved the building from demolition and turned it into the Public Theater.
Papp also founded Shakespeare in the Park.
The Public premiered the musical Hair in 1967, A Chorus Line in 1975, and Hamilton in 2015, all of which went on to Broadway.
You're on the Bowery, at 315 Bowery, near Bleecker Street.
In 1973, a club owner named Hilly Kristal opened a bar here called CBGB, which stood for Country, Bluegrass, and Blues, the kind of music he planned to book.
That's not what happened.
In the 1970s, the Bowery was still skid row, lined with flophouses, and CBGB was a narrow, dingy room with a long bar and a tiny stage.
Kristal had a policy that bands had to play their own original music.
A group of young musicians began playing there, and between about 1974 and 1977, CBGB became the birthplace of American punk rock and new wave.
The Ramones played their early shows here, short, fast, loud songs that stripped rock and roll to its basics.
So did Patti Smith, Television, Blondie, and the Talking Heads.
These bands sounded nothing alike, but they shared a stripped-down, do-it-yourself aesthetic that changed popular music.
CBGB's bathrooms were legendarily filthy, and its awning, with its white letters on a dark background, became an iconic image, endlessly reproduced on T-shirts.
The club closed in 2006 after a rent dispute, and the space later became a high-end clothing store, which preserved some of the graffiti-covered walls.
Now walk a couple of blocks west to East Fourth Street, between the Bowery and Lafayette Street, and look for a red brick house with a Greek Revival doorway at number 29.
This is the Merchant's House Museum, and it's a time capsule from an entirely different world.
Built in 1832, it was bought in 1835 by Seabury Tredwell, a wealthy hardware merchant.
At that time, this street was one of the most fashionable addresses in the city.
The Tredwell family lived here for almost a century.
The youngest daughter, Gertrude Tredwell, was born in the house and lived there until she died in 1933.
As the neighborhood changed around her, she kept the house and furnishings almost exactly as they had been.
A relative turned it into a museum in 1936.
It's one of very few nineteenth-century family homes in New York preserved with original furniture, clothing, and belongings intact.
It's also said to be among the most haunted houses in Manhattan: staff and visitors have reported sightings of Gertrude Tredwell.
The museum offers candlelit ghost tours around Halloween.
It's a reminder that before the Bowery was skid row, and before it was punk, it was the edge of an elegant residential neighborhood.
You're on East Seventh Street, between Second and Third Avenues.
Look for McSorley's Old Ale House, at number 15, with its sawdust floor and dark wood interior.
McSorley's claims to date from 1854, which would make it one of the oldest continuously operating bars in New York, though some historians think it opened a bit later.
Its motto is: Be good or be gone.
McSorley's serves only two kinds of beer, light and dark, and you order them two mugs at a time.
The walls are covered with a dense layer of old photographs, newspaper clippings, and memorabilia, much of it untouched for over a century.
Above the bar hang wishbones, said to have been left by young men going off to fight in World War One, intended to be collected when they returned.
The ones still hanging belonged to those who didn't come back.
For most of its history, McSorley's banned women.
It finally admitted them in 1970, after two lawyers from the National Organization for Women sued and won, and New York City passed a law banning sex discrimination in public places.
Even then, it didn't have a women's restroom until 1986.
Now look east along Seventh Street, toward Second Avenue.
This stretch is the heart of Little Ukraine.
Ukrainians settled here starting in the late nineteenth century, and a larger wave arrived after World War Two, many of them people displaced by the war and fleeing Soviet rule.
Look for St. George Ukrainian Catholic Church, with its large dome, on Seventh Street.
Every year, its parish holds a Ukrainian festival.
At the corner of Second Avenue and Ninth Street, look for Veselka, a Ukrainian restaurant open since 1954, famous for its pierogi, borscht, and blintzes, and open nearly around the clock.
After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Veselka became a gathering place for the community and raised money for relief efforts.
The Ukrainian Museum, on East Sixth Street, holds a fine collection of folk art, including painted Easter eggs called pysanky.
Also on Seventh Street, look for the old building of the Ukrainian National Home, and the occasional blue and yellow flag in windows.
The community has been shrinking for decades, but it remains visible here.
You're on St. Mark's Place, the stretch of Eighth Street between Third Avenue and Avenue A. It's probably the most famous street in the East Village.
It started out respectable.
In the 1830s, the street was lined with fine Federal-style houses.
Look for number 4 St. Mark's Place, the Hamilton-Holly House, built in 1831.
Colonel Alexander Hamilton Junior, the son of the Alexander Hamilton buried at Trinity Church, lived there with his sister Eliza for a time.
By the late nineteenth century, the street was part of Little Germany, lined with German clubs and halls.
At 19 to 25 St. Mark's Place stood the Arlington Hall, and later a Polish social hall called the Polski Dom Narodowy.
In 1966, Andy Warhol rented the space for his multimedia show, the Exploding Plastic Inevitable, featuring the Velvet Underground and Nico, with light shows, film projections, and dancing.
The building later became a nightclub called the Electric Circus, one of the first psychedelic discotheques.
In the late 1960s, St. Mark's Place was the East Coast capital of the hippie counterculture, packed with head shops, poster stores, and young runaways.
In the 1970s and 80s it became the main drag of punk.
The clothing store Trash and Vaudeville, which outfitted punk and rock musicians for decades, was a fixture of the street.
Its owners have said that the Ramones, Debbie Harry, and many others shopped there.
Near Avenue A, look for the pair of tenement buildings at 96 and 98 St. Mark's Place.
Their facade appears on the cover of Led Zeppelin's 1975 album Physical Graffiti, with the windows cut out on the album cover.
The Rolling Stones also filmed their 1981 music video for Waiting on a Friend in front of these buildings.
In recent decades, St. Mark's Place became known for something else: Japanese food.
Starting in the 1980s, a cluster of Japanese restaurants, izakayas, and shops opened on and around the street, giving the area the nickname Little Tokyo.
The famous Gem Spa newsstand, at the corner of St. Mark's Place and Second Avenue, sold what many considered the best egg cream in the city for decades.
An egg cream, by the way, contains neither egg nor cream: it's chocolate syrup, milk, and seltzer.
Gem Spa closed in 2020, another casualty of the neighborhood's changing economics.
At the corner of Second Avenue and East 10th Street, set back from the street in a small churchyard, stands St. Mark's Church in-the-Bowery.
It is one of the oldest churches in New York.
This land was part of Peter Stuyvesant's farm.
Stuyvesant, the peg-legged director-general of New Amsterdam who surrendered the colony to the English in 1664, built a family chapel here in the 1660s.
He was buried in a vault beneath that chapel in 1672.
The current church was built on the same site in 1799, making it among the oldest church buildings in Manhattan, second only to St. Paul's Chapel.
The steeple was added in the 1820s, and the cast iron portico in the 1850s.
Stuyvesant's remains are still in the vault beneath the church, and there's a bust of him in the churchyard.
Some say his ghost walks the grounds, tapping his wooden leg.
Notice that the church doesn't line up with the street grid.
It's oriented to Stuyvesant Street, a diagonal street just to the west, which follows an old road through the Stuyvesant farm.
Stuyvesant Street is one of the only streets in Manhattan that runs true east-west, as opposed to the grid, which is tilted about twenty nine degrees.
It's lined with historic houses, including the Stuyvesant-Fish House, built in 1804, and the charming Renwick Triangle, a group of townhouses designed in the 1860s.
In the twentieth century, St. Mark's became one of the most artistically adventurous churches in the city.
In the 1920s, its rector hosted dancers, poets, and the architect Frank Lloyd Wright, who designed a tower for the property that was never built.
Since 1966, the church has been home to the Poetry Project, where poets like Allen Ginsberg, Patti Smith, and many others have read their work.
It also hosts experimental dance and theater.
In 1978, the church was badly damaged by fire.
It was restored with the help of neighborhood volunteers, many of them young people trained in construction skills as part of the restoration.
A reminder that in this neighborhood, even a two-hundred-year-old church is part of the creative scene.
Walk north along Second Avenue to East 12th Street.
In the early twentieth century, the stretch of Second Avenue from Houston Street to about 14th Street was the Yiddish Rialto, the center of Yiddish theater in America and, arguably, in the world.

At its height, in the 1910s and 1920s, there were more than a dozen Yiddish theaters in the area, presenting everything from melodramas and musical comedies to serious adaptations of Shakespeare and Ibsen in Yiddish.
Audiences of immigrant workers packed the theaters, cheered and booed, and treated stars like royalty.
Some great performers began here.
The actor Paul Muni started in Yiddish theater before becoming a Hollywood star.
Molly Picon became a beloved comedic star.
Boris Thomashefsky and Jacob Adler were among the great actor-managers of the era.
Jacob Adler's daughter, Stella Adler, later became one of the most influential acting teachers in America, teaching Marlon Brando and many others.
Look at the theater at the corner of Second Avenue and 12th Street.
It's now a movie theater, the Village East by Angelika, but it was built in 1926 as the Yiddish Art Theatre, commissioned by the businessman Louis Jaffe for the actor-director Maurice Schwartz.
Its interior features an extravagant Moorish-style ceiling with a giant Star of David.
If you go in to see a movie, look up.
A few blocks south, at the corner of Second Avenue and 10th Street, look down at the sidewalk for small stars with names on them.
This is the Yiddish Walk of Fame, honoring stars of the Yiddish stage.
For decades it was in front of the Second Avenue Deli, a famous kosher deli that operated here from 1954 until 2006, before moving uptown.
Yiddish theater declined as immigration was cut off after 1924, as the children of immigrants assimilated and moved away, and as movies and radio took over.
The Holocaust destroyed the European Yiddish-speaking world that sustained it.
But its influence on American entertainment is enormous: many of the comedians, actors, songwriters, and producers who shaped Broadway, Hollywood, and television came out of this world.
You're in Tompkins Square Park, between Avenues A and B and 7th and 10th Streets.
It has been the center stage of the neighborhood's dramas for over a century and a half.
In the nineteenth century, the park was the heart of Little Germany.
It was also a gathering place for protests.
In January 1874, in the depths of an economic depression, thousands of unemployed workers gathered here to demand public works jobs.
Police charged the crowd on horseback, beating demonstrators indiscriminately.
The Tompkins Square Riot became a landmark event in American labor history.
One young man who was there, a cigar maker named Samuel Gompers, later founded the American Federation of Labor.
He said the experience taught him the importance of practical, disciplined organizing.
Now look for a small marble fountain near the north side of the park, showing a boy and a girl looking out to sea.
This is the General Slocum memorial, and it marks one of the worst disasters in New York history.

On June fifteenth, 1904, the members of St. Mark's Evangelical Lutheran Church, a German congregation on East Sixth Street, chartered a paddle-wheel steamboat called the General Slocum for their annual Sunday school picnic.
More than thirteen hundred people boarded, most of them women and children, since the men were at work.
As the boat steamed up the East River, a fire broke out.
The crew was poorly trained, the life preservers were rotten and useless, and the fire hoses were rotten too.
The captain kept steaming forward instead of beaching the boat immediately.
More than a thousand people died, burned or drowned, within sight of shore.
It was the deadliest single-day disaster in New York City's history until September eleventh, 2001.
The tragedy devastated Little Germany.
So many families lost wives and children that many survivors couldn't bear to stay.
The German community, which had already begun migrating uptown, largely moved away to Yorkville on the Upper East Side.
The park has other stories.
Under one of the large elms, look for a plaque.

In 1966, the Indian spiritual teacher A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada held a public chanting session under this tree, and this is often considered the founding moment of the Hare Krishna movement in America.
The jazz saxophonist Charlie Parker lived in a townhouse facing the park on Avenue B in the early 1950s, and a jazz festival is held here in his honor every summer.
In 1988, the park was the scene of another riot, when police tried to enforce a curfew to clear out homeless encampments, and clashed violently with protesters.
The park was closed for a renovation in 1991 and reopened in 1992.
It's now a lively, much-loved neighborhood park, with a famous dog run, one of the first in the city.
End your walk in Alphabet City, near Avenue C and East Third Street.
Look up at the street signs: on Avenue C, you'll see a second name, Loisaida Avenue.
Loisaida is a Spanglish pronunciation of Lower East Side, popularized by Puerto Rican residents and artists in the 1970s.
Puerto Ricans began arriving in New York in large numbers after World War Two, many in the so-called Great Migration of the 1950s, when cheap airfares made the journey possible.
They came for factory jobs and settled in East Harlem, the South Bronx, Brooklyn, and here.
By the 1970s, much of Alphabet City was Puerto Rican.
Those were brutal years.
The city was nearly bankrupt, landlords abandoned buildings or set them on fire for insurance money, and the city took ownership of thousands of abandoned properties.
Drugs and crime were rampant.
But residents fought back.
Community activists organized to rehabilitate buildings through sweat equity, doing the work themselves in exchange for ownership.
And they turned rubble-strewn lots into community gardens.
The community garden movement has deep roots here.
In 1973, an artist named Liz Christy and a group called the Green Guerillas began throwing seed bombs, balloons filled with seeds and fertilizer, over fences into vacant lots.
They planted a garden at the corner of the Bowery and Houston Street, now the Liz Christy Community Garden, considered the first community garden in New York City.
Dozens of others followed in Alphabet City.
Look for gardens like La Plaza Cultural, at Avenue C and East 9th Street.
In the late 1990s, Mayor Rudy Giuliani tried to auction off many garden lots for development, provoking huge protests.
Many gardens were saved.
At 236 East Third Street, between Avenues B and C, is the Nuyorican Poets Cafe.
Founded in 1973 by the poet and professor Miguel Algarín, along with the playwright Miguel Piñero and others, it began as an informal gathering in Algarín's living room.
The term Nuyorican refers to New Yorkers of Puerto Rican descent, and the café became a home for their poetry, music, and theater.
In the 1990s, it became famous for its poetry slams, competitive performance poetry that helped launch the spoken word movement nationally.
Piñero's play Short Eyes, written about his experiences in prison, was a major success and was nominated for Tony Awards.
In the 1990s, the musical Rent was set in this neighborhood, in the world of artists, squatters, and people living with HIV.

Today, Alphabet City has gentrified dramatically, but the murals, gardens, and casitas, small wooden houses built in community gardens in the style of rural Puerto Rico, preserve the memory of Loisaida.
In the second half of the nineteenth century, the center of New York was not Midtown and not Wall Street.
It was the stretch of Broadway and Fifth Avenue between 14th and 34th Streets.
This was where fashionable New Yorkers shopped, dined, went to the theater, and lived.
The story of this area is the story of the city's relentless northward march.
As commerce pushed up from lower Manhattan, wealthy families kept moving north to stay ahead of it.
In the 1830s and 40s, they built mansions around Union Square and Gramercy Park.
By the 1850s and 60s, Madison Square, at 23rd Street, was the most fashionable address in the city, surrounded by luxury hotels and mansions.
Then the shops followed.
In the 1870s and 80s, a stretch of Broadway and Sixth Avenue became known as Ladies' Mile, lined with enormous department stores that catered to middle- and upper-class women.
Theaters clustered around Union Square and Madison Square.
Restaurants like Delmonico's moved uptown to be near their clientele.
By the early 1900s, the fashionable crowd had moved on again, to upper Fifth Avenue and Midtown, and the department stores followed them to Herald Square and Fifth Avenue.
The neighborhood shifted to light manufacturing, toy companies, publishing houses, and photography studios.
The area around the Flatiron Building became the center of the toy industry, with an annual toy fair.
Later, in the 1990s, the neighborhood got a new identity as Silicon Alley, the hub of New York's first internet startup boom, with companies like DoubleClick, which Google later acquired.

This walk takes you through some of the most important buildings in the history of American architecture and commerce: the Flatiron, which helped define the skyscraper; the Metropolitan Life Tower; the grand cast iron and stone palaces of Ladies' Mile; and the private, gated Gramercy Park, which still requires a key to enter.
Along the way, you'll hear about Tammany Hall, Theodore Roosevelt, Andy Warhol, and the birth of the American popular song.
You're in Union Square.
The name doesn't refer to labor unions, though it would be fitting.
It comes from the union, or junction, of two major roads: Broadway and the old Bowery Road, which met here.
In the nineteenth century, this was a fashionable residential square, and then, as commerce moved in, a center of theaters, hotels, and luxury retail.
Tiffany and Company, for example, had its flagship store on the west side of the square from 1870 to 1906, in a cast iron building that still stands.
Tiffany was founded downtown in 1837 by Charles Lewis Tiffany as a stationery and fancy goods store, and became the most prestigious jeweler in America.
The company followed its customers north, from lower Broadway to Union Square, and later to Fifth Avenue.
Union Square's real identity, though, is as New York's great stage for protest.
On September fifth, 1882, about ten thousand workers marched from City Hall to Union Square in what is considered the first Labor Day parade in the United States.
In the following decades, socialists, anarchists, suffragists, and labor unions rallied here.
In 1927, crowds gathered here to protest the execution of Sacco and Vanzetti, two Italian anarchists convicted of murder in a widely criticized trial.
After September eleventh, 2001, the square became a spontaneous memorial, filled with candles and handwritten messages.
It remains the go-to place for protests in the city.
Look at the equestrian statue of George Washington at the south end.
Sculpted by Henry Kirke Brown, it was dedicated in 1856, and it's one of the oldest public sculptures in New York.
On the east side of the square, at the corner of 17th Street, look for the neo-Georgian building with a peaked roof.
This was the last home of Tammany Hall, the Democratic political machine that dominated New York politics for more than a century.
Tammany provided jobs, favors, and help to immigrants in exchange for votes, and its bosses, including William Tweed, became synonymous with corruption.
Tammany moved into this building in 1929.
Its power faded in the following decades, and today the building houses offices and shops.
At the south side of the square, above the stores, you might see a giant digital display.
Originally an art installation called Metronome, it was reprogrammed in 2020 as the Climate Clock, counting down the time left to limit global warming.
On the west side, at 33 Union Square West, the Decker Building, with its Moorish-style details, was where Andy Warhol moved his studio, The Factory, in 1968.
In June of that year, the radical feminist writer Valerie Solanas shot Warhol there.
He survived, but barely.
On Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays, the square hosts the Union Square Greenmarket, founded in 1976, which helped start the farmers' market movement in New York.
Some of the city's top chefs shop here.
You're on Broadway, around 18th to 20th Streets.
