Look around at the grand buildings on both sides, many with cast iron facades, mansard roofs, and huge plate-glass windows at street level.
These were department stores, and this was Ladies' Mile.
From about the 1860s to the early 1900s, the area along Broadway, Fifth Avenue, and especially Sixth Avenue between roughly 14th and 23rd Streets was the premier shopping district in America.

The department store was essentially invented in this period, and some of the most important American retailers had their flagships here: Lord and Taylor, Arnold Constable, B. Altman, Siegel-Cooper, and R. H. Macy and Company, which was on Sixth Avenue at 14th Street before moving to Herald Square in 1902.
Department stores changed American life.
They offered fixed prices instead of haggling.
They displayed huge varieties of goods under one roof.
They offered amenities like restaurants, restrooms, reading rooms, and delivery.
And critically, they created one of the first public spaces where middle-class women could go alone, without male chaperones, and spend the day.
That's why the area was called Ladies' Mile.
Look for the Lord and Taylor building at Broadway and 20th Street, completed in 1870, with its cast iron facade and corner tower.
Lord and Taylor was founded in 1826 and became one of the oldest department stores in the country, before closing its last stores in 2021.
Over on Sixth Avenue, look for the massive Siegel-Cooper building, between 18th and 19th Streets, completed in 1896.
It was one of the largest stores in the world.
It featured a fountain under its central atrium with a statue of the Republic, and the phrase Meet me at the fountain became a common way for New Yorkers to arrange meetings.
The El, the elevated railway along Sixth Avenue, brought shoppers right to the store doors.
But by the early 1900s, the stores began following their wealthy customers north, to Herald Square and Fifth Avenue in Midtown.
The buildings were taken over by manufacturers and wholesalers.
In 1989, the area was designated the Ladies' Mile Historic District, and in recent decades, retail has returned, with big-box stores and chains filling the old palaces.
The ABC Carpet and Home store on Broadway at 19th Street occupies a building originally built for W. and J. Sloane, a high-end furniture and carpet firm.
The interior, crammed with antiques and rugs, still gives a hint of the old department store atmosphere.
At 28 East 20th Street, between Broadway and Park Avenue South, look for a brownstone with a flag.
This is the Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace National Historic Site.
Theodore Roosevelt was born here on October twenty-seventh, 1858, into a wealthy old New York family of Dutch descent.
His father, Theodore Senior, was a glass importer, banker, and philanthropist who helped found the American Museum of Natural History and the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
Young Theodore was a sickly, asthmatic child, and he famously built up his strength through intense exercise, including in a home gymnasium his father had built for him on the porch.
Roosevelt lived here until he was fourteen.

He went on to become a state legislator, New York City police commissioner, assistant secretary of the Navy, leader of the Rough Riders in the Spanish-American War, governor of New York, vice president, and, after the assassination of William McKinley in 1901, president of the United States.
At forty-two, he was the youngest person ever to become president.
As president, he was a trustbuster, breaking up corporate monopolies, including the Northern Securities railroad trust organized by J. P. Morgan.
He was a conservationist who protected huge areas of public land, and he won the Nobel Peace Prize for mediating an end to the Russo-Japanese War.
Here's a twist: this is not the original house.
The original was demolished in 1916 to make way for a commercial building.

After Roosevelt died in 1919, his family and supporters bought the site and rebuilt the house as a replica, with Roosevelt's sister and widow helping to recreate the interiors from memory and photographs.
Many of the furnishings inside are original to the family.
The reconstruction was designed by Theodate Pope Riddle, one of the first women licensed as an architect in the United States.
It opened in 1923.
The museum is run by the National Park Service, and tours of the rooms are free.
It's a strange and interesting artifact: a historically accurate reconstruction of a house from the 1860s, built in the 1920s, and now itself almost a century old.
You're at Gramercy Park, between 20th and 21st Streets and Park Avenue South and Third Avenue.
Notice something unusual: the park is surrounded by a tall iron fence, and the gates are locked.
Gramercy Park is one of the very few private parks left in New York.
It was created in 1831 by a lawyer and developer named Samuel Ruggles, who bought a marshy farm here, drained it, and laid out sixty-six lots around a private park.
Owners of the lots surrounding the park were given keys, and the right to use the park was written into the property deeds.
To this day, only residents of the buildings facing the park have access, and keys are tightly controlled.
The locks are changed each year.
Hotel guests at the Gramercy Park Hotel have sometimes been given access, and once a year, on Christmas Eve, the park is traditionally opened to the public for a few hours.
The name Gramercy is thought to come from a Dutch name for the marshy area, possibly Krom Moerasje, meaning little crooked swamp, and a creek that ran through it.
Look around at the historic buildings surrounding the park.
On the south side, at 15 Gramercy Park South, is the National Arts Club, housed in a Victorian Gothic mansion that once belonged to Samuel J. Tilden.
Tilden was the governor of New York who helped bring down Boss Tweed, and he ran for president in 1876, winning the popular vote but losing in the Electoral College after a disputed deal.
According to a long-told story, Tilden, fearful of his political enemies, had a secret tunnel built from his house to escape to 19th Street.
The mansion's facade, renovated by Calvert Vaux, features carved portraits of writers like Shakespeare, Goethe, and Dante.
Next door, at number 16, is The Players, a private club founded in 1888 by the actor Edwin Booth, one of the greatest Shakespearean actors of the nineteenth century.
Booth was also the brother of John Wilkes Booth, the man who assassinated Abraham Lincoln.
Edwin was devastated by his brother's crime and withdrew from the stage for months.
Stanford White redesigned the building for the club.
Booth lived in an apartment on the top floor, and his room has been preserved as it was when he died in 1893.
Look for the statue in the center of the park: it's Edwin Booth, as Hamlet.

A short walk east, at Irving Place and 18th Street, is Pete's Tavern, which claims to be the oldest continuously operating bar in New York, open since 1864, and to have stayed open during Prohibition disguised as a flower shop.
The writer O. Henry lived nearby and, according to the bar, wrote his famous Christmas story The Gift of the Magi in one of its booths.
You're looking at one of the most famous buildings in the world, the Flatiron Building, at the intersection of Broadway, Fifth Avenue, and 23rd Street.
When it was completed in 1902, it was officially named the Fuller Building, after the George A. Fuller Company, a pioneering Chicago construction firm that built it as its New York headquarters.
But New Yorkers immediately nicknamed it the Flatiron, because its triangular shape resembled a clothes iron.
The building fills a narrow triangular lot created where Broadway crosses Fifth Avenue on a diagonal.
At its narrowest point, the tip, it's only about six and a half feet wide.
The architect was Daniel Burnham of Chicago, one of the great figures of American architecture.
He had led the design of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
He's famous for the phrase, Make no little plans; they have no magic to stir men's blood.
The Flatiron is a steel-frame skyscraper, but Burnham clad it in limestone and terracotta, with elaborate decoration inspired by the Italian Renaissance.
The facade is divided like a classical column, with a base, a shaft, and a capital.
When it opened, many people thought it would blow over.
The intersection does create strong wind gusts, and there's a well-known story that in the early 1900s, men would gather on 23rd Street to watch the wind lift women's skirts.
When police shooed them away, it was called giving them the twenty-three skidoo.
Etymologists aren't sure this story is the true origin of the phrase, but it's a good one.
The building became a favorite subject for photographers and painters.
Alfred Stieglitz and Edward Steichen both made famous photographs of it, in fog and twilight, which helped establish photography as a fine art.
Stieglitz said it looked like a ship moving forward.
In the 1990s, the area around the building was nicknamed Silicon Alley, as internet startups moved into the neighborhood's old loft buildings.
The Flatiron itself was home to the publishing company Macmillan for decades.
More recently, the building was emptied for a long renovation, and plans have been announced to convert much of it into residences.
The best view is from the small plaza at the north tip, where you can see its prow cutting through the city like the bow of a ship.
You're in Madison Square Park, across from the Flatiron Building.
In the second half of the nineteenth century, Madison Square was the most fashionable place in New York.
The park was surrounded by grand hotels, like the Fifth Avenue Hotel, where presidents stayed and political deals were made, and by mansions.
Delmonico's opened a restaurant on the square.
In the 1870s and 80s, the raised right arm and torch of the Statue of Liberty was displayed in this park for several years, part of a fundraising campaign to pay for the statue's pedestal.
Visitors paid to climb up inside the torch.
Look across Madison Avenue, at the northeast corner of the park.
On that site stood the original Madison Square Garden.

The second Garden, designed by Stanford White and opened in 1890, was one of the grandest entertainment buildings in the country, with a tall tower modeled on the Giralda in Seville, topped by a gilded statue of Diana by Augustus Saint-Gaudens.

On June twenty-fifth, 1906, Stanford White was shot dead in the rooftop theater of the Garden by Harry Kendall Thaw, a deranged millionaire who was obsessed with his wife, Evelyn Nesbit, a famous model and showgirl with whom White had had a relationship.
The trial was called the trial of the century.
The Garden was demolished in 1925, and the name moved uptown.
On the site now stands the New York Life Insurance Building, by Cass Gilbert, completed in 1928, with its golden pyramid roof.
Now look at the tall white tower on the east side of the park, at Madison Avenue and 24th Street, with a giant clock and a gold cupola.
This is the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company Tower, completed in 1909.
Modeled on the Campanile of St. Mark's in Venice, it was the tallest building in the world until the Woolworth Building surpassed it in 1913.
Each of its four clock faces is about twenty-six feet across.
Met Life was one of the giants of the insurance industry, selling small policies to working-class families, and its headquarters here were a symbol of its dominance.
The park has a few more stories.

Baseball's early history is linked to this area: the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club was organized near here in 1845 by players who had been playing on open lots around Madison Square, and its rules became the basis of modern baseball.
At the northwest corner of the park, a granite obelisk marks the grave of General William Worth, a hero of the Mexican-American War, who is actually buried underneath it.
And finally, look for the Shake Shack in the park.
It started in 2001 as a hot dog cart run by the restaurateur Danny Meyer, as part of an art project in the park.
The cart was so popular that he opened a permanent kiosk in 2004.
Shake Shack is now a publicly traded company with hundreds of locations around the world.
End your walk on West 28th Street, between Broadway and Sixth Avenue.
On the north side of the street, look for a row of modest nineteenth-century brick buildings.
This block is Tin Pan Alley, the birthplace of the American popular music industry.
From around the 1890s to the early 1900s, dozens of sheet music publishers had offices on this block.
Before recorded music became widespread, the music business ran on sheet music.
Families bought printed music to play on their parlor pianos, and a hit song could sell millions of copies.
Publishers employed songwriters to write hits and song pluggers, piano players who demonstrated songs for customers, vaudeville performers, and bandleaders.

According to legend, the name Tin Pan Alley came from a journalist who wrote that the sound of dozens of pianos playing different songs at once, through open windows, sounded like people banging on tin pans.
The songs that came out of Tin Pan Alley shaped American culture.

Composers and lyricists associated with this world include Irving Berlin, who wrote Alexander's Ragtime Band, God Bless America, and White Christmas; George Gershwin, who worked as a song plugger as a teenager; Scott Joplin, who lived in New York for a time; and many others.
Songs like Take Me Out to the Ball Game and Give My Regards to Broadway came from this era and this industry.
Tin Pan Alley was also a place where Black composers and performers, Jewish immigrants, and others found a way into American popular culture, often against the odds.
African American composers like James Weldon Johnson, his brother J. Rosamond Johnson, and Bob Cole wrote hit songs for the Tin Pan Alley publishers.
The music business followed the theaters uptown, toward Times Square, and later to the Brill Building at Broadway and 49th Street, where songwriters wrote many of the pop hits of the 1950s and 60s.
In 2019, several buildings on this block were designated as New York City landmarks, after preservationists fought to save them.
Look around, too, at the flower shops nearby.
Sixth Avenue and 28th Street is the heart of the city's Flower District, where wholesalers sell flowers and plants to florists.
Early in the morning, the sidewalks are filled with greenery.
As you leave, imagine the sound of dozens of pianos drifting out of these windows, each one playing a different song, all hoping to be the next big hit.
Midtown Manhattan is the densest concentration of office space in the United States, and arguably the most recognizable urban landscape on Earth.
Hundreds of thousands of people commute into these few square miles every workday.

But for much of the nineteenth century, this area was on the outskirts of the city, a patchwork of farms, rocky outcrops, squatters' shanties, and institutions that wanted to be out of the way, like reservoirs, cattle yards, and rail yards.
The great transformation came at the turn of the twentieth century, driven by transportation.
In 1871, Cornelius Vanderbilt opened the first Grand Central at 42nd Street, consolidating his railroads in one terminal.
In 1904, the first subway line opened, running up the east side to Grand Central, across 42nd Street to Times Square, and up the west side.
In 1910, the Pennsylvania Railroad opened Penn Station at 34th Street, connecting Manhattan by tunnel to New Jersey and Long Island.
In 1913, the new Grand Central Terminal opened.
Suddenly, Midtown was the most accessible place in the region.
Business followed.
Department stores moved to Herald Square and Fifth Avenue.
Theaters moved to Times Square.
The garment industry moved to the West Thirties.
Corporations built headquarters along 42nd Street and Park Avenue.
In the late 1920s, during an extraordinary boom, Midtown became the site of a race for the sky, producing the Chrysler Building and the Empire State Building within a year of each other.
The look of Midtown was shaped by one law in particular.
In 1916, after the massive Equitable Building downtown blocked light and air from its neighbors, New York passed the first comprehensive zoning law in the country.
It required buildings to step back as they rose, so that light could reach the street.
This produced the wedding-cake setbacks that define Art Deco skyscrapers, including the Empire State Building.
As you walk, look up at the towers and you'll notice those setbacks everywhere.

On this walk, you'll see icons of American commerce, the department store, the corporate skyscraper, the advertising sign, and the train terminal, and you'll hear about the people who built them, the companies that paid for them, and the controversies that shaped them.
You're at Fifth Avenue and 34th Street, at the base of the Empire State Building.
Before the skyscraper, this site held the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel, born of a family feud.
In the 1890s, William Waldorf Astor built the Waldorf Hotel here, next to the mansion of his aunt, Caroline Astor, the queen of New York society.
It was partly an act of spite.
Her son, John Jacob Astor the Fourth, responded by building an even taller hotel, the Astoria, next door.
The two hotels were then joined into the Waldorf-Astoria, the most luxurious hotel in the city.
When the hotel moved to Park Avenue in 1931, the old one was demolished.
By the way, John Jacob Astor the Fourth died on the Titanic in 1912.
He was among the wealthiest people aboard.

The Empire State Building was the project of John J. Raskob, a financier and former executive of General Motors and DuPont, and Al Smith, the former governor of New York who had just lost the 1928 presidential election.
Raskob was reportedly in a competition with Walter Chrysler, of the rival automaker, who was building the Chrysler Building a few blocks away.
The design, by the firm Shreve, Lamb and Harmon, was simple and efficient, and construction was astonishingly fast.
Steel went up at a rate of about four and a half stories per week.
The building opened on May first, 1931, after about thirteen and a half months of construction.
President Herbert Hoover pressed a button in Washington to turn on the lights.
At one thousand two hundred fifty feet to its roof, it was the tallest building in the world, a title it held for nearly forty years.
But it opened at the worst possible moment, in the depths of the Great Depression.
For years, much of its office space was empty, and New Yorkers nicknamed it the Empty State Building.
The observation deck's ticket sales helped keep it afloat.
The spire on top was originally meant to be a mooring mast for dirigibles, the airships.
The idea was that passengers would disembark onto a gangplank eighty-six floors up.
A couple of attempts were made, but high winds made it impractical and dangerous, and the idea was abandoned.
In 1933, the building became a movie star, when King Kong climbed to its top.
On July twenty-eighth, 1945, an Army B-25 bomber, flying in heavy fog, crashed into the 79th floor, killing fourteen people.

An elevator operator, Betty Lou Oliver, survived a fall of about seventy-five stories in an elevator whose cables had been damaged, which remains one of the most famous survival stories in the building's history.
The Art Deco lobby is one of the city's finest, with a ceiling mural of gears and planets in gold leaf and an image of the building itself in aluminum relief.
You're at Herald Square, where Broadway crosses Sixth Avenue at 34th Street.
The square takes its name from the New York Herald, a newspaper whose headquarters, designed by Stanford White, once stood here.
Look for the bronze monument at the north end of the square, with a figure of Minerva and two bell ringers with hammers who strike a bell every hour.
The ringers are nicknamed Stuff and Guff.
The monument honors James Gordon Bennett Senior and Junior, the publishers of the Herald.
It was the younger Bennett who sent the reporter Henry Morton Stanley to Africa to find the missionary David Livingstone, producing the famous line, Doctor Livingstone, I presume?
The giant store on the south side of 34th Street is Macy's.
Rowland Hussey Macy, a former whaler from Nantucket, opened a dry goods store on Sixth Avenue at 14th Street in 1858, after several failed retail ventures.
The company's red star logo is said to come from a tattoo Macy got while at sea.
Macy's was innovative: it used fixed prices, sold goods for cash only, and advertised aggressively.
Later, Macy's was taken over by the Straus family, Isidor and Nathan Straus, who had run its china and glassware department.
Isidor Straus and his wife Ida died together on the Titanic in 1912, after Ida reportedly refused to get into a lifeboat without him.
Under the Strauses, Macy's moved here in 1902 and built what it advertised as the World's Largest Store.
Now look at the corner of Broadway and 34th Street.
You'll notice a small, narrow building, covered in giant advertising signs, wedged into the corner of the Macy's block.
Macy's doesn't own it.

When Macy's was assembling the land for its store, an agent working for a rival, Henry Siegel of the Siegel-Cooper store, bought this corner lot first, hoping to force Macy's to buy it at an outrageous price, or to block its access to the corner.
Macy's refused, and built around it.
The holdout building still stands, and Macy's has rented its exterior for its own advertising.
Macy's had a fierce rivalry with Gimbels, a department store that stood a block away.
The rivalry was so famous that it appears in the 1947 film Miracle on 34th Street, in which the Macy's Santa Claus sends customers to Gimbels if Macy's doesn't have what they want.
Gimbels closed in 1987.
Macy's also gave the city one of its biggest traditions: the Thanksgiving Day Parade, first held in 1924.
Its famous giant balloons were introduced in 1927.
The parade ends right here, in front of the store.
You're on Seventh Avenue, around 39th Street.
Look at the street signs: this stretch of Seventh Avenue is also called Fashion Avenue.
Look down: in the sidewalk, you may find bronze plaques of the Fashion Walk of Fame, honoring American designers.
And look at the corner of Seventh Avenue and 39th Street, where a giant sculpture of a needle threading a button stands, along with an information kiosk.
You're in the Garment District, roughly between Fifth and Ninth Avenues, from about 34th to 42nd Streets.
For much of the twentieth century, this was the center of the American clothing industry.
In the early 1900s, the industry was concentrated in the tenement sweatshops of the Lower East Side.
After the Triangle fire and new safety laws, and as the industry grew, manufacturers moved into new loft buildings here, built in the 1920s.
Those tall, setback buildings were designed for garment production, with big windows for light and large open floors for rows of sewing machines.
By the 1950s, this district was producing a large majority of the women's clothing made in the United States, and the industry employed hundreds of thousands of workers in New York.
The streets were jammed with trucks and with workers pushing rolling racks of clothing from factories to showrooms.
Many of the workers were Jewish and Italian immigrants and their children, and later Puerto Rican, Chinese, Dominican, and other immigrants.
The industry was heavily unionized, and the International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union was one of the most powerful unions in the city.
Look for the statue of a garment worker at a sewing machine, a bronze sculpture by Judith Weller, at 555 Seventh Avenue.
It honors the many immigrant workers, especially Jewish workers, who built the industry.
Beginning in the 1960s and accelerating in the 1980s and 90s, most garment manufacturing moved overseas, to Asia and Latin America, where labor was cheaper.
The number of garment jobs in New York collapsed.
The district's buildings were gradually converted to offices, showrooms, hotels, and tech companies.
Still, New York remains a fashion capital, the home of major designers, fashion magazines, and New York Fashion Week.
Nearby schools, including the Fashion Institute of Technology on 27th Street and Parsons School of Design, train designers from around the world.
And you'll still find a few fabric stores, button shops, and trimming suppliers on the side streets, especially around 38th and 39th Streets, where designers come to buy materials.
You're in Bryant Park, behind the New York Public Library, between Fifth and Sixth Avenues and 40th and 42nd Streets.
In the nineteenth century, the site of the library held the Croton Distributing Reservoir, completed in 1842.
It was part of the Croton Aqueduct system, which brought clean water to the city from the Croton River, forty miles north, transforming public health in New York.
The reservoir was surrounded by massive Egyptian-style stone walls, and New Yorkers strolled along a promenade on top of them, looking down at the water.
Next to the reservoir, on the site of today's park, New York hosted its first world's fair in 1853, housed in a giant iron-and-glass building called the Crystal Palace, inspired by the one in London.
It was here, in 1854, that Elisha Otis demonstrated his safety elevator by cutting the rope.
The Crystal Palace burned down in 1858.
The library, built over the old reservoir, opened in 1911.
It was designed by Carrère and Hastings, and it's a masterpiece of Beaux-Arts architecture.
The library was created by combining two private libraries, those of John Jacob Astor and James Lenox, with a large bequest from Samuel Tilden, the former governor you heard about at Gramercy Park.
In front, on Fifth Avenue, are the famous marble lions.
In the 1930s, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia named them Patience and Fortitude, the qualities he said New Yorkers would need to survive the Depression.
If you can, go inside and see the Rose Main Reading Room on the third floor, nearly two blocks long, with a painted ceiling of clouds.
As for the park, it's named for William Cullen Bryant, a poet and longtime editor of the New York Evening Post, who campaigned for the creation of Central Park.
By the 1970s, Bryant Park was a notorious haven for drug dealers and was considered dangerous.
In the 1980s, a private nonprofit, the Bryant Park Restoration Corporation, led by Daniel Biederman, took over its management.
It was redesigned with open sightlines, movable chairs, and food kiosks, and reopened in 1992.
Its turnaround became a model for business improvement districts and public-private park management around the world.
Today, it hosts an ice rink in winter, outdoor movies in summer, and some of the best people watching in the city.
Before you leave, look at the black and gold tower on 40th Street, facing the park.
That's the American Radiator Building, completed in 1924 and designed by Raymond Hood.
It was built for the American Radiator Company, which made heating equipment, and the black brick and gold top were meant to evoke glowing coals.
Georgia O'Keeffe painted it at night.
It's now a hotel.
You're in Times Square, at the junction of Broadway and Seventh Avenue, between 42nd and 47th Streets.
Until 1904, this was Longacre Square, a district of carriage makers and horse stables.
Then the New York Times moved into a new tower at 42nd Street, the narrow building at the south end of the square, now called One Times Square.
The Times's publisher, Adolph Ochs, persuaded the city to rename the square after his newspaper.
The same year, the first subway line opened, with a station right here.
To celebrate the new building, the Times hosted a New Year's Eve celebration with fireworks on December thirty-first, 1904.
A few years later, when fireworks were banned, the paper lowered an illuminated ball from the building's flagpole at midnight.
The first ball drop was on New Year's Eve, 1907, and it's happened almost every year since.
The Times itself moved out of the tower in 1913, but the name stuck.
In 1928, the building installed a news ticker that ran headlines around the building in lights, the famous zipper.
By the 1920s, the area was the center of the American theater, with dozens of Broadway theaters on the side streets.
Electric advertising signs turned Broadway into the Great White Way.
Advertisers competed to create the most spectacular displays.
Look up at the giant screens around you.
Zoning rules actually require buildings in Times Square to have large, illuminated signs.
It's one of the only places in the world where flashy advertising is legally mandatory.
After World War Two, Times Square declined.
By the 1970s, 42nd Street was lined with pornographic theaters, peep shows, and drug dealers, and it became a national symbol of urban decay.
In the 1990s, the city and state launched an aggressive redevelopment.
A key moment came in 1997, when the Walt Disney Company restored the historic New Amsterdam Theatre on 42nd Street, signaling that big corporations were willing to invest here.
Within a few years, the area was transformed into a family-friendly district of chain stores, restaurants, and tourist attractions.
Some New Yorkers mourn the old grit; most are glad to be rid of it.
In 2009, under Mayor Michael Bloomberg and his transportation commissioner, Janette Sadik-Khan, the city closed parts of Broadway to cars and created pedestrian plazas.
The experiment was so popular it was made permanent.

At the north end of the square, look for the red glass steps, which sit atop the TKTS booth, where you can buy discounted same-day theater tickets, and the statue of Father Francis Duffy, the chaplain of the Fighting 69th regiment in World War One.
Behind him is a statue of George M. Cohan, the composer of Give My Regards to Broadway.
Walk west to Shubert Alley, a private pedestrian alley running between 44th and 45th Streets, just west of Broadway.
The alley is named for the Shubert brothers, Lee, Sam, and Jacob, three immigrants from Lithuania who grew up poor in Syracuse, New York, and built the largest theater empire in America.
At their peak, the Shuberts owned, operated, or booked a huge number of theaters across the country.
The Shubert Organization, headquartered in the Shubert Theatre building next to the alley, still owns more Broadway theaters than anyone else.
Shubert Alley was created as a fire exit for the theaters on either side.
It became a gathering place for actors, who would wait here hoping to be noticed by producers, since casting offices were nearby.
Today, the walls are covered with posters for current shows.
The theaters around you, on 44th, 45th, and nearby streets, are the heart of Broadway.
Broadway is technically not the street, but a designation for about forty professional theaters, each with at least five hundred seats, mostly located between 41st and 54th Streets.
Many date from the 1910s and 1920s, the golden age of theater construction.
The Shubert Theatre, next to the alley, opened in 1913, and was home to A Chorus Line for its fifteen-year run.
The Booth Theatre, on the other side, is named after Edwin Booth, the actor whose club you may have visited at Gramercy Park.
On West 44th Street, look for Sardi's, the restaurant famous for the caricatures of Broadway stars covering its walls.
It's been a gathering place for theater people since the 1920s, and for decades, opening night casts would gather there to wait for the reviews in the morning papers.
Broadway is a big business.
In a typical recent season, it has drawn more than twelve million attendees and grossed over a billion and a half dollars, with tourists making up the majority of the audience.

Shows are high-risk investments: most lose money, but a hit, like The Phantom of the Opera, which ran for thirty-five years at the Majestic Theatre on 44th Street, or The Lion King, can earn billions over its life.

If you have time, the stretch of West 44th and 45th Streets between Broadway and Eighth Avenue is the best place to see a cluster of historic theater facades, marquees, and stage doors, where crowds gather after shows to get autographs.
You're at Grand Central Terminal, at 42nd Street and Park Avenue.
Go inside, if you can, and stand in the Main Concourse.
The terminal was built by the New York Central Railroad, the Vanderbilt family's railroad empire.
The first Grand Central opened here in 1871.
In those days, steam locomotives ran down Park Avenue, through an open trench and a smoky tunnel.
In January 1902, two trains collided in the smoke-filled tunnel, killing seventeen people.
Public outrage led to a law banning steam locomotives in Manhattan.
The railroad's chief engineer, William Wilgus, came up with a brilliant plan.
He proposed electrifying the trains, and since electric trains don't produce smoke, the tracks could be put underground and covered over.
Then the railroad could sell the air rights above the tracks to developers.
The new terminal, with two levels of underground tracks, opened in 1913.
It was designed by the architects Reed and Stem and Warren and Wetmore.
The covered tracks became Park Avenue, and the blocks above them were developed into hotels, apartments, and office buildings, a district called Terminal City.
The sale of air rights helped pay for the whole project.
It was one of the great real estate deals in history.
Look up at the ceiling of the Main Concourse: a turquoise sky with gold constellations of the zodiac.
The constellations are painted backward, as if you're looking down at the sky from outside.
Some say it was a mistake; others say it's a view from the heavens.
Look also for a small dark patch near one corner.
During restoration in the 1990s, workers left one area uncleaned, to show how dark the ceiling had become, mostly from decades of tobacco smoke.
At the center of the concourse is the four-faced clock on top of the information booth.
Its faces are made of opal, and it's often said to be worth millions of dollars.
Grand Central's survival is a landmark story.
In 1963, the Pennsylvania Railroad demolished the original Penn Station, a magnificent Beaux-Arts building, to build Madison Square Garden.
The loss shocked the city and led to the creation of the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission in 1965.
In the late 1960s, Grand Central's owners planned to build an office tower on top of the terminal.
The city refused, and with support from Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and other prominent New Yorkers, the case went to the Supreme Court.
In 1978, in Penn Central Transportation Company versus New York City, the court upheld the city's right to protect landmarks, a decision that has shaped historic preservation across the country.
Downstairs, near the Oyster Bar, look for the Whispering Gallery, a low tiled archway where you can whisper into one corner and someone standing diagonally opposite can hear you clearly.
End your walk at Lexington Avenue and 42nd Street, looking up at the Chrysler Building, which many people consider the most beautiful skyscraper in the world.
It was built for Walter Chrysler, a former railroad mechanic who had founded the Chrysler Corporation in 1925, which quickly became one of the big three American automakers.
Chrysler paid for the building himself, rather than with company money, so that his children would inherit it.
The architect was William Van Alen.
The building was at the center of the great race for the sky in 1929 and 1930.
Van Alen's former partner, H. Craig Severance, was designing 40 Wall Street, and the two buildings were competing to be the tallest in the world.
When 40 Wall Street seemed to have won, Van Alen revealed his secret.
A steel spire, called the vertex, had been assembled in pieces inside the building's dome.
In October 1929, it was raised through the top and bolted into place in about ninety minutes.
The Chrysler Building rose to one thousand forty-six feet, the tallest in the world, and the first structure to exceed one thousand feet.
It held the title for less than a year, until the Empire State Building opened.
Look at the details.
The stainless steel crown has rows of triangular windows in a sunburst pattern.

Near the top, at the setbacks, are gleaming steel gargoyles shaped like eagle heads, and lower down, ornaments modeled on Chrysler radiator caps and hubcaps, along with a frieze of stylized car wheels.
It's a temple to the automobile.

If it's open, step into the lobby, which is clad in red Moroccan marble, with a ceiling mural by Edward Trumbull showing transportation and human endeavor, and elevator doors with elaborate wood inlays.
Before you go, look east along 42nd Street.
At 220 East 42nd Street is the Daily News Building, designed by Raymond Hood and completed in 1930, home of the tabloid New York Daily News, once the highest-circulation newspaper in America.
Its lobby has a giant rotating globe.
In the 1978 film Superman, the building appeared as the Daily Planet.
At the end of 42nd Street, along the East River, is the United Nations headquarters, built on land that once held slaughterhouses.
John D. Rockefeller Junior bought the land and donated it to the United Nations in 1946.
The Secretariat Building, completed in 1952, was among the first glass curtain wall skyscrapers in New York.
From railroads and department stores, to newspapers, cars, and the world's diplomats, the businesses that built Midtown are all written into its skyline.
This walk covers the stretch of Midtown that has long been the showroom of American wealth and corporate power: Fifth Avenue, Park Avenue, and 57th Street.
In the second half of the nineteenth century, as the rich moved north from Madison Square, Fifth Avenue between about 50th and 70th Streets became a canyon of mansions.
The Vanderbilts alone built a string of enormous houses along the avenue, each trying to outdo the others, in French château and Italian Renaissance styles.
This was the Gilded Age, the era of railroad, oil, and steel fortunes, and Fifth Avenue was its main street.
Within a few decades, the mansions were gone.
Rising property taxes, the income tax introduced in 1913, the cost of servants, and the relentless pressure of commerce made them impractical.
Families sold them to developers and moved into apartments on the Upper East Side.
Department stores and luxury retailers took over Fifth Avenue: Saks, Bergdorf Goodman, Tiffany, Cartier.
Office buildings rose around them.
Then came Rockefeller Center, built in the 1930s during the Great Depression, a city within a city that became the model for the modern mixed-use urban development.

After World War Two, Park Avenue, which had been lined with elegant apartment buildings, was transformed into a corridor of glass corporate headquarters, starting with Lever House and the Seagram Building, two of the most influential skyscrapers ever built.
In recent years, the newest form of wealth display has appeared along 57th Street: super-tall, super-thin residential towers for the global ultra-rich, known as Billionaires' Row.

As you walk, notice how each era expressed wealth differently: Gilded Age mansions with marble and ornament; the Art Deco optimism of Rockefeller Center; the cool, minimalist glass of mid-century corporate modernism; and the needle-thin towers of today.
Every one of them was built to impress you.
You're at Rockefeller Plaza, between Fifth and Sixth Avenues and 48th to 51st Streets, the heart of Rockefeller Center.
The story begins in 1928.
John D. Rockefeller Junior, the son of the Standard Oil founder, agreed to lease land here from Columbia University to build a new home for the Metropolitan Opera.
Then the stock market crashed in 1929, and the opera pulled out.
Rockefeller was stuck with a long-term lease on a large swath of Midtown real estate.
Rather than walk away, he decided to build a commercial development on his own, with his own money.
Construction began in 1930 and continued through the Depression, employing tens of thousands of workers when jobs were scarce.
The result, completed in the late 1930s, was fourteen Art Deco buildings, organized around plazas, gardens, and a private street, Rockefeller Plaza.
It was one of the first developments to combine offices, shops, restaurants, theaters, and public space in a coherent design, and it's been a model for urban developments around the world ever since.
The centerpiece is 30 Rockefeller Plaza, the tall, slender limestone tower.
It was originally the RCA Building, headquarters of the Radio Corporation of America, which owned NBC.
NBC has broadcast from here since 1933, and shows like Saturday Night Live and The Tonight Show have been produced inside.
The building was later renamed for General Electric, and then for Comcast, which now owns NBC.
During construction, in 1932, a photographer captured eleven ironworkers eating lunch on a steel beam high above the city, their legs dangling over the void.
The image, Lunch atop a Skyscraper, became one of the most famous photographs of the twentieth century.
It was taken on this building.
The center has a famous art controversy.
Rockefeller commissioned the Mexican muralist Diego Rivera to paint a mural in the lobby of the RCA Building.
Rivera, a communist, included a portrait of Vladimir Lenin.
Rockefeller asked him to remove it.
Rivera refused.
The mural was covered and, in 1934, destroyed.
Rivera later recreated it in Mexico City.
Look down into the sunken plaza, where the ice rink is in winter, and the gilded statue of Prometheus by Paul Manship, bringing fire to humanity.
The famous Christmas tree tradition began in 1931, when construction workers set up a small tree on the site.
It became official in 1933.
On Fifth Avenue, in front of the International Building, is the giant bronze statue of Atlas holding the heavens, by Lee Lawrie and Rene Chambellan.
And at Sixth Avenue and 50th Street is Radio City Music Hall, opened in 1932, the largest indoor theater in the world at the time and home of the Rockettes.
Across Fifth Avenue from Atlas is St. Patrick's Cathedral, the largest Gothic Revival Catholic cathedral in the United States.
When construction began in 1858, this site was far north of the city's center, and critics mocked the decision to build a cathedral out in the countryside.
They called it Hughes's Folly, after Archbishop John Hughes, who pushed the project forward.
Hughes was a formidable figure, an Irish immigrant nicknamed Dagger John because of the cross he drew next to his signature and because of his combative defense of Catholics against nativist attacks.
Building a grand cathedral on Fifth Avenue was a statement that Irish Catholics, despised by many Protestant New Yorkers, had arrived.
The project was funded by wealthy donors and by the small contributions of tens of thousands of working-class Irish immigrants.
Construction was interrupted by the Civil War, and the cathedral was finally dedicated in 1879.
Its twin spires, which rise about three hundred thirty feet, were added in 1888.
The architect was James Renwick Junior, who also designed Grace Church downtown and the Smithsonian Castle in Washington.
Inside, look for the great rose window, the bronze doors, and the Lady Chapel behind the altar.

Beneath the altar is a crypt where past archbishops of New York are buried, along with Pierre Toussaint, the formerly enslaved Haitian philanthropist you may have heard about at Old St. Patrick's on the Lower East Side, who is the only layperson buried there.
The cathedral underwent a major restoration in the 2010s that cleaned the marble exterior, which had been blackened by pollution, back to its bright white.
Notice the dialogue between the cathedral and Rockefeller Center across the street.
The Atlas statue faces the cathedral directly, holding up the heavens.
Whether that was meant as a symbol of human ambition facing faith, or simply a coincidence of planning, it's become one of the most photographed juxtapositions in New York.
Next to the cathedral, on Fifth Avenue between 49th and 50th Streets, is Saks Fifth Avenue, which opened its flagship here in 1924.
It was one of the first major department stores on upper Fifth Avenue, helping to cement the avenue's transformation from mansions to luxury retail.
Walk to West 53rd Street, between Fifth and Sixth Avenues.
Here you'll find the Museum of Modern Art.
MoMA was founded in 1929 by three wealthy women: Abby Aldrich Rockefeller, the wife of John D. Rockefeller Junior, and her friends Lillie P. Bliss and Mary Quinn Sullivan.
At the time, established museums like the Met were reluctant to collect contemporary art.
The founders wanted a museum dedicated to the art of their own time.
It opened nine days after the stock market crash, in rented rooms in an office building.
Its first director, Alfred Barr, was just twenty-seven years old.
His vision, that a museum should show modern painting alongside photography, film, industrial design, and architecture, was revolutionary.
The museum moved to 53rd Street in 1939, into a modernist building designed by Philip Goodwin and Edward Durell Stone.
It's been expanded many times since, most recently in 2004 by the Japanese architect Yoshio Taniguchi and in 2019 by Diller Scofidio and Renfro, the firm behind the High Line.
Its collection includes Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night, Pablo Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, Claude Monet's Water Lilies, Andy Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans, and much more.
Its design collection includes everything from a helicopter to the original emoji set.
Now walk east, to East 53rd Street between Fifth and Madison Avenues, and look for a small park with a waterfall.
This is Paley Park, a tiny vest-pocket park opened in 1967.
It was created by William S. Paley, the founder of CBS, in memory of his father, on the site of the famous Stork Club, a nightclub where celebrities and gossip columnists gathered in the mid-century.
Paley Park is only about forty-two by one hundred feet, but it's considered one of the most perfect small urban spaces in the world.
The twenty-foot waterfall at the back drowns out traffic noise.
Honey locust trees provide dappled shade.
Movable chairs let people sit wherever they like.

The urbanist William H. Whyte studied this park and others like it in the 1970s, filming how people used public spaces, and found that small, well-designed spaces with seating, water, food, and trees could attract heavy use.
His findings shaped the city's plaza rules and later the redesign of Bryant Park.
CBS's own headquarters, a dark granite tower nicknamed Black Rock, designed by Eero Saarinen and completed in 1965, stands a block west, at Sixth Avenue and 52nd Street.
You're on Park Avenue, around 52nd and 53rd Streets.
Remember that Park Avenue exists because the railroad tracks going into Grand Central were covered over.
In the 1910s and 20s, this stretch was lined with elegant apartment buildings.
After World War Two, corporations replaced them with glass towers.
Two buildings, across the avenue from each other, started that transformation.
On the west side, at 390 Park Avenue, look for a green glass tower that rises from a low horizontal base lifted on columns.
This is Lever House, completed in 1952.
It was designed by Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings and Merrill for the Lever Brothers company, the British soap maker that produced brands like Lifebuoy and Lux, and is now part of Unilever.
The company wanted a building that looked clean, like its products.

Lever House was among the first glass curtain-wall office buildings in New York, and it was revolutionary: instead of filling its lot, it left most of the ground open, with a courtyard and a slim tower.
Its glass was even cleaned by a gondola that moved along the facade, which was itself a marketing statement.
Across the avenue, at 375 Park Avenue, is the Seagram Building, completed in 1958.
It was the headquarters of Joseph E. Seagram and Sons, the Canadian whiskey distiller.
The founder's daughter, Phyllis Lambert, a young architecture student, persuaded her father to hire Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, the German modernist master.
Mies designed a dark bronze and glass tower set back from the street behind a granite plaza with two reflecting pools.
He used bronze I-beams on the exterior, purely for visual effect, to express the steel structure inside.
It was enormously expensive, and enormously influential.
The Seagram Building became the template for countless corporate towers around the world.
Its plaza inspired a change in the city's zoning law in 1961, which gave developers extra height if they provided public plazas.
Not all of those plazas turned out as well as Seagram's.
Inside the Seagram Building, the restaurant space designed by Philip Johnson housed the Four Seasons, where the power lunch is said to have been invented.
Now look south along Park Avenue, toward 47th Street, at the massive new tower at 270 Park Avenue.
This is the new global headquarters of JPMorgan Chase, completed in the mid-2020s.
To build it, the bank demolished the previous fifty-two-story tower on the site, the former Union Carbide Building, making it the tallest building ever intentionally demolished.
JPMorgan Chase's history, as you may have heard on the Financial District tour, includes J. P. Morgan's bank and Aaron Burr's Manhattan Company.
Its new tower is a sign that, for the biggest banks, Midtown, not Wall Street, is now the center of gravity.
Also on Park Avenue, at 49th Street, is the Waldorf Astoria, the Art Deco hotel that opened in 1931 after the old one was demolished for the Empire State Building.
For decades, it was where presidents stayed in New York.
You're at Fifth Avenue and 57th Street, the most famous luxury shopping intersection in America.
Imagine this corner in the 1890s.
On the west side of Fifth Avenue, from 57th to 58th Street, stood the largest private house ever built in New York City, the mansion of Cornelius Vanderbilt the Second, the grandson of the Commodore.
It was a French château with well over one hundred rooms, and it took up the whole block front.
Vanderbilt family mansions lined Fifth Avenue for blocks to the south.
This was the heart of the Gilded Age.
By 1926, the Vanderbilt mansion was demolished.
Its site became the department store Bergdorf Goodman, founded by Herman Bergdorf, a tailor, and Edwin Goodman, which moved here in 1928.
Bergdorf's is still one of the most exclusive department stores in the world.
The mansion's grand iron gates were saved, and today they stand at the entrance to the Conservatory Garden in Central Park.
On the southeast corner of 57th Street is Tiffany and Company's flagship store, which opened here in 1940.
Above the entrance, look for the statue of Atlas holding a clock, which was moved here from the company's earlier stores.
In the 1961 film Breakfast at Tiffany's, Audrey Hepburn ate a pastry while gazing into these windows.
The store underwent a major renovation in the early 2020s.
Walk back a few blocks south, to Fifth Avenue and 52nd Street, and look for an Italian Renaissance mansion of pale stone, home to the Cartier jewelry store.
Here's one of the best stories in New York real estate.
The mansion was built for Morton Plant, a railroad and steamship magnate.
By 1917, the neighborhood was going commercial, and Plant wanted out.
Meanwhile, Pierre Cartier, the French jeweler, wanted a Fifth Avenue store.
Plant's wife, Maisie, admired a double strand of natural pearls Cartier had.
At the time, natural pearls were extraordinarily valuable, before cultured pearls became widespread.
So they made a trade: the mansion, plus a small sum of cash, for the pearl necklace.
Cartier got its New York flagship, which it still occupies.
A few decades later, after cultured pearls had flooded the market, the necklace sold at auction for a small fraction of its former value.
The house turned out to be the better deal.
Up and down this stretch, flagship stores for luxury brands occupy some of the most expensive retail space in the world.
Upper Fifth Avenue's rents regularly rank among the highest anywhere.
You're at Grand Army Plaza, at Fifth Avenue and 59th Street, the southeast corner of Central Park.
The grand, château-style building facing the park is the Plaza Hotel.
It opened in 1907, designed by Henry Janeway Hardenbergh, who also designed the Dakota apartment building on the Upper West Side.
It was built to be the most luxurious hotel in the world, and the Vanderbilts and other wealthy families took up residence there.
The Plaza has played a starring role in countless stories.
Kay Thompson's Eloise books, published starting in 1955, featured a mischievous six-year-old girl who lives at the Plaza; a portrait of Eloise hangs in the hotel.
In 1964, the Beatles stayed here on their first visit to America.
In 1966, the writer Truman Capote held his Black and White Ball in the hotel's ballroom, a masked party considered by many to be the social event of the century.
The Plaza has a place in financial history too.

In September 1985, finance ministers and central bankers from the United States, Japan, West Germany, France, and the United Kingdom met at the Plaza and agreed to coordinate interventions in currency markets to bring down the value of the US dollar, which had risen sharply.
The agreement, the Plaza Accord, worked.
The dollar fell dramatically over the following two years.
Many economists link the resulting rise of the Japanese yen to Japan's asset bubble in the late 1980s and its collapse into a long stagnation.
In the plaza in front of the hotel is the Pulitzer Fountain, with a statue of Pomona, the Roman goddess of abundance, funded by a bequest from the newspaper publisher Joseph Pulitzer.
North of it, at the park's corner, is a gleaming gilded statue of General William Tecumseh Sherman on horseback, led by a winged figure of Victory, by Augustus Saint-Gaudens, completed in 1903.
It's considered one of the finest equestrian statues in America.
Across Fifth Avenue is the General Motors Building, a white marble tower completed in 1968.
In front of it is a glass cube, the entrance to Apple's Fifth Avenue store, opened in 2006.
The store is underground, open around the clock, and the cube has become one of the most photographed retail designs in the world.
For decades, the GM Building was also home to the toy store FAO Schwarz, founded in 1862 and famous for the giant floor piano played in the 1988 film Big.
The store closed here in 2015 and has since reopened at Rockefeller Center.
End your walk at Seventh Avenue and 57th Street, outside Carnegie Hall.

Carnegie Hall was built by Andrew Carnegie, the Scottish-born steel magnate who was one of the richest men in history, and who later gave away most of his fortune, funding more than two thousand five hundred public libraries around the world.
He built the hall at the urging of a young conductor, Walter Damrosch, and his wife Louise, who was a member of the Oratorio Society.
It opened in 1891, with the Russian composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky conducting on opening night.
Its acoustics are considered among the best in the world.
Everyone from Gustav Mahler to Benny Goodman, Judy Garland, and the Beatles has performed here.
In the 1950s, Carnegie Hall faced demolition after the New York Philharmonic decided to move to the new Lincoln Center.
The violinist Isaac Stern led a campaign to save it, and in 1960, the city bought it.
The main auditorium is now named for Stern.
There's an old joke: a tourist stops a musician on 57th Street and asks, How do you get to Carnegie Hall?
The musician answers, Practice, practice, practice.
Now look up and around you, along 57th Street.
You're on Billionaires' Row, a cluster of super-tall, super-slender luxury residential towers built since the 2010s, mostly along 57th Street at the south edge of Central Park.
They include One57, Central Park Tower, the tallest residential building in the world, and, just east of here, 111 West 57th Street, often called the Steinway Tower.
It's one of the most slender skyscrapers in the world, with a width-to-height ratio of about one to twenty-four.

It incorporates the historic Steinway Hall, built in 1925 as the showroom of Steinway and Sons, the piano company founded by the German immigrant Henry Steinway in 1853, whose pianos are used by most of the world's concert pianists.

These towers were made possible by new engineering techniques and by developers buying up the unused air rights of neighboring buildings, allowing them to build much taller than would otherwise be allowed.
Their apartments have sold for tens of millions of dollars, and some for over one hundred million.
Critics point out that many are owned by international buyers as investments and sit empty much of the year, and that the towers cast long shadows across Central Park.

It's a fitting place to end: a nineteenth-century concert hall built by a steel baron, a twentieth-century piano showroom, and twenty-first-century towers for the global rich, side by side on the same block.
On 57th Street, wealth keeps finding new ways to show itself.
Central Park looks natural.
It isn't.
Almost every rock outcrop, lake, meadow, and hill you see was planned, sculpted, and planted by people.
It's one of the largest and most ambitious works of landscape design ever made, and it's been copied in cities all over the world.
By the 1840s, New York was growing fast and had almost no public green space.
The 1811 grid plan had allotted very little land to parks, on the theory that the rivers on either side would give residents fresh air.
Wealthy New Yorkers, who had seen the great public parks of London and Paris, began to argue that a world-class city needed a great park.
The poet and editor William Cullen Bryant and the landscape designer Andrew Jackson Downing were among the leading advocates.

In 1853, the state legislature authorized the city to acquire the land, and the park was eventually expanded to its current size of about eight hundred forty acres, stretching from 59th Street to 110th Street, and from Fifth Avenue to Central Park West.
The land wasn't empty.

It was rocky, swampy, and considered poor for building, but it was home to about sixteen hundred people, including Irish and German immigrants who raised pigs and goats, and a community of African American property owners called Seneca Village.
All were removed through eminent domain.
You'll hear more about Seneca Village on the northern Central Park tour.
In 1857, the park's commissioners held a design competition.

The winning entry, called the Greensward Plan, came from two men: Frederick Law Olmsted, a journalist, farmer, and failed businessman who had never designed a park, and Calvert Vaux, a young English-born architect.
Their vision was a pastoral escape from the city, a sequence of carefully composed scenes, meadows, woods, water, and rocky outcrops, meant to feel like an unspoiled landscape.
They believed the park could improve the health and spirit of all New Yorkers, rich and poor alike, and offer a democratic space where all classes could mix.
Building it was a colossal undertaking.

Over roughly fifteen years, thousands of workers blasted rock with more gunpowder than was used at the Battle of Gettysburg, according to a frequently repeated claim, moved millions of cubic yards of earth and stone, planted hundreds of thousands of trees and shrubs, and built bridges, arches, and buildings.
One of the cleverest features was the design for traffic.
Olmsted and Vaux sunk four transverse roads below the level of the park, so that crosstown traffic would pass through without disturbing the landscape.
And they separated carriage drives, bridle paths, and footpaths, using bridges and arches so they rarely crossed.
The park declined badly in the mid-twentieth century, and by the 1970s it was covered in graffiti, its lawns were dust bowls, and many considered it dangerous.
In 1980, the Central Park Conservancy, a private nonprofit, was founded to restore it, and it now manages the park in partnership with the city.
This tour covers the southern half, the more formal and heavily visited part of the park.
You're at the southeast corner of Central Park, near Fifth Avenue and 60th Street, beside the body of water called the Pond.
Olmsted and Vaux designed the park's entrances carefully.
They wanted visitors to leave the city behind within a few steps.
Here, the path descends from the busy street to the water's edge, and the noise of the city begins to fade.
Notice how the Pond curves out of sight, so you can't see its full extent.
This was a classic technique of English landscape design: hide the edges, and the space feels larger and more mysterious.
Look for the arched stone bridge over the northern neck of the Pond.
That's Gapstow Bridge.
The current stone bridge dates from 1896, replacing an earlier, more ornate wooden and iron bridge by Jacob Wrey Mould.

It's one of the most photographed spots in the park, because of the view south, with the towers of Midtown, including the Plaza Hotel and the needle-thin towers of Billionaires' Row, rising above the trees.
It's a perfect demonstration of the park's central contrast: wild nature, framed by the city.
On the peninsula jutting into the Pond is the Hallett Nature Sanctuary, a small woodland that was closed to the public for decades to serve as a bird sanctuary.
It's now open on a limited schedule.
It's named after George Hallett, an amateur birder and conservationist.
In winter, the Pond and the rink beyond it fill with skaters.
In the nineteenth century, ice skating was hugely popular in the park, and it was one of the first activities that brought huge crowds to Central Park, even before construction was complete.
Skating was also one of the few activities in Victorian New York where men and women could socialize relatively freely.
The park was the first major landscaped public park in America, and when it opened, there was a lot of debate about how people should behave in it.
The park's early rules were strict: no walking on the grass in many areas, no picnics, no ball playing for adults, and no commercial vehicles.
Over time, as the park became more democratic, those rules loosened.
Walk north along the eastern side of the park, near 64th Street and Fifth Avenue.
The brick building with the corner towers that looks like a fortress is the Arsenal.
It was built between 1847 and 1851, before the park existed, as a storehouse for New York State's munitions.
It's one of only two buildings in the park that predate the park itself.

Later, it served as a museum, a weather station, and a police precinct, and the American Museum of Natural History got its start here in the 1870s, before its building on the Upper West Side was completed.
Today, it's the headquarters of the city's Parks Department.
If you peek in, the lobby has murals from the 1930s, painted as part of a Depression-era federal arts program.
The Central Park Zoo, next to the Arsenal, began informally in the 1860s, when New Yorkers started donating animals to the park: a bear, a swan, monkeys, and others.
They were kept around the Arsenal in what became known as the menagerie.
In 1934, Robert Moses built a formal zoo with brick buildings and cages.
By the 1980s, it was outdated, and the Wildlife Conservation Society, which runs the Bronx Zoo, redesigned it with naturalistic habitats.
It reopened in 1988.
Look for the sea lion pool in the center, and the penguins and snow leopards.

At the north end of the zoo, look up at the Delacorte Musical Clock, an archway topped by a clock and bronze animals: a bear with a tambourine, a hippo with a violin, a goat with pipes, a kangaroo with horns, and others.
Every half hour, they rotate around the clock while it plays nursery rhymes.
The clock was a gift from the publisher George Delacorte, who founded Dell Publishing, and installed in 1965.
Delacorte, a philanthropist, also funded the Delacorte Theater, home of Shakespeare in the Park, and the Alice in Wonderland sculpture near the Conservatory Water.
Nearby is the Tisch Children's Zoo.
And a little to the north is the Conservatory Water, where people race model sailboats on summer weekends, a scene immortalized in the children's book Stuart Little by E. B. White.
Walk west into the park to a small Gothic building with a steep roof and a wooden porch with ornate gingerbread trim.
This is the Dairy, built in 1870 and designed by Calvert Vaux.
The Dairy was part of Olmsted and Vaux's vision for the Children's District, the southern part of the park that was meant to be especially for families.
It served a practical purpose.
In the mid-nineteenth century, milk in New York was dangerous.
Much of it came from cows kept in filthy city stables next to breweries and fed on distillery waste, called swill.
Swill milk was blamed for the deaths of thousands of children every year.
At the Dairy, families could buy fresh, safe milk from cows grazing in the country.
There were even cows grazing on the lawn nearby.
Today the Dairy serves as a visitor center and gift shop.
A short walk west is the Carousel, one of the largest carousels in the United States.
There's been a carousel in this spot since 1871.
The first one was powered by a horse or mule walking in circles in a pit underneath it.

The current carousel, with its colorful hand-carved horses, was built in 1908 by the carvers Solomon Stein and Harry Goldstein, Russian Jewish immigrants who were among the master carvers of Coney Island-style carousels.
It originally stood at an amusement park in Coney Island and was moved here in 1951 after an earlier carousel burned.
Nearby, look for the Chess and Checkers House, a small building where you can borrow game pieces and play at outdoor tables.
Chess hustlers have long been a fixture in New York parks.
And down the hill to the south is the Wollman Rink, which opened in 1950 with money from the philanthropist Kate Wollman.
In winter it's one of the most famous skating rinks in the world, with the skyline of Central Park South rising above it.
You're at the edge of Sheep Meadow, a vast, open lawn of about fifteen acres between roughly 66th and 69th Streets.
On a sunny weekend, it's covered with sunbathers, picnickers, and people reading.
It's a designated quiet zone: no ball games, no loud music, no dogs.
Olmsted and Vaux designed this meadow as a large open pastoral space, something rare and precious in a dense city.
They wanted people to experience the expansiveness of rolling countryside, with a long view toward the trees and the sky.
The original plan actually called it the Parade Ground, but Olmsted resisted using it for military drills.
And it really did have sheep.
From the 1860s to 1934, a flock of purebred sheep grazed here, tended by a shepherd who lived in a building called the Sheepfold.
The sheep kept the grass trimmed and added to the pastoral illusion.
Twice a day, the shepherd would stop traffic on the West Drive to lead the flock across.
In 1934, Robert Moses removed the sheep, sending them to Prospect Park in Brooklyn, and converted the Sheepfold into a restaurant.
That restaurant is Tavern on the Green, at the western edge of the park near 67th Street.
In the 1960s and 70s, Sheep Meadow became a gathering place for the counterculture, with Be-Ins, protests against the Vietnam War, and concerts.
Heavy use turned it into a dust bowl.

In 1980, it was one of the first major restoration projects of the new Central Park Conservancy, which reseeded it and introduced rules to protect it, including closing it in winter and when the ground is wet.
Look south, over the lawn, at the skyline of Central Park South and Billionaires' Row.
The tall, thin towers you see were designed to exploit this view.
It's often said that the view of Central Park is the most valuable view in real estate.
You're at the southern end of the Mall, the wide, straight promenade lined with towering elm trees that runs from about 66th to 72nd Streets.
The Mall is the only formal, straight-line feature in Olmsted and Vaux's design.
Everything else in the park curves and meanders.
But they believed that a great urban park needed one grand promenade, a place where people of all classes could stroll, see and be seen.
In the nineteenth century, it was the most fashionable place in the park, where people paraded in their finest clothes on Sunday afternoons.
Look up at the trees.
These are American elms, and the Mall has one of the largest and finest remaining stands of American elms in North America.
Elms were once the most common street tree in America, until Dutch elm disease, a fungus spread by beetles, killed most of them in the twentieth century.
Central Park's elms survived, thanks partly to the park's relative isolation and careful monitoring by the Conservancy.
Their branches arch overhead like the vaulted ceiling of a cathedral.
At the southern end of the Mall, look for the statues of writers.
This section is called the Literary Walk.
You'll find William Shakespeare, the Scottish poets Robert Burns and Sir Walter Scott, and the American poet Fitz-Greene Halleck.
There's also a statue of Christopher Columbus.
Olmsted and Vaux didn't want statues in their park, which they saw as a landscape, not a museum.
But public pressure to honor famous figures was intense, and statues were installed anyway, mostly here in the southern part of the park.
At the northern end of the Mall, look for the Naumburg Bandshell, a limestone bandshell built in 1923, a gift of the banker Elkan Naumburg.
Free concerts have been held here for a century, and the area in front of it was the site of political rallies and the funerals of famous figures.
Nearby, on summer weekends, you'll often find roller skaters dancing to music, a tradition that dates back to the 1970s.
Before you leave, notice the people around you.
The Mall still does what its designers intended: everyone is here, from tourists and joggers to musicians, families, and old men on benches.
At the northern end of the Mall, walk down the grand staircase, or through the arcade beneath the road, to Bethesda Terrace.
Look up as you pass through the arcade.
The ceiling is covered in about sixteen thousand ornate encaustic tiles made by the English company Minton.
They were designed by Jacob Wrey Mould, Vaux's collaborator, who also designed much of the decorative carving on the terrace.
After decades of neglect, the tiles were removed, stored, and restored, and reinstalled in 2007.
It's one of the most beautiful spaces in the park, and the acoustics make it a favorite spot for musicians.
On the terrace, look closely at the stone carvings on the staircases.
They depict birds, plants, and animals representing the seasons and times of day.
At the center of the terrace is the Bethesda Fountain, topped by a bronze statue called the Angel of the Waters, by the sculptor Emma Stebbins.
Unveiled in 1873, it was the first public sculpture in New York City commissioned from a woman.
The angel refers to the Gospel of John, in which an angel stirs the waters of the Pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem, giving them healing powers.
The symbolism had a local meaning: the fountain celebrated the Croton Aqueduct, which in 1842 had brought clean water to New York for the first time, dramatically reducing diseases like cholera.
Pure water, in other words, was New York's healing angel.
There's another layer.
Emma Stebbins was in a long-term relationship with the actress Charlotte Cushman, and the fountain has become meaningful to the LGBTQ community.
It appears prominently in Tony Kushner's play Angels in America, which ends at this fountain.
Bethesda Terrace was designed as the heart of the park, the place where the formal Mall meets the wild landscape.
Stand at the fountain and look north across the Lake toward the Ramble's woods, and you'll see the composition Olmsted and Vaux intended: the architecture gives way to nature.
In the 1970s, the fountain was dry, covered in graffiti, and a center of drug dealing.
It was among the first places the Conservancy restored, and it's now one of the most beloved spots in the city.
Walk west along the Lake to Bow Bridge, the graceful cast iron bridge arching across the water.
Completed in 1862, Bow Bridge was designed by Calvert Vaux and Jacob Wrey Mould.
Its name comes from its shape, like the curve of an archer's bow.
It's about sixty feet long, with a decorative railing of interlocking circles and planters.
It's one of the oldest cast iron bridges in America, and probably the most romantic spot in the park.
It has appeared in many films, and countless marriage proposals have happened on it.
The bridge connects Cherry Hill and the Bethesda area to the Ramble, the wild woodland on the north shore of the Lake.
That contrast is deliberate.
Crossing Bow Bridge, you move from the formal, social part of the park to the wild, solitary part.
The Lake itself is entirely artificial, created from a swamp.
It covers about twenty acres.
In the nineteenth century, it was the main skating spot in the park, and in winter, tens of thousands of skaters would flock here.
When the ice was thick enough to be safe, the park raised a red ball on a flagpole, and streetcars would display a similar signal, letting New Yorkers across the city know that skating was open.
The Lake is no longer used for skating, now that there are rinks.
In summer, you can rent rowboats at the Loeb Boathouse, on the east side of the Lake, where there's also a restaurant.
Rowing on the Lake has been a popular activity since the 1860s.
In the nineteenth century, the park also had gondolas, and even a gondolier imported from Venice.
Look around at the trees and the skyline beyond.
From the middle of the bridge, the towers of the Upper West Side, including the twin-towered San Remo and the Dakota, rise above the trees, perfectly framed by the park's landscape.
Just west of the bridge is Cherry Hill, a raised plaza with a small fountain.
Originally it was a turnaround for carriages, and the fountain was a watering trough for horses.
End your walk at Strawberry Fields, a teardrop-shaped garden on the western edge of the park, near West 72nd Street.
This is a memorial to John Lennon.
On the evening of December eighth, 1980, Lennon was shot and killed outside the Dakota, the apartment building where he lived with Yoko Ono, just across Central Park West from here.
He was forty years old.
The killing devastated fans around the world, and on the following Sunday, hundreds of thousands of people gathered in Central Park for ten minutes of silence.
Yoko Ono, who continued to live at the Dakota, worked with the city to create a memorial in the park.
Strawberry Fields, named after the Beatles song Strawberry Fields Forever, was dedicated in 1985, on what would have been Lennon's forty-fifth birthday.
It was designed by the landscape architect Bruce Kelly.
Ono invited countries around the world to contribute plants, and many did.
At the center of the garden, look for the black and white mosaic with a single word: Imagine.
The mosaic was a gift from the city of Naples, Italy, and it's modeled on ancient Roman mosaics.
On any given day, you'll find flowers left on it, often arranged into a peace sign, and musicians playing Beatles songs.
On December eighth and on Lennon's birthday, October ninth, crowds gather here to sing.
The area is designated a quiet zone, meant for contemplation, though it's often busy with visitors.
Look across the street at the Dakota, the dark, gabled building with its own fortress-like entrance.
You'll hear more about it on the Upper West Side tour.
It's one of the most famous apartment buildings in the world.
This is a good place to reflect on the park as a whole.
Olmsted and Vaux designed Central Park as a place of escape and renewal.
More than a century later, it's become something they couldn't have foreseen: the city's collective memory, a place where New Yorkers come to celebrate, protest, mourn, and remember.
The northern two-thirds of Central Park are quieter, wilder, and less visited than the southern end, and many New Yorkers consider them the best part of the park.
Olmsted and Vaux designed the park as a sequence of moods.
The south end, near the city's busiest streets, has the more formal and social features: the Mall, the Dairy, the Carousel, the zoo.
As you move north, the landscape becomes more rugged and more pastoral.
The Ramble, north of the Lake, is a dense, winding woodland.
Above it, at Vista Rock, Belvedere Castle overlooks the park.
Beyond that are the great open lawns and the Reservoir.
And in the far north, above 100th Street, the North Woods were designed to evoke the Adirondack Mountains, with a ravine, a stream, and waterfalls.
The northern section also holds the park's deepest history.

During the Revolutionary War, British and Hessian troops built fortifications on the high ground near the northern end, and during the War of 1812, Americans built a blockhouse there that still stands, the oldest structure in the park.

And on the west side, between about 82nd and 89th Streets, there once stood Seneca Village, a community of African American property owners, along with Irish and German immigrants, that was destroyed to build the park.
The north end of the park was also slower to be completed, and for much of the twentieth century it was less maintained and less safe than the south end.
In the 1970s and 80s, much of it was overgrown and neglected.
The restoration of the north end by the Central Park Conservancy, beginning in the 1980s and continuing to this day, has been one of its biggest achievements.
Projects completed in recent years include a rebuilt Lasker Rink and pool area near the Harlem Meer, reconnecting the park's landscape to the water.
This tour starts in the Ramble, just north of the Lake, and ends at the Conservatory Garden on Fifth Avenue at 105th Street.
It's a long walk, a little over two miles if you take a direct path, so feel free to take it in pieces.
You're in the Ramble, about thirty-six acres of woodland just north of the Lake, roughly between 73rd and 79th Streets.
Olmsted called it a wild garden.
It was designed to feel like a natural forest, with winding paths, rocky outcrops, a small stream called the Gill, and dense trees and shrubs.
But it's as carefully designed as any part of the park.
The stream is artificial and fed by city water.
The rocks were placed.
The paths were laid out to disorient you, so that you lose your sense of the city around you.
It's very easy to get lost in the Ramble, and that's exactly the point.
The Ramble is one of the best birding spots in North America.
Central Park sits on the Atlantic Flyway, a major migration route for birds traveling between South and Central America and Canada.
For migrating birds flying over a vast expanse of concrete, Central Park looks like an oasis, and they drop in to rest and feed.
More than two hundred species of birds have been recorded in the park.
In the spring and fall migration seasons, especially May, the Ramble fills with warblers, thrushes, tanagers, and orioles, and with birders carrying binoculars.
Look for small feeders near the Azalea Pond in winter.
The park's most famous birds, though, have lived in the surrounding city.

In the 1990s, a red-tailed hawk nicknamed Pale Male built a nest on the facade of a luxury apartment building on Fifth Avenue, overlooking the park, and he and his mates raised chicks there for years.
When the building's co-op board removed the nest in 2004, birders protested, and the nest was eventually allowed to be rebuilt.
