More recently, a Eurasian eagle-owl named Flaco, who escaped from the Central Park Zoo in 2023, became a city celebrity during the year he lived free in the park and around Manhattan.
In the twentieth century, the Ramble also became known as a gathering place for gay men, who found privacy in its winding paths during an era when gay life was largely hidden.
It's part of the park's history that is now openly acknowledged.
Climb up to Belvedere Castle, the small stone castle perched on Vista Rock, the second highest natural point in the park.
Calvert Vaux and Jacob Wrey Mould designed it, and it was completed in 1869.
It's a folly, an ornamental building with no real defensive purpose, a fantasy castle designed to be seen from a distance as a romantic focal point.
The name Belvedere means beautiful view in Italian, and from the castle's terraces, you get one of the best views in the park, over Turtle Pond, the Great Lawn, and the surrounding skyline.
Originally, the castle had open windows and no doors.
It was meant as a lookout, not a building.
In 1919, the United States Weather Bureau set up a station here, and the castle was enclosed.
Today, automated instruments here and nearby measure the official weather for Central Park, which is often cited in weather reports as the weather for New York City.
When you hear on the news that Central Park got six inches of snow, those measurements come from instruments here and nearby.
By the 1970s, the castle had been vandalized and was in ruins.
It was restored in the 1980s, and again in 2019.
It now houses a visitor center with nature exhibits for children.
Below the castle is Turtle Pond, which, as its name suggests, is home to many turtles, mostly red-eared sliders, many of them abandoned pets.
Look for them basking on rocks and logs on sunny days.
The pond is what's left of the old Lower Reservoir, which was drained in the 1930s.
West of the pond is the Delacorte Theater, the open-air amphitheater that has been home to Shakespeare in the Park since 1962.
The producer Joseph Papp began staging free Shakespeare in the 1950s, and fought Robert Moses, who wanted to charge admission.
Papp won, and the theater was built with funding from George Delacorte.
Performances are still free, and people line up for hours, sometimes overnight, for tickets.
Stars like Meryl Streep, Al Pacino, and Denzel Washington have performed here.
Next to the theater is the Shakespeare Garden, planted with flowers and plants mentioned in Shakespeare's plays and poems.
North of the castle and Turtle Pond is the Great Lawn, a vast oval field of about fifty-five acres, with baseball diamonds and broad lawns.
It wasn't originally a lawn at all.

In Olmsted and Vaux's plan, this space was occupied by the Lower Reservoir, a rectangular reservoir built in the 1840s as part of the Croton water system, which predated the park and was incorporated into it.
By the 1930s, the reservoir was no longer needed and was drained.
While it sat empty during the Great Depression, homeless New Yorkers built a shantytown in the empty reservoir bed.
They called it Hooverville, or Hoover Valley, after President Herbert Hoover, whom they blamed for the Depression.
Shacks were made of scrap wood, cardboard, and tin, and some residents, unemployed bricklayers and carpenters, built surprisingly substantial structures.
Hoovervilles sprang up all over the country, but this one, in the middle of the richest city in America, was a powerful symbol.
The camp was cleared in 1933, and the reservoir bed was filled in to create the Great Lawn.
Since then, the Great Lawn has been the site of some of the largest gatherings in American history.
In September 1981, Simon and Garfunkel reunited for a free concert here, drawing about half a million people.
In June 1982, about a million people gathered here for a rally against nuclear weapons, one of the largest political demonstrations in American history.
Pope John Paul the Second celebrated mass here in 1995, and in 1997, Garth Brooks drew an enormous crowd for a free concert.
All those crowds took a toll.
By the 1990s, the Great Lawn was a dust bowl.
The Conservancy rebuilt it in the late 1990s with new drainage, irrigation, and soil, and now closes it during wet weather and in winter to protect the grass.
Big concerts are mostly gone, but the New York Philharmonic and the Metropolitan Opera still hold free summer performances here.
Look around at the skyline framing the lawn: the towers of Fifth Avenue to the east, and Central Park West to the west, rise just above the trees, like walls around a giant room.

On a small hill just east of the Great Lawn, behind the Metropolitan Museum of Art, stands the oldest man-made object in Central Park, and one of the oldest outdoor monuments anywhere in the Americas: a granite obelisk nicknamed Cleopatra's Needle.
It has nothing to do with Cleopatra.
It was carved around 1450 BC, more than a thousand years before Cleopatra's time, for the Egyptian pharaoh Thutmose the Third, and erected at the temple city of Heliopolis.
Look for the hieroglyphics carved on its sides, though they're badly weathered on some faces.
Around 12 BC, the Romans moved it to Alexandria, where it stood outside a temple built by Cleopatra in honor of Julius Caesar, or Mark Antony, depending on the source.
That's how it got its nickname.
In the 1870s, the ruler of Egypt, Khedive Ismail Pasha, offered the obelisk to the United States as a gift, hoping to win friendship and support.
A similar obelisk had gone to London.
The cost of moving it, more than one hundred thousand dollars, was paid by William Henry Vanderbilt, the son of the Commodore.
A Navy officer named Henry Gorringe engineered the move.

The obelisk, about seventy feet tall and weighing over two hundred tons, was lowered, loaded into the hold of a steamship through a hole cut in its hull, shipped across the Atlantic, floated to the Hudson River, and hauled across Manhattan on a special railway over several months.
It was erected here in January 1881, with a Masonic ceremony attended by thousands.
New York's climate, with its freeze-thaw cycles and air pollution, has been much harder on the stone than three thousand years in Egypt.
Some of the hieroglyphics have eroded significantly since it arrived.
Look at the base, at the corners.
You'll see bronze crabs.
They're replicas of crabs the Romans placed under the obelisk to support it when they moved it to Alexandria.
The originals are in the Met.
Speaking of which, the massive building next to you is the back of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
Look for the glass wall of the Sackler Wing.

Inside, visible through the glass, is the Temple of Dendur, an Egyptian temple built around 15 BC, given to the United States by Egypt in the 1960s, in gratitude for American help in saving monuments threatened by the Aswan High Dam.
So here, two ancient Egyptian monuments face each other across a park in Manhattan.
Walk west across the park to the area near West 85th Street, near Central Park West.
Here, between roughly 82nd and 89th Streets, stood Seneca Village.
In 1825, a young African American shoeshiner named Andrew Williams bought three lots of land here from a white landowner named John Whitehead.
Other Black New Yorkers followed, buying lots of their own.
At that time, slavery had not yet been fully abolished in New York State; final emancipation came in 1827.
Seneca Village was one of the first communities of African American property owners in New York.
Owning property mattered for another reason.
In 1821, New York State had changed its voting laws, eliminating property requirements for white men, but requiring Black men to own at least two hundred and fifty dollars in property to vote.
In Seneca Village, many Black residents met that threshold.
Property ownership was a path to political rights.
By the 1850s, Seneca Village had about two hundred twenty-five residents, mostly African American, along with Irish and German immigrants.
It had three churches, including an African Methodist Episcopal Zion church, a school, and cemeteries.
Residents worked as laborers, servants, cooks, and in various trades.
It was a stable, settled community, far from the crowded neighborhoods downtown.
In 1857, the city took the land by eminent domain to build Central Park.
Residents were compensated, though many contested the amounts as inadequate.
The village was destroyed.
Newspapers of the time sometimes described the area's residents dismissively, calling their homes shanties, which helped justify the removal.
Where the residents went is largely unknown.
For more than a century, Seneca Village was mostly forgotten.

In the 1990s, historians began to recover its story, and in 2011, archaeologists excavated the site, finding foundations of houses and thousands of artifacts, including household items like ceramics, a toothbrush, and a child's shoe.
In recent years, the Conservancy has installed signs and a display here explaining the history.
As you stand here, look at the landscape around you: the gentle slope, the rocks, the playground nearby.
It's a reminder that the park's pastoral beauty was built on top of a real community, with real homes and families.
Climb to the Reservoir, the vast body of water covering much of the park between 86th and 96th Streets.
Officially, it's the Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis Reservoir.
It was built between 1858 and 1862, as part of the Croton water system, to hold water from the Croton Aqueduct.
It covers about one hundred six acres, and holds about a billion gallons of water.
Olmsted and Vaux had to design the park around it, and its huge size is one reason the park is so narrow in places.
For more than a century, it was part of the city's water supply.
In 1993, it was decommissioned, after a newer system of underground water tunnels made it obsolete.
The water you see today is no longer for drinking.
Running around it is a track of about one point six miles, one of the most famous running paths in the world.
Joggers have used it since the jogging craze of the 1970s, and on a nice morning, it's packed with runners.
Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, who lived on Fifth Avenue facing the park, was a regular jogger here, and after her death in 1994, the reservoir was renamed in her honor.
She was also a passionate advocate for the city's landmarks and was instrumental in saving Grand Central Terminal.

Look around: the view across the water is one of the most spectacular in the city, especially at sunrise or sunset, with the skylines of the Upper East and Upper West Sides on either side, and Midtown's towers to the south.
The open water also attracts birds, especially in winter, when ducks, geese, gulls, and grebes gather here.
Look for the old gatehouses on the north and south ends of the Reservoir.
These stone buildings housed the machinery that controlled the flow of water.
Along the reservoir's edges, notice the beautiful iron fences.
They were replaced in the 2000s with replicas of the original 1920s designs.
North of the Reservoir lies the North Meadow, a large area with baseball and soccer fields, and the Central Park Tennis Center, where New Yorkers have played tennis for decades.
Walk to the northern end of the park, into the North Woods, around 102nd to 106th Streets on the west side.
Olmsted and Vaux designed this area to evoke the Adirondack Mountains of upstate New York.
It's the most rugged part of the park, with steep slopes, rocky outcrops, and dense woods.
Through it runs the Loch, Scottish for lake, a stream that flows through a ravine, over small waterfalls, into the Harlem Meer.
The stream is artificial; its water comes from the city supply.
But the effect is strikingly real.
Standing in the ravine, it's easy to forget you're in Manhattan.
Look for the stone arches that carry paths and roads over the ravine.
The Glen Span Arch, at the western entrance to the ravine, is a rustic stone arch.
And the Huddlestone Arch, near the east end, is made of huge, rough boulders, some weighing many tons, held together only by gravity, without any mortar.
Now climb to the top of the rocky hill at the northwest corner of the North Woods, near 109th Street.
Here you'll find the Blockhouse, a small stone fort and the oldest structure in Central Park.
It was built in 1814, during the War of 1812.
The British had burned Washington, D.C., that August, and New Yorkers feared a British invasion from the north, by way of the Harlem River.
Volunteers built a line of fortifications across upper Manhattan, including this blockhouse, on high ground overlooking the approaches to the city.
The British never came.
The blockhouse never saw combat.
Olmsted and Vaux kept it as a picturesque ruin.
Today it's an empty stone shell, but its walls and gun ports are still visible.
This area also saw action in the Revolutionary War.
In 1776, after the Battle of Brooklyn, George Washington's army retreated north through Manhattan.
The British later built fortifications in this area, near a tavern called McGown's Pass Tavern, which stood on a hill near the east side of the park, overlooking the old Post Road.
The steep ridge here made it a strategic chokepoint.
End your walk on the east side of the park, at the Harlem Meer and the Conservatory Garden.
The Harlem Meer is an eleven-acre lake in the park's northeast corner.
Meer is the Dutch word for lake, a nod to the Dutch village of Haarlem that stood nearby in the colonial era.
The Meer was dredged and restored in the 1990s and is now stocked with fish for catch-and-release fishing.
On its north shore is the Dana Discovery Center, a visitor center.
On the south side, look for the newly rebuilt pool and rink complex, which has reopened the shoreline to the public.
Now walk to Fifth Avenue at about 105th Street, and look for an ornate wrought iron gate.

These are the Vanderbilt Gates, which once stood at the entrance to the Cornelius Vanderbilt the Second mansion on Fifth Avenue at 58th Street, which you may have heard about on the Fifth Avenue tour.
They were made in Paris in 1894.
When the mansion was demolished, the gates were donated to the city, and they were installed here in 1939.
Walk through the gates into the Conservatory Garden, the only formal garden in Central Park.
It's six acres, divided into three sections, each in a different style.
The central garden, in the Italian style, has a large lawn surrounded by hedges and an iron pergola covered with wisteria.
The north garden, in the French style, has concentric beds of flowers around a fountain called the Untermyer Fountain, with three dancing maidens.
The south garden, in the English style, has lush perennial borders and a small pool with a statue of two children, inspired by the characters in Frances Hodgson Burnett's novel The Secret Garden.
The garden's name comes from a large glass conservatory that stood here from 1899 to 1934, when it was demolished.
Robert Moses then created the formal garden, which opened in 1937.
By the 1970s, it had fallen into disrepair.
It was restored in the 1980s and is now one of the most beautiful and peaceful places in the city.
It's a popular spot for wedding photos.
It's a fitting end for a walk through the park.
Olmsted and Vaux designed Central Park to give people of all classes access to beauty, peace, and nature.
Here, in the northern end, near Harlem and East Harlem, that vision is as alive as ever.
The Upper East Side has been, for more than a century, the most famous wealthy neighborhood in America.
Its name is shorthand for old money, private schools, charity galas, and Park Avenue co-ops with famously selective boards.
It wasn't always that way.
In the mid-nineteenth century, much of the area was rocky, rural land, dotted with farms, country estates along the East River, and shantytowns.
The New York and Harlem Railroad ran up Fourth Avenue, now Park Avenue, in an open cut, belching smoke and noise.

Elevated trains rumbled along Second and Third Avenues starting in the late 1870s, and the blocks near them filled with tenements for working-class immigrants: Germans, Irish, Hungarians, Czechs, and others.
The transformation came in two stages.
First, after Central Park opened, the very rich began building mansions along Fifth Avenue facing the park, moving north from the Gilded Age mansions in the Fifties.
By the early 1900s, Fifth Avenue from 59th Street to 96th Street was lined with palaces built by the families of the industrial age: steel, oil, railroads, banking, and tobacco.
Second, after Grand Central's tracks were covered in the early twentieth century, Park Avenue became a grand boulevard, and luxury apartment buildings rose along it.
The rich discovered that a large apartment with a doorman was much easier to run than a mansion with dozens of servants.
As the mansions became impractical, many of them were demolished, but many were converted into museums, consulates, schools, and cultural institutions.
That's why Fifth Avenue along the park, from the Met at 82nd Street north to about 105th Street, has so many museums that it's called Museum Mile.
Many of these museums are the former homes and private collections of the people who made the great American fortunes.
East of Lexington Avenue, the story is different.
The area known as Yorkville was a working-class neighborhood of German, Hungarian, and Czech immigrants, with breweries, beer halls, and churches.
Elevated trains kept it modest for decades.
After the elevated trains were torn down in the 1940s and 50s, high-rise apartments replaced the tenements, and the neighborhood became more uniformly affluent.
And at the far east, along the river, is Gracie Mansion, the official home of New York's mayor.
On this walk, you'll see how private wealth became public culture, and how a working-class immigrant neighborhood became part of the city's most famous zip codes.
You're at Park Avenue and 66th Street, in front of a massive brick building that looks like a medieval fortress, with towers and crenellations.
This is the Park Avenue Armory, completed in 1880 as the headquarters of the Seventh Regiment of the New York State Militia.
The Seventh Regiment was nicknamed the Silk Stocking Regiment, because so many of its members came from New York's wealthiest families.
It was a social club as well as a military unit.
It also had a practical role: in the nineteenth century, the city's militia was used to put down riots and labor disturbances, including the deadly Draft Riots of 1863.
Armories built in this era often had fortress-like designs, reflecting the fears of the wealthy that the city's working classes might rise up.
The building was paid for not by the government but by the members themselves, and they spared no expense.
The interior rooms were designed by some of the most celebrated designers of the era, including Louis Comfort Tiffany, the son of the jeweler, and Stanford White.
The Veterans Room, designed by Tiffany's firm, is a masterpiece of the Aesthetic Movement, with dark wood, metalwork, and stained glass.
Behind the front building is the drill hall, a vast iron-trussed space of about fifty-five thousand square feet, one of the largest unobstructed interior spaces in New York.
It was modeled on the great train sheds of the era.
The regiment drilled here, and it was also used for sporting events and exhibitions.
In the 2000s, a nonprofit took over the building and turned it into a cultural center.
The drill hall now hosts large-scale art installations, theater, music, and performances that couldn't fit anywhere else, along with the famous Winter Show, an antiques fair.
Look around the neighborhood, too.
Just north is Hunter College, a public college founded in 1870 as a teacher-training school for women.

Along Park Avenue, look at the elegant apartment buildings, mostly built in the 1910s and 20s, many designed by the architect Rosario Candela, whose buildings are considered among the most desirable in the city.
At Fifth Avenue and 70th Street, facing Central Park, stands a low, elegant mansion of limestone set back behind a garden.
This is the Frick Collection.
It was built between 1912 and 1914 as the home of Henry Clay Frick, designed by Thomas Hastings of Carrère and Hastings, the architects of the New York Public Library.
Frick was one of the most ruthless industrialists of the Gilded Age.
He made his fortune producing coke, a fuel used in steelmaking, in western Pennsylvania, and became the chairman of Carnegie Steel, Andrew Carnegie's company.
In 1892, during a strike at the Homestead steel works near Pittsburgh, Frick brought in hundreds of armed Pinkerton agents.
A battle broke out between the strikers and the Pinkertons, and people were killed on both sides.
The state militia then occupied the town, and the strike was broken.
Weeks later, an anarchist named Alexander Berkman burst into Frick's office, shot him twice and stabbed him.
Frick survived, and reportedly returned to work within about a week.
Frick and Carnegie eventually had a bitter falling out.
Frick moved to New York, and built his mansion a few blocks north of Carnegie's.
Some say he wanted to make Carnegie's house look like a miner's shack.
Frick spent his later years collecting European art, and he intended from the beginning that his house and collection would become a museum after his death.
He died in 1919, and the museum opened in 1935.

The Frick has an extraordinary collection, including works by Vermeer, Rembrandt, Holbein, Goya, Titian, and Turner, displayed as they would have been in a private home, among furniture and decorative objects.
Many visitors find it the most intimate and beautiful museum in the city.
The Frick underwent a major renovation and expansion in the early 2020s, opening up the second floor of the mansion, where the family's private rooms were, for the first time.
During the renovation, the collection was displayed temporarily in the Breuer building on Madison Avenue, the former home of the Whitney Museum.
You're on Fifth Avenue at 82nd Street, at the foot of the famous steps of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

The Met was founded in 1870 by a group of businessmen, financiers, artists, and civic leaders, including Theodore Roosevelt Senior, who wanted New York to have an art museum to rival the great museums of Europe.
Its first home was in a building on Fifth Avenue downtown.
In 1880, it moved into a red brick Gothic building inside Central Park, designed by Calvert Vaux and Jacob Wrey Mould.
That original building is now buried within the museum; part of its brick facade is visible inside, in the Lehman Wing.
The grand Beaux-Arts facade you see on Fifth Avenue was designed by Richard Morris Hunt and completed in 1902, after his death, by his son.
Look up at the tops of the paired columns.
Above them, there are large rough blocks of stone.
They were intended to be carved into sculptures representing great periods of art, but the money ran out, and they've been left uncarved for more than a century.
Today, the Met is the largest art museum in the Americas, with a collection of around one and a half million objects spanning five thousand years.

Its galleries include Egyptian art, including the Temple of Dendur; European paintings, including works by Rembrandt, Vermeer, and Van Gogh; an American Wing, with entire period rooms; arms and armor; and much more.
The museum's annual fundraising gala, the Met Gala, held each May for the Costume Institute, has become one of the biggest celebrity events in the world.
The steps themselves are one of the great public spaces in the city.
People sit here to eat lunch, meet friends, watch street performers, and people-watch.

In the beloved 1967 children's novel From the Mixed-Up Files of Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler, two children run away from home and secretly live inside the Met, sleeping in an antique bed and bathing in a fountain.
If you go to the roof garden in the warmer months, you'll get a spectacular view over Central Park and the skyline.
Walk north along Fifth Avenue.
At 86th Street, look for an elegant Beaux-Arts mansion on the corner, built in 1914 for the industrialist William Starr Miller and later home to Grace Vanderbilt.
Today it's the Neue Galerie, a museum of early twentieth-century German and Austrian art and design, founded by the cosmetics heir Ronald Lauder and the art dealer Serge Sabarsky.
Its star is Gustav Klimt's 1907 portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer, the dazzling gold painting often called The Woman in Gold.
The painting was seized by the Nazis from the Bloch-Bauer family in Vienna, and after the war it hung in an Austrian state museum for decades.
Adele's niece, Maria Altmann, who had fled to the United States, fought a long legal battle and won its return in 2006.
Lauder then bought it for a reported one hundred thirty-five million dollars, at the time a record price for a painting.
Downstairs, Café Sabarsky serves Viennese coffee and pastries in an elegant, wood-paneled room.
Continue north to 89th Street, where you'll see one of the most famous buildings of the twentieth century: the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright.
Solomon Guggenheim came from a family that made an enormous fortune in mining and smelting, especially copper and silver.
Advised by the artist Baroness Hilla von Rebay, he collected what they called non-objective art, abstract painting by artists like Wassily Kandinsky.
In 1943, they commissioned Wright to design a museum for the collection.
The project took sixteen years, through endless disputes with city officials, the museum's board, and Wright's own stubbornness.
Wright died in April 1959, about six months before the museum opened that October.
The design is a radical departure from traditional museums.
Instead of a series of rooms, it's a single continuous spiral ramp, coiling up around a central atrium, under a glass skylight.
Visitors typically take an elevator to the top and walk down the ramp.
Wright, who mostly despised cities, designed the building as a kind of organic shell, set apart from the grid of Manhattan.
Some artists objected that the curved, sloping walls were terrible for displaying paintings.
The building's admirers say the building is itself the greatest work of art in the collection.
Look at the building from across the street.
Its white, inverted, stacked spirals widen as they rise.
When it opened, critics compared it to a washing machine, an inverted cupcake, and a snail.
At Fifth Avenue and 91st Street, look for a large red brick and limestone mansion set within a garden.
This was the home of Andrew Carnegie, built between 1899 and 1902.
When Carnegie built here, this area was considered remote, and the land around his mansion was still partly empty and rocky, with shanties nearby.
He chose it for the space and sunlight.
He wanted a big garden, and he deliberately bought up surrounding lots to protect his light and air.
The neighborhood around it came to be known as Carnegie Hill.

Carnegie, as you may have heard at Carnegie Hall, was born in Scotland in 1835, emigrated to Pittsburgh as a poor boy, and worked as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill and a telegraph messenger before rising in the railroad industry and then founding the steel company that made him one of the richest people in history.
In 1901, he sold Carnegie Steel to J. P. Morgan, who combined it with other companies to form U.S. Steel, the first company in the world valued at over one billion dollars.
Carnegie then devoted himself to giving his fortune away.
In an essay called The Gospel of Wealth, he argued that the rich had a moral obligation to use their wealth for the public good, and that the man who dies rich dies disgraced.
Carnegie described the house as the most modest, plainest, and most roomy house in New York, though it had more than sixty rooms.

It was one of the first private homes in the United States to have a structural steel frame, appropriately enough for a steel magnate, and it included an Otis passenger elevator and an early form of air conditioning and central heating.
Today, the mansion is home to the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, the only museum in the United States devoted entirely to historic and contemporary design.
The museum was founded in 1897 by Sarah, Eleanor, and Amy Hewitt, the granddaughters of Peter Cooper, the founder of Cooper Union.
Its collection includes everything from wallpaper and textiles to furniture, product design, and graphic design.
A block north, at 92nd Street, is the Jewish Museum, housed in the French Gothic mansion of the banker Felix Warburg, completed in 1908.
The Warburgs were among the leading families of the German Jewish financial elite in New York, along with the Schiffs, the Loebs, and the Lehmans, a group sometimes called Our Crowd.
Walk east to East 86th Street and Second Avenue.
You're in Yorkville, the eastern part of the Upper East Side.
Starting in the late nineteenth century, Yorkville became a working-class immigrant neighborhood.
After the General Slocum disaster in 1904, which you may have heard about on the East Village tour, many German families left the Lower East Side and resettled here.
86th Street became known as the German Broadway, lined with beer halls, cafés, bakeries, butchers, dance halls, and German-language theaters and movie houses.
Hungarians, Czechs, Slovaks, and Irish also lived in the neighborhood, with their own churches and social clubs.
Yorkville also had a dark chapter.
In the 1930s, the German American Bund, a pro-Nazi organization, was active here, holding rallies and parades along 86th Street.
Its activities provoked counter-protests and violent confrontations.
Its leader, Fritz Kuhn, was convicted of embezzling the group's funds in 1939, and the Bund collapsed after the United States entered World War Two.
A few traces of German Yorkville survive.
Look for Schaller and Weber, a German butcher and grocer on Second Avenue, open since 1937, and its sausage shop next door.
Glaser's Bake Shop, on First Avenue, operated from 1902 until 2018.
There are still a few German restaurants nearby.
A few blocks north, between Second and Third Avenues and 90th to 93rd Streets, stood the Jacob Ruppert Brewery, one of the largest breweries in the country, makers of Knickerbocker beer.
Jacob Ruppert Junior, the brewery's heir, used his fortune to buy the New York Yankees in 1915.
He bought Babe Ruth from the Boston Red Sox in 1919 and built the original Yankee Stadium in 1923, turning the Yankees into the most successful franchise in American sports.
The brewery closed in 1965 and was demolished.
Apartment towers, named Ruppert Towers, now stand on the site.
Underneath Second Avenue runs the Second Avenue Subway.
It was first proposed in the 1920s, and construction started and stopped several times over the decades.
The first phase, from 63rd Street to 96th Street, finally opened on January first, 2017.
The station at 86th Street has large, bright mosaic artworks by the artist Chuck Close.
It's worth a peek.
End your walk at Carl Schurz Park, along the East River at the end of East 86th Street, and at Gracie Mansion, the official residence of the mayor of New York City.
Gracie Mansion was built in 1799 as a country house for Archibald Gracie, a Scottish-born merchant and shipping magnate.
In his time, this was the countryside, far north of the city, and wealthy merchants built summer estates along the East River.
Gracie entertained prominent guests here, including Alexander Hamilton, John Quincy Adams, and the future King Louis Philippe of France.
Gracie lost his fortune in the economic turmoil around the War of 1812 and sold the house in 1823.
After passing through several owners, the city took over the property in 1896 and made it part of the park.
For decades, it housed the Museum of the City of New York, and a concession stand.
In 1942, at the urging of Robert Moses, it became the official residence of the mayor.
Fiorello La Guardia was the first mayor to live here.
Most mayors since have lived in the house, though Michael Bloomberg, who was a billionaire with his own townhouse, chose not to.
The park is named after Carl Schurz, a German revolutionary who fled to America after the failed revolutions of 1848 in Germany.
He became a general in the Civil War, a United States senator from Missouri, Secretary of the Interior, and a journalist and reformer.
He's credited with a famous version of the phrase My country, right or wrong: if right, to be kept right; and if wrong, to be set right.
The park honored him because of the large German population in Yorkville.
He lived nearby, at the end of his life.
Walk to the promenade along the river.
Look out at the water.
This stretch of the East River, where the river meets the Harlem River and Long Island Sound, is called Hell Gate, from the Dutch Hellegat.
Its swirling currents and submerged rocks wrecked hundreds of ships.
In the 1870s and 1880s, the Army Corps of Engineers undertook a huge project to clear the rocks.
In 1885, they detonated about three hundred thousand pounds of explosives to blow up Flood Rock.
It was one of the largest planned explosions in history before the atomic bomb, and it reportedly was felt as far away as Princeton, New Jersey.
Across the water, you'll see Roosevelt Island, Randall's Island, and Queens.
From the promenade, you can watch boats and barges pass by, and the lights of the Triborough Bridge, now the Robert F. Kennedy Bridge, in the distance.
The Upper West Side developed later than the Upper East Side, and it has always had a different personality.
If the East Side was old money and Society with a capital S, the West Side was intellectual, artistic, liberal, and a little bohemian.

It's the neighborhood of musicians, writers, academics, psychoanalysts, and serious eaters, and the setting for countless novels and films, from West Side Story to When Harry Met Sally to You've Got Mail.
In the mid-nineteenth century, this area was mostly countryside, called Bloomingdale, from the Dutch Bloemendael, or valley of flowers.
The old Bloomingdale Road, which followed a Native American trail, ran through it; it later became upper Broadway.
There were country estates along the Hudson, farms, villages, and shantytowns, as well as institutions like the Bloomingdale Insane Asylum, which stood on the site of today's Columbia University.
Development was slow until transportation arrived.
The Ninth Avenue elevated train reached the area in 1879.
Developers began building rowhouses on the side streets, and a few ambitious apartment buildings, like the Dakota.
But the real boom came with the first subway, the IRT, which opened in 1904 and ran up Broadway.
Almost overnight, the West Side became accessible to the middle class, and giant apartment buildings rose along Broadway, Central Park West, West End Avenue, and Riverside Drive.
Many of them were built for a new population: upwardly mobile, often Jewish families moving up from the Lower East Side and other parts of the city.
The neighborhood went through hard times in the mid-twentieth century.
Many large apartments were cut up into single-room-occupancy hotels, and parts of the neighborhood were considered dangerous by the 1970s.
Urban renewal projects demolished whole neighborhoods, most notably San Juan Hill, for Lincoln Center.
Then, starting in the 1980s, the West Side gentrified dramatically.
Today, it's one of the most expensive neighborhoods in the country, though it retains its reputation as a place of books, music, and lively street life.

On this walk, you'll explore some of the most famous apartment buildings in the world, great cultural institutions, and a few beloved food shops, and you'll end on the banks of the Hudson in Riverside Park.
You're at Columbus Circle, at the southwest corner of Central Park, where Broadway, Eighth Avenue, Central Park West, and 59th Street converge.
In the center of the circle, atop a tall granite column, stands a marble statue of Christopher Columbus by the Italian sculptor Gaetano Russo.

It was erected in 1892, for the four hundredth anniversary of Columbus's first voyage, and was paid for by Italian Americans through a fundraising campaign led by the Italian-language newspaper Il Progresso.
At the time, Italian immigrants faced intense discrimination, and Columbus was embraced as a symbol of Italian contributions to America.
In recent years, the statue has been the subject of debate over how Columbus should be remembered, given his treatment of Indigenous people.
A fun fact: Columbus Circle is the official point from which distances to and from New York City are measured on highway signs.
Look at the twin glass towers on the west side of the circle.
This is the Deutsche Bank Center, formerly the Time Warner Center, completed in 2003, on the site of the old New York Coliseum, a convention hall built by Robert Moses.
It houses offices, luxury condos, a hotel, restaurants, and Jazz at Lincoln Center's concert halls, with a window behind the stage overlooking Central Park.
On the south side of the circle, at 2 Columbus Circle, is a curious white marble building with round porthole-like openings at its base.
It was designed by Edward Durell Stone and completed in 1964 as a museum for the collection of the A&P supermarket heir Huntington Hartford.
Critics mocked it; the architecture critic Ada Louise Huxtable called it a die-cut Venetian palazzo on lollipops.
It was controversially remodeled in the 2000s, and now houses the Museum of Arts and Design.
A block south, at Eighth Avenue and 57th Street, look for the Hearst Tower, a glass skyscraper with a distinctive diagonal grid pattern, rising from a six-story Art Deco stone base.
William Randolph Hearst, the newspaper and magazine baron who built a media empire on sensational yellow journalism, commissioned the base in 1928 as the foundation for a skyscraper.
The Depression halted the plan.
Nearly eighty years later, in 2006, the Hearst Corporation finally completed the tower, designed by Norman Foster, rising from the old base.
The company, publisher of magazines like Cosmopolitan and Esquire, still has its headquarters there.
You're at Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts, between 62nd and 66th Streets, Columbus and Amsterdam Avenues.
Walk into the main plaza and stand near the Revson Fountain.
Around you are three great halls.
Straight ahead is the Metropolitan Opera House, with its five tall arched windows.
Inside, visible through the windows, hang two enormous murals by Marc Chagall.
To the left is the David H. Koch Theater, home of the New York City Ballet.
To the right is David Geffen Hall, home of the New York Philharmonic.
Nearby are the Juilliard School, the Vivian Beaumont Theater, the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts, and other institutions.
Lincoln Center was built between 1959 and the late 1960s, championed by John D. Rockefeller the Third and Robert Moses.
It was the first major center of its kind in the world, bringing together opera, symphony, ballet, theater, and education in one complex.
President Dwight Eisenhower broke ground in 1959.
But there's a story underneath the plaza.
Before Lincoln Center, this area was a neighborhood called San Juan Hill.
In the early twentieth century, it was one of the largest African American neighborhoods in Manhattan, before Harlem became the center of Black New York.
Its name may refer to the Battle of San Juan Hill in the Spanish-American War, in which Black soldiers fought.
San Juan Hill was a crowded neighborhood of tenements, with a vibrant musical culture.
The stride pianist James P. Johnson lived and played here, and he said the dance the Charleston was inspired by the dances of Gullah dockworkers from South Carolina he saw in the neighborhood.
The jazz pianist Thelonious Monk lived on West 63rd Street for decades.
By the 1940s and 50s, the neighborhood was largely Black and Puerto Rican.
In the 1950s, the city declared the area a slum and cleared it as part of the Lincoln Square urban renewal project.
Thousands of families were displaced.

Before the buildings were demolished, the film crew for the 1961 movie version of West Side Story shot its opening scenes in the neighborhood's streets, a story about Puerto Rican and white gangs fighting over the very neighborhood that was about to be destroyed.
Lincoln Center has acknowledged this history in recent years with exhibitions and programs.
As you look around this elegant plaza, it's worth remembering the neighborhood that was erased to make room for it.
At Central Park West and 72nd Street stands the Dakota, one of the most famous apartment buildings in the world.
Look at its steep roofs, gables, dormers, and towers, its yellow brick and sandstone, and its moat-like areaway surrounded by an iron fence.
The Dakota was completed in 1884, designed by Henry Janeway Hardenbergh, who later designed the Plaza Hotel.
It was built by Edward Clark, the lawyer who was president of the Singer Manufacturing Company, the sewing machine giant.
Clark had made a fortune from Singer and invested heavily in West Side real estate.
At the time, wealthy New Yorkers lived in private houses, and apartments were associated with tenements.
Clark set out to create apartments luxurious enough to attract the rich.

The Dakota had large apartments, some with as many as twenty rooms, with high ceilings, elaborate woodwork, and modern amenities, including central heating, its own electrical generating plant, and hydraulic elevators.
Its interior courtyard was large enough for carriages to drive in.
A popular story says it was called the Dakota because it was so far uptown, so remote from the city, that it might as well have been in the Dakota Territory.
Historians think it was more likely just part of Clark's fondness for western names; he also proposed renaming the West Side avenues after western states.
But the story stuck.
The Dakota became a home for artists, musicians, and actors, including Leonard Bernstein, Lauren Bacall, Boris Karloff, Judy Garland, and Rudolf Nureyev.
The building's co-op board is famously selective, and it reportedly turned down several celebrities who wanted to buy in.
Its gloomy, Gothic exterior made it the setting for Roman Polanski's 1968 horror film Rosemary's Baby.
And, most famously, it was the home of John Lennon and Yoko Ono.
On December eighth, 1980, Lennon was shot and killed just outside the building's entrance, the arched carriage gate on 72nd Street.
Yoko Ono continued to live in the building for many years.
The Strawberry Fields memorial in Central Park is just across the street.
Look up and down Central Park West.

The avenue is lined with grand apartment buildings, many of them built in the 1920s and 30s, including the twin-towered San Remo at 74th Street and the Majestic and the Century, with their Art Deco towers.
Their twin towers create one of the most recognizable skylines in the city, especially viewed from across the park.
Walk west to Broadway and 73rd Street.
Look up at the huge, ornate Beaux-Arts building with rounded corner towers, iron balconies, and a mansard roof.
This is the Ansonia, completed in 1904, one of the grandest and strangest apartment hotels ever built.
Its developer was William Earl Dodge Stokes, a wealthy and eccentric heir to a copper and real estate fortune.
He named it after his grandfather, Anson Greene Phelps, whose company, Phelps Dodge, became a mining giant.
Stokes's ambitions were enormous.
The Ansonia had hundreds of apartments, a grand lobby, Turkish baths, and one of the world's largest indoor swimming pools at the time.
And on the roof, Stokes kept a small farm, with chickens, goats, ducks, and reportedly a small bear.
He sold fresh eggs to residents at a discount.
In the lobby, there was a fountain with live seals.
The city's health department eventually shut down the farm.
The Ansonia's thick walls made it nearly soundproof, which attracted musicians and singers.
The opera star Enrico Caruso, the composer Igor Stravinsky, the conductor Arturo Toscanini, and the singer Lily Pons all lived here at various times.
Baseball fans have a reason to visit too.
Babe Ruth lived here in the early 1920s, after joining the Yankees.

And in 1919, members of the Chicago White Sox reportedly met in a room at the Ansonia with gamblers to plan the fixing of the World Series, the infamous Black Sox scandal, in which eight players were banned from baseball for life.
In the 1970s, the building's basement was home to the Continental Baths, a gay bathhouse where Bette Midler got her start, singing for patrons with Barry Manilow accompanying her on piano.
Later, the space became Plato's Retreat, a notorious swingers' club.
Just to the north is Verdi Square, a small triangular park with a statue of the Italian composer Giuseppe Verdi, surrounded by characters from his operas.
In the 1960s and 70s, this park became notorious as Needle Park because of open drug use, and was the setting for the 1971 film The Panic in Needle Park, an early starring role for Al Pacino.
Today, the park has been restored, and the neighborhood is a world away from those days.
Across Broadway, the subway station at 72nd Street has its original 1904 control house, a small Beaux-Arts building, the entrance to one of the first subway stations in the city.
You're on Central Park West, between 77th and 81st Streets, at the American Museum of Natural History, one of the largest natural history museums in the world.
It was founded in 1869 by the naturalist Albert Bickmore and a group of wealthy New Yorkers, including Theodore Roosevelt Senior.
Its first home was in the Arsenal in Central Park.
In 1877, it moved into its first building here, on what was then a rocky, rural site called Manhattan Square.
Today, the museum complex is a patchwork of more than two dozen interconnected buildings, built over a century and a half, in different styles.

The main entrance on Central Park West is the Theodore Roosevelt Memorial, completed in 1936, honoring Theodore Roosevelt Junior, the former president, naturalist, and conservationist, who was a lifelong supporter of the museum.
For decades, a bronze equestrian statue of Roosevelt flanked by an African man and a Native American man stood on the front steps.
Critics argued that it portrayed the two men as subordinate, and it was removed in 2022.
It's been relocated to North Dakota.
Inside, the museum is famous for its dinosaur halls, which hold one of the greatest collections of fossils in the world, including a Tyrannosaurus rex.
Its dioramas of animals in their habitats, created in the early twentieth century, are masterpieces of naturalistic art.
The Milstein Hall of Ocean Life features a life-size model of a blue whale, ninety-four feet long, suspended from the ceiling.
On the north side, on 81st Street, look at the giant glass cube enclosing a sphere.
This is the Rose Center for Earth and Space, which opened in 2000, and houses the Hayden Planetarium.

Shortly after it opened, its exhibits grouped Pluto with the Kuiper Belt objects, not with the planets, a decision that caused a public uproar, years before astronomers officially reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet in 2006.
The planetarium's director, Neil deGrasse Tyson, became a celebrity partly through that controversy.
On the Columbus Avenue side, look for the newest addition, the Richard Gilder Center for Science, Education, and Innovation, which opened in 2023.
Designed by Jeanne Gang's firm, Studio Gang, its flowing, cave-like atrium is inspired by natural canyons and geological formations.
Behind the museum, on Columbus Avenue, there's a popular Sunday flea and farmers' market.
Walk to Broadway and 80th Street.
Here, you'll find Zabar's, the most famous food store on the Upper West Side.
Zabar's was founded in 1934 by Louis and Lillian Zabar, Jewish immigrants from Ukraine, who started with a small counter selling smoked fish.
They grew it into a sprawling gourmet store, now spread across a full block front.
Inside, you'll find smoked fish, coffee, cheese, breads, and cooking equipment upstairs.
The store is still run by the Zabar family.
Its bright orange signs and shopping bags are an icon of the neighborhood.
Zabar's is part of the larger story of the Upper West Side's Jewish culture.
After the subway opened in 1904, many Jewish families moved here from the Lower East Side and Harlem, and the West Side became one of the most important centers of Jewish life in America.
The neighborhood is home to many synagogues, delis, and bakeries.

Nearby on Broadway, H and H Bagels was a famous bagel shop for decades; Barney Greengrass, on Amsterdam Avenue at 86th Street, has been selling smoked fish and appetizing since 1908, calling itself The Sturgeon King.
Look up and down Broadway.
Notice how wide it is, with a planted median down the middle.
That's because the old Bloomingdale Road was widened into a grand boulevard in the 1860s and 70s, called the Boulevard, before it was renamed Broadway in 1899.
The subway runs right underneath it.

At Broadway and 78th to 79th Streets, look for the Apthorp, a giant Italian Renaissance apartment building, completed in 1908, built by William Waldorf Astor, the same Astor who built the Waldorf Hotel.
It has a large interior courtyard with gardens and fountains, and grand iron gates at its entrances.

It was among the first and largest courtyard apartment buildings in the city, and it was the model for a style of luxury living that defined the Upper West Side: big, solid buildings with plenty of light and air.
The neighborhood was also home to the Thalia, a repertory cinema on West 95th Street, which appears in Annie Hall, and Symphony Space, which still hosts readings and concerts.
End your walk in Riverside Park, at Riverside Drive and 89th Street, at the Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument.
Riverside Park stretches for about four miles along the Hudson, from 59th Street up to 158th Street.
Frederick Law Olmsted, one of the designers of Central Park, designed the original park and Riverside Drive in the 1870s.
The drive curves along the contours of the land, unlike the rigid street grid, and was designed for carriages, with views of the river and the New Jersey Palisades.
There was one big problem: the New York Central Railroad's tracks ran along the shore at the bottom of the park, with smoke, noise, and soot.
In the 1930s, Robert Moses covered the tracks with a deck, extended the park on landfill, and built the Henry Hudson Parkway along the water, as part of the West Side Improvement Project.
The rail line is still there, in a tunnel under the park, and is used today by Amtrak trains.
Moses's project also created the 79th Street Rotunda and Boat Basin, where people still live year-round on houseboats.

The white marble monument in front of you, a circular temple of Corinthian columns, is the Soldiers' and Sailors' Memorial, completed in 1902 to honor the Union soldiers and sailors who fought in the Civil War.
It was modeled on the ancient Choragic Monument of Lysicrates in Athens.
Look out over the river from the monument's terrace.
The views of the Hudson and the New Jersey Palisades are among the best in the city, especially at sunset.
Riverside Drive is lined with handsome apartment buildings and a few surviving mansions.

Some of its most famous residents included the newspaper publisher William Randolph Hearst, who lived in a vast apartment at the Clarendon, at Riverside Drive and 86th Street, which he expanded until it took up several floors, and the composer George Gershwin, who lived on Riverside Drive in the 1920s.

Up and down the park, look for other monuments: a statue of Joan of Arc at 93rd Street, a statue of Eleanor Roosevelt at 72nd Street, and a garden at 91st Street that featured prominently in the final scene of the 1998 film You've Got Mail.
Riverside Park is less famous than Central Park, but many West Siders love it more: quieter, more local, and with a river view.
Morningside Heights is a plateau high above Harlem, bounded by the cliffs of Morningside Park on the east and the Hudson River on the west.

Around the turn of the twentieth century, it became home to so many major institutions, a university, a cathedral, seminaries, a hospital, and a monumental tomb, that it was nicknamed the Acropolis of America.
Before that, it was rural and isolated.
In the colonial era, it was farmland.
In September 1776, it was the site of the Battle of Harlem Heights, one of George Washington's few early successes in the New York campaign.

After a string of defeats on Long Island and in lower Manhattan, Washington's troops fought the British to a standstill in the fields around what is now 120th Street and Broadway, near the Columbia campus.
The victory was small, but it boosted the morale of an army that badly needed it.
In the nineteenth century, the plateau was dominated by the Bloomingdale Insane Asylum, a psychiatric hospital surrounded by gardens, and the Leake and Watts Orphan House.
The asylum was considered progressive for its time, offering patients fresh air and landscaped grounds.
When the city grew northward and land became valuable, those institutions moved out and new ones moved in.
In the 1890s, Columbia University bought the asylum's land, the Episcopal Church began building a massive cathedral nearby, and General Grant's Tomb rose on Riverside Drive.
The subway arrived in 1904, and the neighborhood filled with apartment buildings for professors, students, and middle-class families.
Morningside Heights has also been a place of conflict.

Columbia's relationship with its Harlem neighbors has often been tense, as the university expanded, bought up buildings, and, in 1968, proposed building a gymnasium in Morningside Park, which triggered one of the most famous student uprisings in American history.

On this walk, you'll see one of the largest cathedrals in the world, which is still unfinished more than a century after construction began; the campus where the first nuclear fission experiment in the United States was carried out; a soaring Gothic church built by John D. Rockefeller Junior; and the tomb of Ulysses S. Grant, whose story ends with a financial scandal you won't expect.
You're at Morningside Park, the long, narrow park that runs along a steep cliff from 110th Street to 123rd Street, separating Morningside Heights above from Harlem below.
The park was designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, the designers of Central Park, in the 1870s and 80s.
The cliff was too steep for buildings, so the city turned it into a park.

Olmsted and Vaux designed it with a walkway along the top of the cliff, offering sweeping views east across Harlem, and paths and stairs winding down through rocky outcrops to the flatter area at the bottom.
For much of the twentieth century, the park was neglected, and it became known as dangerous.
It also became a symbol of the divide between Columbia, at the top of the cliff, and Harlem, at the bottom.
That divide exploded in 1968.
Columbia planned to build a new gymnasium in the park, on land leased from the city.
The plan included a separate, smaller entrance on the Harlem side, at the bottom of the cliff, for community residents, while Columbia students would enter from the top.
Critics called it Gym Crow, comparing it to the Jim Crow segregation laws of the South.

In April 1968, student protesters, led by groups including the Students for a Democratic Society and the Student Afro-American Society, occupied several campus buildings, including the president's office in Low Library.
They protested the gym, and the university's ties to the Institute for Defense Analyses, a think tank doing research for the Vietnam War.
After a week, the police stormed the buildings, arresting more than seven hundred people, with violence that injured many students and turned much of the campus against the administration.
The university canceled the gym, and the protests became a turning point in the student movement of the 1960s.
Look for the pond and waterfall at the bottom of the park, near 113th Street.
They were built on the site where gym construction had begun, as a kind of healing gesture.
The park has been substantially restored since the 1990s and is now well used by both Columbia and Harlem residents.
At Amsterdam Avenue and 112th Street stands the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, the mother church of the Episcopal Diocese of New York, and one of the largest cathedrals in the world.
The cornerstone was laid on December twenty-seventh, 1892, the feast day of St. John.
The original design, by the architects George Heins and Christopher Grant LaFarge, was in a Romanesque and Byzantine style.
After Heins died in 1907, the church hired Ralph Adams Cram, the leading Gothic Revival architect in America, who redesigned the nave in a French Gothic style.
That's why the building looks like a mix of styles.
The eastern end, with its rounded arches, is from the original design.
The long nave, with its pointed arches and soaring vault, is Cram's.
Construction has stopped and started many times, interrupted by two world wars, the Depression, and financial troubles.
The cathedral has never been finished.
Its towers on the west front are incomplete stumps, and the planned central tower was never built.
New Yorkers nicknamed it St. John the Unfinished.
In the 1980s, the cathedral ran a program training young people from Harlem in medieval stone carving, and they carved some of the statues on the west front portal.
Look closely and you'll find some surprising details, including an apocalyptic scene with a recognizable depiction of the Manhattan skyline being destroyed.
Step inside, if you can.
The nave is about six hundred feet long, longer than two football fields, and its vaulted ceiling rises over one hundred twenty feet.

The cathedral regularly hosts concerts, art installations, and events, and every October, it holds a Blessing of the Animals for the Feast of St. Francis, in which people bring dogs, cats, birds, and even camels and elephants to be blessed.
In 2001, a fire badly damaged the north transept, which was home to the cathedral's gift shop.
It took years to clean and restore.
Look for the peacocks.
The cathedral keeps a few of them, and they roam the grounds.
In the garden on the south side, look for the Peace Fountain, a large bronze sculpture by Greg Wyatt, depicting the struggle between good and evil, with the archangel Michael and a giant crab.

Across Amsterdam Avenue is the Hungarian Pastry Shop, a beloved café for Columbia students and faculty for decades, where writers have worked on dissertations, novels, and screenplays over endless cups of coffee.
Walk to the main gate of Columbia University, at Broadway and 116th Street, and walk onto the College Walk.
Columbia was founded in 1754 as King's College, by royal charter from King George the Second.
It's the oldest institution of higher learning in New York, and the fifth oldest in the country.

Among its early students were Alexander Hamilton; John Jay, the first chief justice of the United States; Gouverneur Morris, who wrote the final draft of the Constitution; and Robert Livingston, who helped draft the Declaration of Independence.
After the Revolution, it was renamed Columbia.
The college's first home was near City Hall Park.
In 1857, it moved to Midtown, at 49th Street and Madison Avenue.
In 1897, it moved here, to the former grounds of the Bloomingdale Asylum.
The president of the university, Seth Low, hired the firm McKim, Mead and White to design the new campus, which was conceived as an academic city, inspired by Greek and Roman architecture.
At the center of the campus is Low Memorial Library, with its great dome and columned portico, completed in 1897 and named in honor of Seth Low's father, a merchant in the China trade.
Low himself paid for it.
It was the university's main library until 1934, when the larger Butler Library, across the quadrangle, opened.
Look at Butler's facade: carved across the top are the names of great writers and thinkers from antiquity, including Homer, Herodotus, Sophocles, Plato, Aristotle, Demosthenes, Cicero, and Virgil.
On the steps of Low Library sits the bronze statue of Alma Mater, by Daniel Chester French, the sculptor of the Lincoln Memorial.
Look closely in the folds of her robe for a small owl, a symbol of wisdom.
Tradition says that the first freshman of each class to find it will become class valedictorian.
During the 1968 protests, the statue was damaged by a bomb.
Columbia is also tied to modern finance.
The Columbia Business School was where Benjamin Graham, the father of value investing, taught for decades, starting in the 1920s.
His most famous student was Warren Buffett, who enrolled in 1950 after reading Graham's book The Intelligent Investor.
Graham's classes, and his book Security Analysis, written with David Dodd, have shaped generations of investors.
Walk to the northwest corner of the campus, near Broadway and 120th Street, and look for Pupin Hall, the physics building, a tall brick and limestone tower with a small observatory dome on the roof.
It's named for Michael Pupin, a Serbian immigrant who arrived in New York in 1874 with almost nothing, worked as a laborer, put himself through Columbia, and became a renowned physicist and inventor.
His inventions, including loading coils that dramatically improved long-distance telephone lines, made him wealthy.
AT&T bought the rights to his patent.
His autobiography, From Immigrant to Inventor, won the Pulitzer Prize in 1924.
But Pupin Hall is famous for what happened in its basement in January 1939.
Just weeks earlier, scientists in Germany had discovered that uranium atoms could be split, releasing energy, a process called nuclear fission.
When the news reached the United States, physicists at Columbia, led by John Dunning, set out to confirm it.

On January twenty-fifth, 1939, using a cyclotron, a particle accelerator, in the basement of Pupin Hall, Dunning's team observed fission, among the first such experiments carried out in the United States.
The Italian physicist Enrico Fermi, who had just fled fascist Italy, came to Columbia and worked here on nuclear chain reactions.
Fermi and Leo Szilard, also at Columbia, conducted early research on the possibility of a nuclear chain reaction.

Szilard drafted the famous letter that Albert Einstein signed in August 1939, warning President Franklin Roosevelt that Germany might build an atomic bomb, and urging the United States to start its own research.

When the United States launched its effort to build the bomb, the Army Corps of Engineers set up the Manhattan Engineer District, headquartered at first in an office building at 270 Broadway, near City Hall.
That's why the program became known as the Manhattan Project.
Much of the early research took place here at Columbia, before the work shifted to Chicago, Oak Ridge, Hanford, and Los Alamos.
Pupin Hall was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1965.
The cyclotron was dismantled in 2008.
Standing outside this ordinary-looking academic building, it's sobering to think that the atomic age began, in part, in its basement.
Walk west to Riverside Drive and 120th Street, to Riverside Church, with its massive Gothic tower rising over the Hudson.
The church was built by John D. Rockefeller Junior, the son of the Standard Oil founder, and completed in 1930.
Rockefeller was a devout Baptist, and he wanted to create a great interdenominational church, open to all Christians.

He chose as its minister Harry Emerson Fosdick, one of the most famous preachers of the era, a liberal Protestant who had been forced out of his previous pulpit for challenging fundamentalist doctrine.
The architecture was modeled largely on Chartres Cathedral in France, but the building has a steel frame, like a skyscraper.
The tower is about three hundred ninety feet tall, and contains offices, classrooms, and meeting rooms, as well as the Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Carillon, named for Rockefeller's mother.
The carillon has seventy-four bells.
Its largest bell, the bourdon, weighs about twenty tons, and is said to be the largest tuned carillon bell in the world.
On Sundays, you can hear the bells ring across the neighborhood.
You can sometimes take an elevator up the tower, for a tremendous view of the Hudson and upper Manhattan.
Riverside Church has been a center of progressive activism.
On April fourth, 1967, exactly one year before his assassination, the Reverend Martin Luther King Junior delivered his speech Beyond Vietnam: A Time to Break Silence, from the pulpit here.
In it, King publicly denounced the Vietnam War, calling the United States government the greatest purveyor of violence in the world today.
The speech was condemned by much of the press and many of his allies at the time, and it marked a decisive shift in his public stance.
In 1990, Nelson Mandela spoke here, just months after his release from prison in South Africa.
Many presidents, foreign leaders, and religious leaders have spoken here.
The church has also been active in the anti-apartheid movement, the sanctuary movement for refugees, and LGBTQ rights.
Look at the west portal, which is modeled on the portal at Chartres, with carved figures of saints and prophets.
Mixed in with the traditional figures are carvings of modern figures, including scientists and philosophers, including Albert Einstein.
Einstein is said to be the only living person included when the carvings were made.
End your walk across the street, at Riverside Drive and 122nd Street, at the General Grant National Memorial, better known as Grant's Tomb.
Here's a trivia question made famous by Groucho Marx on his quiz show You Bet Your Life, who used it to make sure every contestant went home with a prize: Who is buried in Grant's Tomb?
The technical answer is: nobody.
Ulysses S. Grant and his wife Julia are not buried underground.
Their sarcophagi rest in a crypt, above ground, inside the monument.
They're entombed, not buried.
Ulysses S. Grant was the commanding general of the Union Army who won the Civil War, and he served two terms as president, from 1869 to 1877.
After his presidency, he and Julia settled in New York, in a house on East 66th Street.
And here's the part of Grant's story that many people don't know.
Grant's son, Ulysses Junior, known as Buck, had gone into business with a charming young Wall Street financier named Ferdinand Ward.
Their firm, Grant and Ward, seemed to be wildly successful, and the former president invested nearly all his money in it and lent the firm his name.
But Ward was running a fraud, borrowing against the same securities multiple times and paying old investors with new investors' money, a scheme that would today be called a Ponzi scheme.
In May 1884, the firm collapsed, and the Grants were ruined.
Grant was left nearly penniless.
Ward went to prison.
That same year, Grant was diagnosed with throat cancer.
Desperate to provide for his family, he began writing his memoirs.
His friend Mark Twain offered him a generous publishing deal through Twain's own publishing company.
Grant raced against death to finish, writing in great pain, and completed the manuscript just days before he died in July 1885.
The Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant became a massive bestseller, earning his widow a fortune, and are still regarded as among the finest military memoirs ever written.
Grant had requested to be buried in New York, and around ninety thousand people contributed to build this tomb, which was completed in 1897.
It was designed by John Duncan, and inspired by the ancient Mausoleum at Halicarnassus.
It's the largest mausoleum in North America.
More than a million people attended the dedication parade.
Look around the back and sides of the tomb, at the colorful, wavy mosaic benches.
They were created in the 1970s by the artist Pedro Silva, with community volunteers, inspired by the work of Antoni Gaudí in Barcelona.
The benches caused controversy, since some felt they didn't match the solemn monument, but they've become a beloved part of the site.
Look north along Riverside Drive.
Nearby is a small, easily missed monument, the Amiable Child memorial, marking the grave of a five-year-old boy named St. Claire Pollock, who died in 1797 when this land was a private estate.
It's one of the only private graves on public land in New York City.
Harlem is one of the most famous neighborhoods in the world, a name that stands for African American culture, music, politics, and creativity.
But Harlem was not always Black, and the story of how it became the capital of Black America is one of the most interesting in New York history.
The Dutch founded the village of Nieuw Haarlem in 1658, named after the city of Haarlem in the Netherlands.
For two centuries, Harlem was farmland and country estates, connected to the city by the old Post Road.

In the late nineteenth century, elevated trains arrived, and developers built elegant brownstones and apartment buildings for middle- and upper-middle-class white families, many of them German and Jewish immigrants and their children.
Harlem became a fashionable suburb within the city.
Then came a crash.
Developers, anticipating the arrival of the first subway line along Lenox Avenue in 1904, built far more apartment buildings than the market could fill.
Prices collapsed, and landlords were left with empty buildings.
Enter Philip A. Payton Junior, a Black real estate entrepreneur, who founded the Afro-American Realty Company in 1904.

Payton persuaded white landlords to rent their vacant buildings to Black tenants, who were desperate for decent housing, since they were confined to crowded, run-down neighborhoods like the Tenderloin and San Juan Hill.
Payton's company leased and bought buildings, and Black New Yorkers began moving in.
White residents resisted, sometimes forming associations to keep Black tenants out, but the movement was unstoppable.
The Great Migration, the movement of millions of African Americans out of the rural South starting around 1915, along with immigration from the Caribbean, filled Harlem.
By the 1920s, it was the largest Black urban community in the country.
The result was the Harlem Renaissance, a flowering of Black literature, music, art, and political thought in the 1920s and 30s.

Writers like Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Claude McKay, and Countee Cullen; musicians like Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong, Bessie Smith, and Fats Waller; and intellectuals like W. E. B. Du Bois and Alain Locke made Harlem a cultural capital.

Harlem's later history includes the Great Depression, which hit it hard; the political activism of Adam Clayton Powell Junior and Malcolm X; decades of disinvestment, crime, and abandonment in the 1970s and 80s; and, since the 1990s, a dramatic and contested wave of gentrification.
Through it all, Harlem has remained a center of Black culture, faith, and politics.
As you walk, notice the remarkable architecture.
Harlem has some of the finest rows of brownstones and townhouses in the city, built for wealthy white families who left long ago.
You're at Marcus Garvey Park, between 120th and 124th Streets, at Madison Avenue and Fifth Avenue.
Originally called Mount Morris Park, it was renamed in 1973 for Marcus Garvey.
Garvey was a Jamaican-born activist who arrived in New York in 1916.

He founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association, the UNIA, which became the largest mass movement of people of African descent in history, with chapters around the world and, by some estimates, millions of members and supporters.
Garvey preached Black pride, self-reliance, and Pan-Africanism, the idea that people of African descent around the world shared a common destiny, and that Africa should be free of colonial rule.
He held huge parades through Harlem, with uniformed marchers, and rallies at the UNIA's Liberty Hall on West 138th Street.
In 1919, Garvey launched the Black Star Line, a shipping company owned by Black shareholders, which would carry passengers and goods between America, the Caribbean, and Africa.
It was a bold idea: an international business controlled by Black people, at a time when they were shut out of most industries.
Tens of thousands of supporters bought shares, some for as little as five dollars.
But the company was badly managed, bought old, unseaworthy ships, and collapsed within a few years.

In 1923, Garvey was convicted of mail fraud related to the sale of Black Star Line stock, in a prosecution that many saw as politically motivated, encouraged by J. Edgar Hoover's Bureau of Investigation.
He was imprisoned and then deported to Jamaica in 1927.
His ideas, though, influenced generations of activists, from Malcolm X to the leaders of African independence movements.
Now look up at the rocky hill in the center of the park.
On top stands the Harlem Fire Watchtower, a cast iron tower built in 1857.
In the days before telephone alarms, watchmen stood here scanning the area for smoke, and rang the bell to call firefighters.
It's the last surviving fire watchtower of its kind in the city.
It was dismantled for restoration and reinstalled in 2019.
Around the park, look at the Mount Morris Park Historic District, with some of the most beautiful brownstones and townhouses in Harlem, built in the 1880s and 90s.
A few blocks away, at 20 East 127th Street, is the townhouse where the poet Langston Hughes lived for the last twenty years of his life.
Walk west to 125th Street, Harlem's main commercial street, and look for the red and white vertical sign of the Apollo Theater, at 253 West 125th Street.
The building opened in 1914 as Hurtig and Seamon's New Burlesque Theater.
Like many theaters in Harlem at the time, it was for white audiences only.
In 1934, new owners reopened it as the Apollo Theater, presenting variety shows for Black audiences.
It quickly became the most famous venue for Black performers in America.
Its most famous institution is Amateur Night, held on Wednesday nights since 1934.
The audience is famously tough.
If they like a performer, they cheer; if not, they boo, and a figure called the Executioner sweeps the performer off the stage.
In November 1934, a seventeen-year-old girl named Ella Fitzgerald, who had planned to dance, lost her nerve and decided to sing instead.
She won.
It launched her career.
Other performers who were discovered or got early breaks at the Apollo include Billie Holiday, Sarah Vaughan, James Brown, Gladys Knight, the Jackson Five, Stevie Wonder, Lauryn Hill, and many more.
Look for the Tree of Hope, a stump on the stage.
It's a piece of an elm that once stood outside on Seventh Avenue, between the Lafayette Theatre and Connie's Inn.
Performers rubbed the tree for luck.
When it was cut down in the 1930s, a piece was saved and placed on the Apollo stage, and amateur performers still rub it for luck before they go on.
James Brown recorded his album Live at the Apollo here in October 1962.
Released in 1963, it became one of the most celebrated live albums ever made.
Look along 125th Street.
It's officially named Martin Luther King Junior Boulevard.
Throughout the twentieth century, it was the commercial and political heart of Harlem, lined with stores, theaters, and restaurants.
For decades, many of its stores were owned by white merchants who refused to hire Black workers.
In the 1930s, Harlem activists launched the Don't Buy Where You Can't Work campaign, boycotting and picketing stores until they hired Black employees.
The campaign was one of the first major direct-action civil rights campaigns in the North.
Since the 1990s, national chains have moved onto 125th Street, and in 2008, the city rezoned the street for taller buildings, changes that have been both welcomed and resented.
Walk to the corner of 125th Street and Adam Clayton Powell Junior Boulevard, also known as Seventh Avenue.
Look at the tall white terracotta building on the corner.
This is the former Hotel Theresa.
When it opened in 1913, the Theresa was a hotel for white guests only, even as the neighborhood around it became predominantly Black.
In 1940, under new ownership, it opened to Black guests and quickly became the most important Black hotel in the country.
It was nicknamed the Waldorf of Harlem.
At a time when most hotels in Midtown Manhattan wouldn't accept Black guests, the Theresa hosted Black celebrities, athletes, and musicians.
Joe Louis, the heavyweight boxing champion, celebrated his victories here, with crowds filling the street below.
Jimi Hendrix, Little Richard, Duke Ellington, Josephine Baker, and Dinah Washington stayed here.
In September 1960, the Theresa became the center of world attention.
Fidel Castro, the new leader of Cuba, came to New York for a meeting of the United Nations General Assembly.
After a dispute with his Midtown hotel, he moved his entire delegation to the Theresa in Harlem, a deliberate political statement.
He was visited there by Malcolm X and by the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev, who came up to Harlem to meet him.
Crowds gathered on the street outside.
A few weeks later, the presidential candidate John F. Kennedy campaigned outside the Theresa.
Malcolm X later rented offices in the Theresa for his new Organization of Afro-American Unity, which he founded in 1964 after splitting from the Nation of Islam.
In February 1965, Malcolm X was assassinated while giving a speech at the Audubon Ballroom in Washington Heights.
The hotel closed in 1966 and was converted into offices.
Its distinctive white facade remains.
Across the street, the tall office tower is the Adam Clayton Powell Junior State Office Building, completed in the 1970s, on the site where Black activists had hoped to build a community center.
Its construction led to protests and an occupation of the site in 1969.
In front of it, look for the statue of Adam Clayton Powell Junior, whom you'll hear about at Abyssinian Baptist Church.
Walk north on Malcolm X Boulevard, also known as Lenox Avenue, to 135th Street.
On the corner is the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, one of the world's leading research libraries devoted to the history and culture of people of African descent.
It began with the collection of Arturo Alfonso Schomburg, an Afro-Puerto Rican scholar and collector who arrived in New York in 1891.
As a schoolboy in Puerto Rico, Schomburg had been told by a teacher that Black people had no history.
He spent his life proving the teacher wrong, gathering books, manuscripts, art, and artifacts documenting the achievements of people of African descent.
In 1926, the New York Public Library bought his collection, with funding from the Carnegie Corporation, and placed it here, in the 135th Street branch library.
Schomburg later became the curator.
The library, and its neighborhood, became a hub of the Harlem Renaissance.
Writers met, read, and debated at the library.
The poet Countee Cullen and the writer Zora Neale Hurston were among the many who used its resources.
Step into the lobby and look down.
Under the floor of the atrium, beneath a cosmogram, a circular design inspired by African and African American symbols, lie the ashes of the poet Langston Hughes.
The design incorporates the words of his poem The Negro Speaks of Rivers, with rivers radiating out from the center.
Hughes's interment here honors his deep connection to this library.

Langston Hughes was the leading poet of the Harlem Renaissance, and his poetry, with its jazz and blues rhythms and its portraits of everyday Black life, made him one of the most important American writers of the twentieth century.
