His poem Harlem, which asks what happens to a dream deferred, inspired the title of Lorraine Hansberry's play A Raisin in the Sun.
Across Lenox Avenue, look for Harlem Hospital, which has a series of murals painted in the 1930s by Black artists, including Charles Alston, as part of the Works Progress Administration.
They were among the first government commissions given to Black artists, and they depict Black life, history, and medicine.
Walk to West 138th Street, between Lenox Avenue and Adam Clayton Powell Boulevard.
Look for the Gothic stone church, Abyssinian Baptist Church, one of the oldest and most influential Black churches in the United States.
Its origins go back to 1808, in lower Manhattan.
Black members of the First Baptist Church, along with some Ethiopian merchants and sailors visiting the city, were forced to sit in segregated seating.
They walked out and founded their own congregation, naming it Abyssinian, after the old name for Ethiopia.
The church moved several times, following its members uptown, and in 1923, it built this church in Harlem.
The church's most famous pastors were a father and son.
Adam Clayton Powell Senior led the church from 1908 to 1937 and oversaw its move to Harlem.
Under his leadership, it became one of the largest Protestant congregations in the country.
His son, Adam Clayton Powell Junior, succeeded him as pastor and became one of the most important Black political figures in American history.
In the 1930s, he led protests and boycotts, including the Don't Buy Where You Can't Work campaign.
In 1944, he was elected to Congress, the first Black congressman from New York.

In Congress, he became chairman of the powerful Education and Labor Committee, where he helped pass major legislation of the 1960s, including laws on minimum wage, education, and anti-poverty programs.
He was also flamboyant, defiant, and controversial, and he was eventually expelled from Congress in 1967 over ethics charges, though the Supreme Court later ruled the expulsion unconstitutional.

Another historical connection: the German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, who later became famous for resisting the Nazis, spent a year in New York in 1930 and 1931, studying at Union Theological Seminary.
He worshipped at Abyssinian and taught Sunday school here.
He said that his experience in the Black church in Harlem shaped his theology, and his commitment to standing with the oppressed.
Today, Abyssinian's Sunday services, with their powerful gospel music, draw so many tourists that the church has had to set rules to make sure members have seats.
If you go, dress respectfully and arrive early.
Walk to Lenox Avenue between 140th and 141st Streets.
Today, there's an apartment complex here.
Look for a plaque marking the site of the Savoy Ballroom, which stood here from 1926 to 1958.
The Savoy took up an entire block front, with a dance floor that held thousands of people, and two bandstands at either end, so the music never stopped.
It was nicknamed the Home of Happy Feet.
Crucially, it was integrated: Black and white dancers danced together, at a time when that was rare and, in many places, illegal.
The Savoy is where the Lindy Hop was born, a fast, acrobatic swing dance that became a national craze.

According to a widely told story, in 1928, a dancer named George Shorty Snowden was asked what the dance was called, and, thinking of Charles Lindbergh's recent solo flight across the Atlantic, called it the Lindy Hop.
Dancers like Frankie Manning, who invented the first aerial moves, took the dance to new heights, literally.
The Savoy was also famous for its battles of the bands.
The house band, led by the drummer Chick Webb, with a young Ella Fitzgerald as his singer, famously took on visiting bands.
In a celebrated 1937 battle, Webb's band went up against Benny Goodman's orchestra, and many in the crowd thought Webb won.
A few blocks south, at the corner of Lenox Avenue and 142nd Street, stood the original Cotton Club.

It was owned by gangsters, including Owney Madden, and it was a whites-only club, despite being in Harlem, featuring Black performers in shows that often played to racist stereotypes of the jungle and the plantation.
It was nonetheless a launching pad for some of the greatest musicians of the era.
Duke Ellington's orchestra played there from 1927 to 1931, broadcasting on the radio nationwide, which made Ellington famous.
Cab Calloway, Lena Horne, and Ethel Waters also performed there.

Farther south, at West 118th Street, Minton's Playhouse, in the Hotel Cecil, was where in the early 1940s musicians including Thelonious Monk, Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker, and Kenny Clarke jammed late at night and helped invent bebop, the fast, complex style that became the foundation of modern jazz.
And at Lenox Avenue and 126th Street, look for Sylvia's, opened in 1962 by Sylvia Woods, known as the Queen of Soul Food.
It became a Harlem institution, visited by presidents, celebrities, and tourists from around the world.
Walk west to West 138th and 139th Streets, between Adam Clayton Powell Junior Boulevard and Frederick Douglass Boulevard.
These two blocks, officially the St. Nicholas Historic District, are known as Strivers' Row, and they're among the most beautiful residential blocks in New York.
They were built in 1891 to 1893 by a developer named David King, who hired three of the leading architectural firms of the day to design them, each with a distinct style.
James Brown Lord designed the red brick Georgian houses on the south side of 138th Street.
Bruce Price and Clarence Luce designed the yellow brick and limestone Colonial Revival houses on the north side of 138th and the south side of 139th.
And McKim, Mead and White, the most prestigious firm in the country, designed the dark brick Italian Renaissance houses on the north side of 139th Street.
Together, they form a rare example of a unified, planned development, with houses sharing rear alleys and service courts.
Look for the signs on the gateposts to the rear alleys, reading Walk your horses.
The alleys were used for deliveries and for horses and carriages to reach the stables.
Originally, the houses were built for wealthy white families.
But the houses were built just before an economic downturn, and as Harlem's population changed, they didn't sell well to white buyers.
By 1919 and 1920, the houses were sold to African American buyers, many of them doctors, lawyers, musicians, and other professionals.
The neighborhood got its nickname because it was seen as a place for ambitious, upwardly mobile Black Harlemites, strivers.

Residents over the years included the composer and bandleader W. C. Handy, known as the Father of the Blues; the bandleader Fletcher Henderson; and the surgeon Louis T. Wright, one of the first Black doctors on the staff of a New York City hospital.
Strivers' Row remains one of the most prestigious addresses in Harlem.
As you walk along the blocks, notice how carefully the houses have been maintained, with their stoops, ironwork, and doorways.
It's a reminder of the Black middle and upper class that has always been part of Harlem's story.
End your walk on the hill to the west, near St. Nicholas Park and West 141st Street.
This is Hamilton Heights, and just to the north is Sugar Hill.
In St. Nicholas Park, look for a yellow Federal-style house with a porch.
This is Hamilton Grange, the only house Alexander Hamilton ever owned.
He built it in 1802 as a country retreat, on a thirty-two-acre estate, naming it after his father's ancestral home in Scotland.
He only lived here for about two years before he was killed in his duel with Aaron Burr in 1804.
The house has moved twice.
In 1889, as the neighborhood was developed, it was moved a short distance to make way for the street grid and squeezed between a church and an apartment building, on Convent Avenue.

In 2008, the National Park Service moved it again, lifting the entire house over the church's portico and rolling it down the street to its current location in the park, closer to its original setting.
Inside, you can see rooms restored to Hamilton's era.
Tours are free.

Up the hill to the west is the campus of the City College of New York, with its striking Gothic buildings, built from dark Manhattan schist excavated during construction of the subway, and trimmed with white terracotta.
City College was founded in 1847 as the Free Academy, offering free higher education to the children of the working class.
For decades, it was called the Harvard of the proletariat, and it educated generations of immigrants and their children, including many future Nobel Prize winners.

Sugar Hill, the area north of here roughly between 145th and 155th Streets, got its name in the 1920s and 30s because it was where Harlem's sweet life was lived: the most prosperous and successful Black New Yorkers lived here.
Two apartment buildings on Edgecombe Avenue became legendary.

At 409 Edgecombe Avenue lived W. E. B. Du Bois, the civil rights leader and scholar; Thurgood Marshall, who argued Brown versus Board of Education and became the first Black Supreme Court justice; Walter White and Roy Wilkins, leaders of the NAACP; and many others.
At 555 Edgecombe Avenue lived the actor and singer Paul Robeson, the bandleader Count Basie, and the boxer Joe Louis, among others.
Duke Ellington's famous theme song, Take the A Train, written by Billy Strayhorn in 1939, was about the subway line that took you to Sugar Hill.
North of Harlem, Manhattan narrows and rises.
The island's spine becomes a ridge of rock, with cliffs dropping to the Hudson River on the west and the Harlem River on the east.
This is Washington Heights, and at the very top of the island, Inwood.
Many New Yorkers who live downtown have never been up here, which is a shame, because this part of Manhattan has some of the city's most dramatic landscapes and some of its deepest history.
The neighborhood's name comes from Fort Washington, a Revolutionary War fortification built on the highest ground in Manhattan in 1776.
That November, the fort fell to the British in one of the worst American defeats of the war, and almost three thousand American soldiers were captured.
Many died in the horrific conditions of British prison ships in Wallabout Bay, in Brooklyn.
For the rest of the war, the British held all of Manhattan.
For most of the nineteenth century, the area remained rural, with farms and grand country estates.
The naturalist John James Audubon had his estate here.
Development came with the subway in the early 1900s, and apartment buildings filled the ridge.

The neighborhood became home to successive waves of immigrants: Irish, then Greek, and in the 1930s and 40s, so many German Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi persecution that the area was nicknamed Frankfurt on the Hudson.
The future Secretary of State Henry Kissinger grew up here, after his family fled Germany in 1938.
From the 1960s onward, Washington Heights became the center of the Dominican community in the United States.
Today, it's often called Little Dominican Republic, and you'll hear Spanish and bachata everywhere, especially along St. Nicholas Avenue and 181st Street.
Lin-Manuel Miranda, who grew up in nearby Inwood, set his musical In the Heights here, and he wrote parts of Hamilton in a historic house you'll visit on this walk.
This tour covers a long stretch, from 160th Street to the northern tip of Manhattan at about 218th Street.
It's best done in pieces, using the A train or the 1 train, which run up the length of the neighborhood.
You're at the Morris-Jumel Mansion, at West 160th Street and Edgecombe Avenue, the oldest surviving house in Manhattan.
It was built in 1765 as a summer villa for Roger Morris, a British army officer, and his wife Mary Philipse, from one of the wealthiest families in the colony.
It's in the Palladian style, with a grand columned portico, and it sat on a hilltop with views of both the Hudson and Harlem Rivers and all the way down to the harbor.
When the Revolution came, the Morrises, who were loyalists, fled.
In September and October 1776, George Washington made the house his headquarters, during the weeks around the Battle of Harlem Heights.
From here, he could watch British movements.
After Washington left, the British and their Hessian allies used it as a headquarters too.
After the war, in 1790, Washington returned for a dinner here with members of his cabinet, including John Adams, Thomas Jefferson, and Alexander Hamilton.
In 1810, the house was bought by Stephen Jumel, a wealthy French-born wine merchant, and his wife Eliza.
Eliza Jumel was born into poverty in Rhode Island and rose to become one of the richest women in America.
After Stephen died in 1832, Eliza married Aaron Burr, the former vice president who had killed Alexander Hamilton, in this house in 1833.
She was in her late fifties; he was seventy-seven.
The marriage quickly fell apart when Burr started speculating with her money.
She filed for divorce, and the divorce was finalized on the very day Burr died, in 1836.
Her divorce lawyer was Alexander Hamilton Junior, the son of the man Burr had killed.
Lin-Manuel Miranda was given permission to write here while working on Hamilton, and he reportedly wrote parts of the musical in Aaron Burr's bedroom.
As you leave, look across the street at Sylvan Terrace, a short cobblestone lane lined with two rows of small yellow wooden houses, built in 1882 as housing for working people.
It looks like a village street from another century, because it is.
Walk to Broadway and West 165th Street, where you'll see a building with an ornate terracotta facade, with figures of Neptune and sea creatures, attached to a modern glass research building.
This is the former Audubon Ballroom.
It was built in 1912 by William Fox, a Hungarian Jewish immigrant who had started out in the garment business and moved into the new business of movies.
Fox built a chain of theaters, and later founded the Fox Film Corporation, which merged in 1935 to become Twentieth Century-Fox, one of the great Hollywood studios.
The Audubon was a theater and ballroom, used for vaudeville, movies, dances, and meetings.
Labor unions, political groups, and community organizations rented its ballroom.

On February twenty-first, 1965, Malcolm X was speaking to a meeting of his Organization of Afro-American Unity in the ballroom when he was shot and killed by several gunmen in front of his wife, Betty Shabazz, and their children.
Three members of the Nation of Islam were convicted of the murder.
In 2021, after a reinvestigation, two of the three men's convictions were vacated, after it emerged that authorities had withheld evidence.
The case remains a subject of investigation and debate.
In the 1980s and 90s, Columbia University, which owned the building, planned to demolish it for a biomedical research center.
Preservationists and activists protested, and in a compromise, part of the facade and ballroom were preserved and incorporated into the new research building.
Today, the building houses the Malcolm X and Dr. Betty Shabazz Memorial and Educational Center, with a mural depicting Malcolm X's life.

The research building is part of the vast Columbia University Irving Medical Center and NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital complex, which opened here in 1928, as the first academic medical center in the world, combining a hospital, medical school, and research in one place.
A few blocks south, at 155th Street and Broadway, is the Trinity Church Cemetery and Mausoleum, the only active cemetery in Manhattan.
John James Audubon, the naturalist and painter of The Birds of America, is buried there.
He owned an estate, called Minnie's Land, along the Hudson in this neighborhood, which is why the Audubon name appears all over the area.
Walk east to Highbridge Park, near West 173rd Street and Amsterdam Avenue, at the edge of the cliff overlooking the Harlem River.
Here you'll find the High Bridge, the oldest standing bridge in New York City.
The High Bridge was completed in 1848 as part of the Croton Aqueduct, the great water system you may have heard about at Bryant Park and Bethesda Fountain.
Before the aqueduct, New Yorkers relied on wells and polluted cisterns, and epidemics of cholera and other diseases ravaged the city, while fires burned unchecked because there wasn't enough water.
The Croton Aqueduct brought clean water from the Croton River in Westchester County, forty-one miles to the north, flowing entirely by gravity.
The aqueduct had to cross the Harlem River, and engineers built this bridge, modeled on the arched aqueducts of ancient Rome, to carry the water pipes over it.
When it opened, the bridge was a sensation.
A promenade on top became a favorite destination for New Yorkers on Sunday outings.
It was the Victorian equivalent of the High Line.
In the 1920s, several of the original stone arches over the river were replaced with a single steel arch, to allow bigger ships to pass underneath.
The bridge stopped carrying water in the mid-twentieth century, and it was closed to the public in the 1970s.
After a long restoration, it reopened to pedestrians and cyclists in 2015, connecting Manhattan to the Bronx.
Next to the bridge on the Manhattan side stands the High Bridge Water Tower, an octagonal granite tower completed in 1872.
It held water in a tank at the top to provide pressure to supply the growing neighborhoods on the high ground of northern Manhattan.
Its design, with its bell tower, makes it look more like a church tower than a piece of infrastructure.
The Croton system set New York on the path to having one of the best municipal water supplies in the world.

Today, the city's water comes mainly from reservoirs in the Catskill Mountains and the Delaware River watershed, upstate, and it's so clean that it's one of the few big city water systems in the United States that doesn't need to be filtered.
Walk west to Fort Washington Park, along the Hudson, beneath the George Washington Bridge, near West 178th Street.
Here you'll find a small red lighthouse right at the foot of the bridge.
Look up at the bridge.
The George Washington Bridge opened in 1931, connecting Manhattan with Fort Lee, New Jersey.
Its chief engineer was Othmar Ammann, a Swiss immigrant, who later designed the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge.
When it opened, its main span, about thirty-five hundred feet, was nearly double the length of the previous record holder, an astonishing leap.
The towers were originally meant to be covered in concrete and granite, but the Depression put a stop to that, and they were left as bare steel latticework.
The Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier called it the most beautiful bridge in the world, praising the honesty of its exposed steel.
A second, lower deck was added in 1962.
Today, it's one of the busiest motor vehicle bridges in the world, carrying hundreds of thousands of vehicles a day.
Now look at the lighthouse.
It's officially called the Jeffrey's Hook Lighthouse.
It was built in 1880 at Sandy Hook, New Jersey, and moved here in 1921 to warn ships away from the rocky point.
When the bridge was built, its bright lights made the lighthouse obsolete, and it was decommissioned in 1948.
The Coast Guard planned to auction it off.
But the lighthouse had become famous.

In 1942, a children's book called The Little Red Lighthouse and the Great Gray Bridge, by Hildegarde Swift and Lynd Ward, told the story of a little lighthouse that felt useless next to the giant bridge, until one foggy night, it saved a ship.
Children who loved the book wrote letters and protested to save it, and in 1951, the Coast Guard gave the lighthouse to the city.
It was restored and is occasionally open for tours.
High on the ridge above you, near 183rd Street and Fort Washington Avenue, is Bennett Park, the highest natural point in Manhattan, at about two hundred sixty-five feet above sea level.
It's also where Fort Washington stood.
You can still see the outline of the fort marked in the park.
On November sixteenth, 1776, about eight thousand British and Hessian troops attacked the fort from several directions.
It fell within hours.
It was a devastating blow to the American cause, and it forced Washington into a long retreat across New Jersey.
Take the A train to 190th Street, or walk north, to Fort Tryon Park, one of the most beautiful parks in New York, perched on cliffs high above the Hudson.
In the park is The Met Cloisters, a branch of the Metropolitan Museum of Art devoted to the art and architecture of medieval Europe.
The park and the museum were gifts of John D. Rockefeller Junior.
In the 1910s and 20s, he bought up the land here, including the former estate of the industrialist C. K. G. Billings.
He hired the Olmsted Brothers firm, run by the sons of Frederick Law Olmsted, to design a park, and gave it to the city, which opened it in 1935.
Rockefeller also bought land across the Hudson, along the Palisades in New Jersey, and donated it to the public, to ensure that the view from the park would never be spoiled by development.
It still hasn't been.
The museum began with the collection of an American sculptor named George Grey Barnard, who had gathered medieval sculptures and architectural fragments from ruined abbeys and churches in France.
Rockefeller bought the collection in 1925 for the Met and funded a new building to house it.
The Cloisters, which opened in 1938, was designed by the architect Charles Collens.

It incorporates parts of five medieval cloisters, the covered walkways around a monastery's garden, from France and Spain, along with chapels, doorways, and windows, reassembled into a building that evokes a medieval monastery.
Inside, you'll find some of the greatest treasures of medieval art, including the Unicorn Tapestries, seven tapestries woven in the Netherlands around 1500, depicting the hunt for a unicorn.
The gardens, planted with species that were grown in the Middle Ages, are especially beautiful in spring and summer.

The park takes its name from Fort Tryon, an American outpost that was captured by Hessian troops during the Battle of Fort Washington in 1776, and renamed by the British for William Tryon, the last British governor of New York.
Near the park's entrance, look for Margaret Corbin Circle.
Margaret Corbin fought here in that battle.
Her husband was a gunner, and when he was killed, she took his place at the cannon and kept firing until she was seriously wounded.
She later became the first woman in the United States to receive a military pension.
Walk to Broadway and West 204th Street, where you'll find a small white clapboard and fieldstone farmhouse with a gambrel roof and a front porch, sitting on a little hill above the street.
This is the Dyckman Farmhouse Museum, the last surviving Dutch colonial farmhouse in Manhattan.
The Dyckman family were among the early Dutch settlers of upper Manhattan.
Jan Dyckman arrived in the 1660s, and the family farmed land here for generations, eventually owning hundreds of acres.
During the Revolutionary War, British and Hessian troops occupied the area and burned the original Dyckman house.

After the war, around 1784, William Dyckman built this farmhouse, in the Dutch colonial style, with fieldstone and brick walls, a steep roof, and a porch called a stoep, from which the New York word stoop comes.
The family lived here and farmed until the mid-nineteenth century.
By the early twentieth century, the house was in poor condition, surrounded by new apartment buildings.

In 1915, two Dyckman descendants, Mary Alice Dyckman Dean and Fannie Fredericka Dyckman Welch, bought the house, restored it, filled it with family furniture and heirlooms, and donated it to the city as a museum in 1916.
Look around the garden behind the house.
There's a reconstruction of a hut used by Hessian soldiers during the British occupation, and a smokehouse.
In this neighborhood of busy streets and apartment buildings, the farmhouse is a startling reminder that all of Manhattan was once countryside.

Inwood, the neighborhood around you, is one of the most residential and affordable parts of Manhattan, with a large Dominican population, and a mix of Irish and Jewish families who have been here for generations.
The area along Dyckman Street, with its restaurants, bars, and music, comes alive on summer nights.
End your walk in Inwood Hill Park, at the northern tip of Manhattan.
Walk in from the entrance at Seaman Avenue and 207th Street, past the ballfields, to the salt marsh.
Inwood Hill Park contains the last natural forest and the last natural salt marsh in Manhattan.
Unlike Central Park, which was entirely designed and rebuilt, much of the woods here were never cleared for farming or development.
Some of the trees are very old.
Walking the trails up the hill, among large tulip trees, oaks, and rock outcrops, you can get a sense of what the island looked like before Europeans arrived.
The Lenape lived and fished here for thousands of years.
Archaeologists have found evidence of their camps, and on the hillside, you'll find rock shelters, natural caves formed by fallen boulders, which were used by the Lenape.
Near the salt marsh, look for a boulder with a plaque.
This is Shorakkopoch Rock.
It marks the spot where a giant tulip tree stood until 1938, when it died.

Local tradition holds that this was where, in 1626, Peter Minuit of the Dutch West India Company bought Manhattan from the Lenape for trade goods worth sixty guilders, an amount that later writers calculated as twenty-four dollars.
Historians doubt the story's details, including the location.
And the Lenape likely understood the transaction very differently from the Dutch, as an agreement to share the land rather than a permanent sale.
But it's the closest thing to a founding site Manhattan has.
Walk to the water's edge.
The water to the north is Spuyten Duyvil Creek, which separates Manhattan from the Bronx.
The name is Dutch, and its meaning is debated: it may mean in spite of the devil or spouting devil, referring to its strong currents.
Look across the creek at the cliff on the Bronx side.
You'll see a giant blue C painted on the rock.
It was first painted in the 1950s by members of the Columbia University rowing team, who train on the river nearby, and it's been repainted many times since.
Columbia's athletic facilities, including its football stadium, are just to the east.
Spanning the creek is the Henry Hudson Bridge, a steel arch bridge built by Robert Moses in 1936.

According to tradition, somewhere near here in 1609, the explorer Henry Hudson, sailing for the Dutch East India Company, anchored his ship, the Half Moon, on his voyage up the river that now bears his name, looking for a passage to Asia.
You're standing about as far as you can get from Wall Street and still be in Manhattan, in the place where the island's story began.
Before the Brooklyn Bridge, Brooklyn was a separate city, and for much of the nineteenth century, it was the third largest city in the United States, after New York and Philadelphia.
The only way to get to Manhattan was by boat.
The ferry from the foot of Fulton Street was the main link, and the area around the ferry landing became the commercial heart of Brooklyn.
The waterfront north and south of the ferry developed into one of the busiest port districts in the world.
Massive warehouses, called stores, lined the shore, holding coffee, sugar, tobacco, grain, and other goods unloaded from ships.
Factories sprang up in the blocks behind them, making paper boxes, machinery, soap, and other products.
The neighborhood that we now call DUMBO, for Down Under the Manhattan Bridge Overpass, was one of the great industrial districts of the country.
Some of its businesses became household names.
Others invented things you use every day without knowing where they came from.
Then came the bridges.
The Brooklyn Bridge opened in 1883, followed by the Williamsburg Bridge in 1903 and the Manhattan Bridge in 1909.
In 1898, Brooklyn voted, narrowly, to merge with New York, becoming one of its five boroughs.
Many Brooklynites still call it the Great Mistake of 1898.
After World War Two, the waterfront declined.
Container shipping moved the port to New Jersey, the warehouses emptied, and factories moved out.
By the 1970s, the area under the Manhattan Bridge was a desolate industrial zone, with a few artists living illegally in the empty lofts.
In 1978, residents coined the name DUMBO, reportedly on purpose to make it sound unappealing and keep developers away.
It didn't work.

A developer named David Walentas began buying buildings in the early 1980s, and over the following decades, he and others transformed DUMBO into one of the most expensive neighborhoods in New York, filled with tech companies, designers, and luxury apartments.
Meanwhile, the piers along the water were transformed into Brooklyn Bridge Park.
This tour begins on the Brooklyn Bridge and ends in the park.
If you're starting in Manhattan, walk across the bridge, and the first stop will play as you approach the first tower.
You're on the Brooklyn Bridge.
Look up at the massive granite towers with their Gothic arches, and the web of steel cables radiating from them.
The bridge was designed by John Augustus Roebling, a German immigrant engineer who had pioneered the manufacture of wire rope and built several suspension bridges.
In 1869, while surveying the site, Roebling's foot was crushed by a ferry against the pilings at the Fulton Ferry landing.
His toes were amputated, and he died of tetanus a few weeks later.
He was sixty-three.
His son, Washington Roebling, a thirty-two-year-old Civil War veteran and engineer, took over.
To build the towers' foundations, workers labored inside caissons, huge upside-down wooden boxes sunk to the river bottom, filled with compressed air to keep water out.
As the caissons sank deeper, workers began suffering from a mysterious illness: crippling joint pain, paralysis, and sometimes death.
They called it caisson disease.
Today we know it as decompression sickness, or the bends, caused by nitrogen bubbles forming in the blood when people come out of high pressure too quickly.
Several workers died.
Washington Roebling himself was struck by it in 1872 and left partially paralyzed and in pain for the rest of his life.
Unable to visit the site, Roebling directed construction from his bedroom window in Brooklyn Heights, watching through a telescope.
His wife, Emily Warren Roebling, became his link to the project.
She learned higher mathematics, the strength of materials, and cable construction, and relayed his instructions to the engineers.
Over time, she effectively became a manager of the project.
On opening day, May twenty-fourth, 1883, she was given the honor of the first ride across the bridge, carrying a rooster as a symbol of victory.
A plaque on the bridge honors her, along with her husband and father-in-law.
The bridge was an engineering marvel.
Its main span, about sixteen hundred feet, was the longest in the world.
It was the first suspension bridge to use steel wire for its cables.
There was a scandal during construction: the contractor supplying the wire, J. Lloyd Haigh, was caught substituting defective wire.
Some of it had already been woven into the cables.
Roebling compensated by adding extra wires, and the bridge was built to be several times stronger than necessary, which is part of why it's still standing.
A week after it opened, on May thirtieth, a rumor that the bridge was collapsing caused a stampede on the crowded walkway, and twelve people were crushed to death.
To prove the bridge was safe, in 1884, the showman P. T. Barnum led a parade of twenty-one elephants across it.
You're at Fulton Ferry Landing, at the foot of Old Fulton Street, on the water just north of the Brooklyn Bridge.
This was the gateway to Brooklyn for centuries.
Ferries crossed here as early as the 1600s, rowed or sailed across the treacherous East River.
In 1814, Robert Fulton, the steamboat pioneer buried at Trinity Church, launched steam ferry service here.
The street leading up the hill was renamed Fulton Street in his honor, and it became Brooklyn's main street.
This landing was also the site of one of the most important moments of the American Revolution.
In August 1776, the British defeated George Washington's army at the Battle of Brooklyn, also called the Battle of Long Island, the largest battle of the war.
Washington's army was trapped in Brooklyn Heights, with the British army in front and the East River behind.
On the night of August twenty-ninth, Washington ordered a secret retreat.

Using every boat they could find, soldiers from a Massachusetts regiment of fishermen and sailors from Marblehead, led by Colonel John Glover, ferried about nine thousand troops, with their supplies and artillery, across the river to Manhattan, in total silence, through the night.
As dawn broke, a thick fog rolled in, hiding the last boats from the British.
By the time the fog lifted, the entire army was gone.
If the British had captured Washington's army that night, the Revolution might well have ended.
Walt Whitman, the great poet, was a Brooklyn man, and he rode this ferry constantly.

In his poem Crossing Brooklyn Ferry, published in 1856, he imagined future generations making the same crossing, looking at the same river and sky, and he addressed them directly: Just as you feel when you look on the river and sky, so I felt.
Whitman also worked as editor of the Brooklyn Daily Eagle, the newspaper whose former warehouse, the Eagle Warehouse, still stands just up Old Fulton Street, now converted to apartments.
Look around the landing.
The barge moored nearby is Bargemusic, a floating concert hall that has hosted chamber music concerts since 1977.
Nearby is the River Café, a celebrated restaurant opened in 1977, when this area was still desolate.
And up the street are two of the most famous pizzerias in the city, which have long attracted lines of tourists.
Walk north along the water into Brooklyn Bridge Park, to the long row of massive brick warehouses facing the river.
These are the Empire Stores, built in two phases between 1869 and 1885.
In the nineteenth century, a warehouse was called a store, because it stored goods.
Ships from around the world unloaded their cargoes here: coffee from Brazil, sugar from the Caribbean, jute, hides, and other goods.
The thick brick walls and small windows kept goods safe and the temperature stable.
Workers used iron shutters to protect the cargo, and you can still see some of them on the windows.
The waterfront here was dominated by coffee and sugar.
One of the most important companies was Arbuckle Brothers, a coffee company founded in Pittsburgh.
Arbuckle had a brilliant innovation: it sold coffee already roasted, sealed in one-pound paper packages, at a time when most people bought green coffee beans and roasted them at home.
The coffee was coated with a glaze of sugar and egg to keep it fresh.
Their brand, Ariosa, became so popular in the American West in the late nineteenth century that it was called the coffee that won the West.
Arbuckle moved its operations to Brooklyn, along this waterfront, and also went into sugar refining, challenging the powerful sugar trust in a famous price war.
The Empire Stores sat empty for decades after the shipping industry declined.
They were redeveloped in the 2010s into offices, shops, and restaurants, with a rooftop terrace.
Next door, the roofless brick ruin with arched openings is the Tobacco Warehouse, built in the 1870s and used to store tobacco during inspection.
The roof was removed in the 1990s, and part of it is now home to St. Ann's Warehouse, a theater.
Now look at the glass box by the water.
Inside is Jane's Carousel, a carousel built in 1922 by the Philadelphia Toboggan Company for an amusement park in Youngstown, Ohio.

In 1984, Jane Walentas, an artist and the wife of the developer David Walentas, bought it at auction and spent more than two decades restoring it by hand, stripping away layers of paint to reveal the original colors of its forty-eight horses.
In 2011, it reopened here, inside a transparent pavilion designed by the French architect Jean Nouvel.
The carousel survived Hurricane Sandy in 2012, when the pavilion flooded but the carousel was undamaged, and photos of it lit up in the storm went viral.
Walk up to Washington Street, at Water Street, and turn to face the Manhattan Bridge.

This is one of the most photographed views in New York: the narrow street framed by brick warehouses, with the Manhattan Bridge's tower filling the gap at the end, and the Empire State Building visible through the bridge's arch.
The buildings around you were once part of Gairville, the factory empire of Robert Gair, a Scottish immigrant who invented a product you've probably used today: the folding cardboard box.
Gair ran a business printing and making paper bags.
In 1879, one of his workers made a mistake: a metal printing rule, used to crease paper, shifted, and it cut through a stack of paper bags instead of creasing them.
Gair realized that he could use the same principle to cut and crease cardboard in one operation, producing flat, pre-cut boxes that could be folded into shape.
Before this, boxes had to be cut and assembled by hand, slowly and expensively.
Gair's machines could produce thousands quickly and cheaply.
The innovation transformed packaging.
Gair's company became one of the largest producers of boxes in the world.

One of his most important customers was the National Biscuit Company, Nabisco, which used Gair's boxes for its Uneeda Biscuits, the first crackers sold in sealed packages, which you may have heard about on the Chelsea tour.
The cardboard box was essential to the rise of national brands, because it allowed companies to package, label, and ship products directly to consumers.
Gair bought and built more and more buildings in this area.
They were among the first large reinforced concrete factory buildings in the city.
Look for the building at 1 Main Street with a clock tower on top.
That was one of Gair's buildings.
Its clock tower penthouse, with enormous clock faces as windows, was converted into one of the most expensive apartments in Brooklyn.
The Gair company moved out in the 1920s, and the buildings were used by other manufacturers.
Today, many of them house tech companies, design studios, and media firms.
DUMBO is part of what the city has promoted as the Brooklyn Tech Triangle, along with the Navy Yard and Downtown Brooklyn.
It's fitting that a neighborhood built on a packaging innovation is now full of startups trying to invent the next one.
Walk south, under the Brooklyn Bridge, to the corner of Columbia Heights and Old Fulton Street, at the foot of Brooklyn Heights.
Look up at the large buildings climbing the hillside above you.
For most of the twentieth century, these buildings were home to two very different organizations.
The first was E. R. Squibb and Sons, the pharmaceutical company.
Edward Robinson Squibb was a Navy doctor who was horrified by the poor quality of the medicines given to sailors.
In 1858, he set up a laboratory here in Brooklyn to manufacture pure, standardized drugs, especially ether, an anesthetic, and chloroform.
During the Civil War, his company supplied medicines to the Union army.
Squibb was a crusader for drug quality and an early advocate of federal regulation of food and drugs.
His company became one of the leading pharmaceutical companies in the country, and it's an ancestor of today's Bristol Myers Squibb.
The second organization was the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, the headquarters of the Jehovah's Witnesses.

The Witnesses moved their headquarters to Brooklyn in 1909, and over the decades, they bought many buildings in Brooklyn Heights and DUMBO, including the old Squibb buildings, for their offices, residences, and printing plants.
They printed hundreds of millions of copies of their magazines, The Watchtower and Awake!, here, distributing them around the world.
For decades, a giant red sign reading Watchtower, with the time and temperature, sat on top of one of the buildings, and it became a familiar sight for anyone crossing the Brooklyn Bridge.
In the 2010s, the Witnesses moved their headquarters to Warwick, in upstate New York, and sold their Brooklyn properties to developers for large sums.
The Watchtower sign was taken down in 2017.
The buildings have been converted into offices and apartments.

Up the hill, along Columbia Heights, is the beginning of Brooklyn Heights, America's first designated historic district, and the Brooklyn Heights Promenade, which you can explore on the Brooklyn Heights tour.
It was from a house on Columbia Heights, near here, that Washington Roebling watched the Brooklyn Bridge being built through his telescope.
End your walk on Pier 1 in Brooklyn Bridge Park, just south of the Brooklyn Bridge, on the water.
Look out at the view: the towers of lower Manhattan rising across the river, the Statue of Liberty in the harbor to the south, and the Brooklyn Bridge arching overhead.
It's one of the best views in New York.
This waterfront was once among the busiest port areas in the world.

In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the New York Dock Company and other companies operated a continuous line of piers, warehouses, and rail yards along the Brooklyn shore, from here south to Red Hook.
Brooklyn's docks handled a huge share of the cargo coming into the Port of New York.
Thousands of longshoremen, many of them Irish and Italian immigrants, loaded and unloaded ships by hand.
The work was brutal, and the docks were controlled by corrupt unions and organized crime, as dramatized in the 1954 film On the Waterfront.
Then came the shipping container.
In 1956, a trucking entrepreneur named Malcolm McLean shipped containers from Port Newark, in New Jersey, on a converted tanker, launching the container revolution.
Containers could be lifted by crane directly from ship to truck or train, eliminating most of the labor of loading and unloading.
But they needed huge open spaces for stacking and handling, which Brooklyn's narrow piers didn't have.
The shipping industry moved to the vast container terminals in New Jersey.
By the 1980s, Brooklyn's piers were nearly abandoned.
In the 2000s, after years of community advocacy, the piers were transformed into Brooklyn Bridge Park, designed by the landscape architecture firm Michael Van Valkenburgh Associates.
The park stretches about a mile and a half along the waterfront, from here to Atlantic Avenue.
Each pier has a different use: lawns, playgrounds, sports fields, a salt marsh, and even a beach for kayaks.

The park was designed to be financially self-sustaining: luxury apartment buildings and a hotel were built within its boundaries, and their fees pay for the park's maintenance, a model that has been both praised and criticized.
The park also uses salvaged materials.
Look for benches made of wood from the old pier sheds, and parts of the old industrial waterfront incorporated into the design.
Stand at the end of the pier and imagine this view a century ago, filled with ships, ferries, and barges.
Brooklyn Heights is often called America's first suburb.
In the early nineteenth century, it was a bluff of farmland and estates above the East River, directly across from lower Manhattan.

When steam ferry service began at Fulton Ferry in 1814, a merchant could live up here, in a quiet, leafy neighborhood with fresh air and a stunning view, and commute to his counting house on Wall Street in minutes.
Real estate promoters advertised the neighborhood exactly that way, and the idea of commuting from a residential district to a business district was born.
The key figure was Hezekiah Pierrepont, a merchant who made his fortune in shipping and, notably, in gin.
He owned the Anchor Gin distillery on the Brooklyn waterfront.
Pierrepont bought up much of the land on the Heights, invested in the steam ferry, and divided his property into lots for townhouses.
Other landowners followed.
Several of the streets are named after the families who owned the land: Pierrepont, Remsen, Joralemon, Hicks, Middagh.
Others are named for fruits: Orange, Pineapple, and Cranberry Streets.

According to a long-told local story, an early resident, Lady Middagh, was annoyed by her neighbors naming streets after themselves, tore down their street signs, and replaced them with the names of fruits.
The city eventually accepted her names.
Brooklyn Heights became one of the most beautiful residential neighborhoods in the country, with streets of Federal, Greek Revival, Gothic Revival, Italianate, and Romanesque townhouses.
It was the home of prosperous merchants, ministers, and, later, writers and artists.

In the twentieth century, as the wealthy moved elsewhere, many houses were split into rooming houses and apartments, and the neighborhood attracted writers drawn by cheap rents, beautiful streets, and views of Manhattan.

In the 1950s, the neighborhood fought to protect itself from Robert Moses's highway plans and from urban renewal, and in 1965, it became the first neighborhood protected as a historic district under New York City's new landmarks law.

The south end of this walk takes you down to Atlantic Avenue, with its Middle Eastern shops and a remarkable secret beneath the street, and to Borough Hall, the old City Hall of the independent City of Brooklyn.
You're on the Brooklyn Heights Promenade, a walkway running about a third of a mile along the edge of the bluff, from Remsen Street to Orange Street.
The view across the East River to lower Manhattan, the Brooklyn Bridge, and the Statue of Liberty is one of the most famous in the world.
The Promenade exists because of a highway.
In the 1940s, Robert Moses planned the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, and his original route ran right through the middle of Brooklyn Heights, which would have destroyed blocks of historic houses.
The residents fought back.
The compromise was ingenious.
Instead of cutting through the neighborhood, the highway was built along the edge of the bluff, in a stack of three cantilevered levels.
Two levels of highway traffic, one in each direction, are stacked on top of each other, and on top of the highway is the Promenade, which opened in 1950.
It's a rare example of a highway built to fit a neighborhood, rather than the other way around.

That structure, known as the triple cantilever, is now around seventy-five years old and has been deteriorating, and its future has been the subject of a long, contentious debate over how to repair or replace it.
During the Revolutionary War, this bluff was strategically important.

In August 1776, as the British closed in after the Battle of Brooklyn, George Washington held a council of war in a house that stood near here, the Four Chimneys, the home of Philip Livingston, a signer of the Declaration of Independence.
It was there that Washington decided to retreat across the East River to Manhattan, the escape you can hear about at Fulton Ferry Landing.
Look across the river at the skyline.
From here, you can trace the history of lower Manhattan, from the old church steeples to the skyscrapers of Wall Street, to One World Trade Center.
Many New Yorkers watched the Twin Towers burn from this Promenade on September eleventh, 2001.
Some residents of the Heights were among those killed, and the Promenade became a gathering place for vigils.
Walk north from the Promenade to Columbia Heights and Willow Street, where some of the most famous writers in American history have lived.
At 110 Columbia Heights, which no longer stands, Washington Roebling lived while he supervised the building of the Brooklyn Bridge from his window.

In a remarkable coincidence, more than forty years later, the poet Hart Crane rented a room in the same building, and he discovered that it was the very room from which Roebling had watched the bridge.
Crane, inspired, wrote his epic poem The Bridge, published in 1930, which uses the Brooklyn Bridge as a symbol of America.
Now walk to 70 Willow Street, a large yellow Greek Revival house built in the 1830s.
In the 1950s and 60s, Truman Capote rented a basement apartment here, from a friend who owned the house.
It was here that he wrote Breakfast at Tiffany's, published in 1958, and much of In Cold Blood, published in 1966.
He described the neighborhood in an essay, A House on the Heights, which captures its atmosphere in the 1950s.
The house sold in 2012 for a then-record price for a Brooklyn single-family home.

Other writers who lived in the Heights include Arthur Miller, who lived here in the years around Death of a Salesman; Norman Mailer, who wrote much of The Naked and the Dead while living in the Heights and later lived on Columbia Heights for decades; W. H. Auden and Carson McCullers, who shared a famous house on Middagh Street in the early 1940s with other artists, including the burlesque star Gypsy Rose Lee and the composer Benjamin Britten; and Marianne Moore, who lived in Fort Greene nearby.
Thomas Wolfe lived here too.
Look around at the houses on Willow Street and the side streets.
Notice the variety of styles, from early nineteenth century Federal houses, with their small dormers and simple doorways, to grand Italianate brownstones from the mid-1800s.
At 155 to 159 Willow Street, look for three small Federal-style houses, among the oldest in the neighborhood.
And on the corner of Willow and Middagh Streets, look for 24 Middagh Street, a charming wooden Federal house built in 1824, one of the oldest houses in the Heights.
Walk to Orange Street, between Hicks and Henry Streets, to Plymouth Church, a plain brick church with a courtyard and a bronze statue.
Plymouth Church was founded in 1847, and its first minister was Henry Ward Beecher, the most famous preacher in America in the mid-nineteenth century.
Beecher came from a remarkable family.
His father, Lyman Beecher, was a renowned preacher, and his sister was Harriet Beecher Stowe, the author of Uncle Tom's Cabin.
Henry Ward Beecher was a passionate, theatrical speaker and an outspoken opponent of slavery.
People came by ferry from Manhattan in such large crowds to hear him that the ferries were nicknamed Beecher Boats.
Beecher dramatized the evils of slavery by staging mock slave auctions in the church.
Most famously, in 1860, he brought a young enslaved girl, nicknamed Pinky, before the congregation and asked them to contribute money to buy her freedom.
The congregation filled the collection plates, and she was freed.
The church is believed to have been a stop on the Underground Railroad, sheltering people escaping slavery in its basement, though documentation is limited.
Beecher also helped raise money to send rifles to anti-slavery settlers in Kansas, which were shipped in boxes labeled Bibles, and they were nicknamed Beecher's Bibles.
In February 1860, Abraham Lincoln attended a service here, just before his Cooper Union speech in Manhattan.
The pew where he sat is marked.
Beecher's career was later tarnished by scandal.
In 1874, his friend Theodore Tilton accused him of having an affair with Tilton's wife, Elizabeth.
Tilton sued Beecher, and the trial in 1875 was a national sensation, covered by newspapers across the country.
The jury couldn't reach a verdict, and Beecher remained in his pulpit, but his reputation never fully recovered.
In the courtyard, look for the bronze statue of Beecher by Gutzon Borglum, the sculptor who carved Mount Rushmore.
It includes figures of two enslaved people at its base.
On the wall nearby is a relief of Lincoln.
Inside the church, there's a stained glass window commemorating Beecher, and a piece of Plymouth Rock in Massachusetts.
Walk south to Montague Street, the main commercial street of Brooklyn Heights, lined with shops, restaurants, and grand bank buildings.
Look for the building at 215 Montague Street.
In the 1940s, this was the headquarters of the Brooklyn Dodgers baseball club.
On August twenty-eighth, 1945, the Dodgers' president, Branch Rickey, met here with a young Black baseball player named Jackie Robinson.
For three hours, Rickey questioned him and warned him about the abuse he would face as the first Black player in the major leagues.
Rickey famously told him he was looking for a player with the guts not to fight back.
Robinson agreed.
He signed with the Dodgers organization, and on April fifteenth, 1947, he took the field at Ebbets Field, breaking baseball's color barrier.
A plaque on the building marks the meeting.
Montague Street was also the financial center of Brooklyn.

Look for the grand bank buildings near the corner of Clinton Street, like the former Brooklyn Trust Company building at 177 Montague Street, designed by York and Sawyer, the architects of the Federal Reserve Bank in Manhattan, and modeled on a Renaissance palazzo.
Today, it's a Chase branch.
At the corner of Pierrepont and Clinton Streets, look for the elaborate red brick and terracotta building with busts on the facade.
This is the Center for Brooklyn History, originally built in 1881 for the Long Island Historical Society, designed by George B. Post, the architect of the New York Stock Exchange.

The busts on the facade depict famous figures, including Christopher Columbus, Benjamin Franklin, Shakespeare, Beethoven, and Michelangelo, and there's a Viking and a Native American representing Long Island's history.
Inside, the library is one of the most beautiful historic reading rooms in New York.
Nearby, on Montague Street, the church of St. Ann and the Holy Trinity has some of the earliest figural stained glass windows made in America, from the 1840s.
The Heights has had many prominent residents in business, too.
Charles Pratt, of the Astral Oil Company, whose story you'll hear on the Williamsburg and Greenpoint tour, built mansions nearby, on Clinton Avenue in Clinton Hill.
And the neighborhood's banks, insurance companies, and law firms made Montague Street the Wall Street of Brooklyn.
Walk to Joralemon and Court Streets, to the white marble building with a columned portico and a cupola.
This is Brooklyn Borough Hall, completed in 1848 as the City Hall of the City of Brooklyn.
Brooklyn was an independent city from 1834 to 1898.
It grew rapidly, fed by ferries, the Navy Yard, the port, and industry, and by the 1890s it was the fourth largest city in the United States, with nearly a million people.
Brooklyn had its own newspapers, its own museums, its own parks, and a strong civic identity.
In 1894, voters in New York, Brooklyn, and the surrounding towns voted on whether to consolidate into one city.
In Brooklyn, the vote was extremely close: consolidation passed by only a few hundred votes, out of more than a hundred and twenty thousand.
On January first, 1898, Greater New York was born, with five boroughs: Manhattan, Brooklyn, the Bronx, Queens, and Staten Island.
This building became Borough Hall.
Many Brooklynites resented the merger, which they called the Great Mistake.
Some still do.
The building's design is Greek Revival.
The cupola was added later, after a fire, in 1898.
Today, it's the office of the Brooklyn Borough President.
Notice the statue of Justice that was planned for the top but only installed in the 1980s, over a century after it was first designed.
Look around the plaza.
Columbus Park, in front of Borough Hall, has a statue of Henry Ward Beecher, whom you may have heard about at Plymouth Church.
To the north, the massive building with columns is the Brooklyn Municipal Building, and the large building to the east is the New York State Supreme Court.

Downtown Brooklyn has been transformed since a rezoning in 2004, with dozens of residential towers, including the first skyscraper in Brooklyn to exceed one thousand feet, completed in the early 2020s.
Court Street, running south from here, leads into the neighborhoods of Cobble Hill and Carroll Gardens.
A farmers' market is held in front of Borough Hall several days a week.
End your walk on Atlantic Avenue, near Court Street.
Look along the street for the Middle Eastern shops, restaurants, and grocery stores.

Starting in the late nineteenth century, immigrants from the Ottoman province of Syria, including what is now Lebanon, settled in lower Manhattan, in a neighborhood called Little Syria, on Washington Street.
Most were Christians, and many were merchants, selling textiles and lace.
When the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel construction and other projects destroyed much of Little Syria in the 1940s, many of these businesses moved here, to Atlantic Avenue.
The most famous is Sahadi's, a grocery store that opened in Manhattan in 1895 and moved here in 1948.
It's still run by the Sahadi family, selling dried fruits, nuts, spices, olives, and other foods.
Now here's a secret: beneath your feet is the oldest subway tunnel in the world.
In 1844, the Long Island Rail Road built a tunnel under Atlantic Avenue, about half a mile long, from near the waterfront to about Boerum Place.
It was the first railroad tunnel under a city street in the world.
It was used for less than twenty years, closed in 1861, and sealed off.
Over time, it was forgotten.
Legends grew up around it: that it held the body of a murdered man, or an old steam locomotive, or the lost pages of John Wilkes Booth's diary.

In 1980, a young engineering student named Bob Diamond, who had heard the stories, tracked down the tunnel, found a manhole under the street, crawled through it, and broke through a wall to discover it.
He ran tours of the tunnel for years, until the city closed it in 2010.
The tunnel is still there, sealed under the pavement.
A few blocks east, at Boerum Place and Schermerhorn Street, is the New York Transit Museum, housed in a decommissioned subway station from 1936.
On its platforms, you can walk through a collection of historic subway cars, from early wooden cars to sleek cars from the 1960s.
It's a fun place to end this walk, and a reminder of how transportation, from ferries to bridges to railroads and subways, shaped every part of Brooklyn.

This walk covers the neighborhoods just east of Downtown Brooklyn: the Brooklyn Navy Yard on the waterfront, the brownstone neighborhood of Fort Greene, and the commercial heart of the borough around Fulton Street and Atlantic Avenue.
For more than a century and a half, the Brooklyn Navy Yard was one of the most important shipyards in the United States.
Ships built here fought in every American war from the War of 1812 to Vietnam.
At its peak in World War Two, the yard employed around seventy thousand people working around the clock, making it one of the largest industrial employers in the country.
The yard's workers, and the businesses that served them, filled the surrounding neighborhoods.
Fort Greene takes its name from a Revolutionary War fort, built in 1776 under the direction of General Nathanael Greene, as part of the defenses of Brooklyn.
In the nineteenth century, the area developed into a neighborhood of handsome brownstones and townhouses for the merchants and professionals of the independent City of Brooklyn.

In the twentieth century, it became one of the centers of Black middle-class life in Brooklyn, and in the 1980s and 90s, it was home to a creative renaissance of Black artists, filmmakers, musicians, and writers, including Spike Lee, whose film company is based here.
Downtown Brooklyn, around Fulton Street, Flatbush Avenue, and Atlantic Avenue, was the shopping and business center of Brooklyn, with department stores, banks, and theaters.
Like downtowns across America, it declined in the mid-twentieth century.
In recent decades, it has been transformed by a rezoning, new towers, and the Barclays Center arena.
There's also a story here about the most painful loss in Brooklyn's history: not a battle or a fire, but a baseball team.
As you walk, you'll find out why the Brooklyn Dodgers left for Los Angeles, and what that has to do with the arena at the corner of Atlantic and Flatbush.
You're at the Brooklyn Navy Yard, at Flushing Avenue and Carlton Avenue, outside Building 92, a brick building that serves as the yard's visitor center and museum.
The site sits on Wallabout Bay, a curve of the East River.
During the Revolutionary War, the British anchored prison ships here, decaying old warships where they held American prisoners of war.
Conditions were horrific: prisoners were crammed below decks, starved, and ravaged by disease.
More than eleven thousand prisoners are believed to have died on these ships, more than died in all the battles of the Revolution combined.
Their bodies were often buried in shallow graves along the shore, and for years afterward, bones washed up on the beach.
You'll see their memorial in Fort Greene Park.
The federal government bought the site in 1801 and established the New York Navy Yard, commonly known as the Brooklyn Navy Yard.
Over the following century and a half, it built and repaired many of the Navy's most important ships.
The USS Maine, whose explosion in Havana harbor in 1898 helped spark the Spanish-American War, was built here.
The battleship USS Arizona, sunk at Pearl Harbor on December seventh, 1941, was built here and launched in 1915.
And the battleship USS Missouri, on whose deck Japan signed its surrender ending World War Two, in September 1945, was built here and launched in 1944.

During World War Two, the yard was a city of its own, with dry docks, foundries, machine shops, and cranes, and around seventy thousand workers, including thousands of women and African Americans who found industrial jobs here for the first time.
The Navy closed the yard in 1966, a devastating blow to Brooklyn.
The city bought it and turned it into an industrial park.

Today, it's home to hundreds of businesses employing thousands of people: manufacturers, artists, designers, and film studios, including Steiner Studios, one of the largest film and television production facilities on the East Coast.
There's a rooftop farm, a distillery, and companies making everything from furniture to food.
If you have time, Building 92's exhibits tell the yard's story, and tours of the yard are offered.
Walk south to Fort Greene Park, and climb to the top of the hill, where a tall Doric column rises from a broad granite stairway.
This hill was the site of Fort Putnam, built in 1776 under General Nathanael Greene, to defend Brooklyn against the British.
It was rebuilt during the War of 1812 and renamed Fort Greene in his honor.
The park was among the first public parks in Brooklyn.
The poet Walt Whitman, as editor of the Brooklyn Daily Eagle in the 1840s, campaigned for its creation, arguing that the working people of the crowded city needed open space.
It was laid out in 1847, and then redesigned in 1867 by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, the designers of Central Park and Prospect Park.

The monument at the top is the Prison Ship Martyrs Monument, dedicated in 1908 to the more than eleven thousand American prisoners who died on British prison ships in Wallabout Bay during the Revolution, which you heard about at the Navy Yard.
For decades, their remains, collected from the shore, were kept in various vaults.
In 1873, they were placed in a crypt here, beneath the stairway.
Then, the architects McKim, Mead and White designed this monument: a column about one hundred forty-nine feet tall, at the time among the tallest Doric columns in the world, topped by a bronze urn.
President-elect William Howard Taft dedicated it in November 1908.
The crypt is beneath the stairway, though it's not open to the public.
The prisoners on the ships came from all thirteen colonies and from many countries, including sailors captured on American privateers, and some were of African descent.
Each year, a ceremony is held here to remember them.
From the top of the hill, look around at the view, and at the neighborhood of brownstones surrounding the park.
On a clear day you can see the Manhattan skyline to the northwest.
Walk to South Portland Avenue and South Oxford Street, between DeKalb and Lafayette Avenues, two of the most beautiful residential blocks in Brooklyn.
These rows of brownstones and Italianate townhouses were built mostly in the 1850s to 1870s, for prosperous merchants and professionals.
Brownstone is a type of sandstone, quarried mostly in Connecticut and New Jersey, that was hugely popular in nineteenth-century New York.
It was relatively cheap, easy to carve, and gave a sense of solid respectability.
Most brownstone houses are actually brick buildings with a brownstone veneer on the front.
Fort Greene went through many changes.
In the early twentieth century, as wealthier residents moved to newer neighborhoods, many houses were divided into rooming houses.
After World War Two, Black families, many working at the Navy Yard, moved into the neighborhood.
Fort Greene developed a strong Black middle-class community.
The novelist Richard Wright wrote much of his landmark 1940 novel, Native Son, while living on Carlton Avenue, nearby.
In the 1980s and 90s, Fort Greene became the center of what was sometimes called a Black Bohemia or a Black Renaissance in Brooklyn.
The filmmaker Spike Lee, who grew up in Fort Greene, set up his production company, 40 Acres and a Mule Filmworks, in a converted firehouse on DeKalb Avenue.
His films, like She's Gotta Have It and Do the Right Thing, were rooted in Brooklyn.
Writers, jazz musicians like Branford Marsalis, artists, and actors lived in the neighborhood.
Since the 2000s, Fort Greene has gentrified, and brownstones now sell for millions of dollars.
The Black population has declined significantly, a change that's been the subject of much discussion, including Spike Lee's own outspoken criticism.
Look for the Lafayette Avenue Presbyterian Church, at Lafayette Avenue and South Oxford Street.
It was founded in 1857 by abolitionists and was reportedly a stop on the Underground Railroad.
Inside, there's a collection of Tiffany stained glass windows.
Walk west on Lafayette Avenue to the Brooklyn Academy of Music, known as BAM, in the large building with a terracotta and brick facade on the corner of Ashland Place.
BAM was founded in 1861, making it one of the oldest performing arts centers in the United States.
Its first building was in Brooklyn Heights, on Montague Street, but it burned down in 1903.
The current building, the Peter Jay Sharp Building, opened in 1908.

In its early years, BAM hosted the biggest names in the performing arts: the opera singer Enrico Caruso, the actress Sarah Bernhardt, the dancer Isadora Duncan, and the Metropolitan Opera, which performed here regularly.
Like much of Brooklyn, BAM declined in the mid-twentieth century.
Its turnaround came in 1967, when Harvey Lichtenstein became its director.
Lichtenstein transformed BAM into one of the world's leading centers for avant-garde and experimental performance.
He brought companies and artists that were too daring for Manhattan's establishment venues.

In 1983, he launched the Next Wave Festival, which showcased artists like the composer Philip Glass, the director Robert Wilson, the choreographers Merce Cunningham and Pina Bausch, and the performance artist Laurie Anderson.
BAM became a destination, drawing audiences from Manhattan to Brooklyn at a time when few people crossed the river for culture.

BAM's growth has been an anchor for the Brooklyn Cultural District, which now includes theaters, galleries, and other institutions, and BAM itself has expanded with additional theaters and cinemas in the neighborhood.
Look around at the area.
Mark Morris, the choreographer, built his dance center across the street.
And the large modern buildings nearby are part of the district's growth, many with arts spaces on their lower floors.
Look up at the tall tower with a gold-domed top and four large clock faces, at One Hanson Place, at the corner of Ashland Place and Flatbush Avenue.
This is the Williamsburgh Savings Bank Tower, completed in 1929.
For eighty years, it was the tallest building in Brooklyn, at about five hundred twelve feet.
It was built for the Williamsburgh Savings Bank, one of the largest savings banks in Brooklyn, a type of bank that held the deposits of working people and made mortgage loans.
The tower was designed to be visible from all over Brooklyn, a symbol of the bank's strength and stability, completed just before the stock market crash.
Its four clock faces, each about twenty-seven feet across, were among the largest in the world when it was built.
They became a landmark for generations of Brooklynites.
Step inside, if possible, to see the former banking hall, now an event space.
It's one of the most spectacular interiors in Brooklyn, with soaring arches, mosaics, and marble.
Its decoration is full of symbols of thrift, industry, and security, the virtues a savings bank wanted its depositors to associate with it.
For many decades, the upper floors of the tower were filled with dentists' offices.
It's a piece of Brooklyn trivia: if you went to the dentist in Brooklyn in the mid-twentieth century, there's a good chance it was here.
In the 2000s, the tower was converted to luxury condominiums.
The banking hall became an event venue.
Next to the tower is the Atlantic Terminal, a hub for the Long Island Rail Road and nine subway lines.
It's one of the busiest transit hubs in New York.
Walk south across Flatbush Avenue to the corner of Atlantic and Flatbush Avenues, to the Barclays Center, the arena with the rusted steel skin and a giant oculus over its entrance plaza.
This intersection holds one of the great what-ifs of New York history.
In the 1950s, the Brooklyn Dodgers were one of the most beloved teams in baseball.
They played at Ebbets Field, in the Flatbush neighborhood, but it was small, aging, and lacked parking.

The team's owner, Walter O'Malley, wanted to build a new, modern stadium, possibly a domed one, right here, at Atlantic and Flatbush, above the Long Island Rail Road terminal, where subway lines and commuter trains converged.
O'Malley needed the city's help to acquire the land.
But Robert Moses, who controlled much of the city's development, refused to support a stadium here.
He wanted the team to move to a site in Flushing Meadows, in Queens.
O'Malley refused to move the team to Queens.
Meanwhile, Los Angeles offered O'Malley a large tract of land for a new stadium.
After the 1957 season, the Dodgers left Brooklyn for Los Angeles.
Brooklynites felt betrayed.
For many, O'Malley was the villain, though historians have argued that Moses deserves a large share of the blame.
Ebbets Field was demolished in 1960 and replaced with apartment buildings.
A few years later, the Mets began playing in Queens, in Shea Stadium, on the very site Moses had offered the Dodgers.
More than half a century later, major league sports finally came back to this corner.
In 2012, the Barclays Center opened here, as part of a large and controversial development called Atlantic Yards, now called Pacific Park.
It is home to the Brooklyn Nets basketball team, who moved from New Jersey, the first major professional sports team in Brooklyn since the Dodgers.
The development involved the use of eminent domain to acquire property, and it led to years of protests and legal battles by neighborhood residents.
The arena's design, with its weathered steel exterior, was meant to evoke the borough's industrial heritage.
End your walk on Fulton Street, between Flatbush Avenue and Adams Street, in the pedestrian-friendly shopping area known as the Fulton Mall.
For most of the twentieth century, Fulton Street was Brooklyn's downtown, its equivalent of Herald Square, lined with department stores, movie palaces, and banks.
The biggest department store was Abraham and Straus, known as A and S. It was founded in 1865 by Abraham Abraham, a Jewish merchant.
In the 1890s, he brought in partners from the Straus family, the same family that ran Macy's.
A and S became one of the largest department stores in the country, and its building at Fulton and Hoyt Streets became a landmark.
In 1995, A and S was merged into Macy's, and the building became a Macy's store.
Fulton Street declined in the 1970s and 80s, as shoppers moved to the suburbs.
In 1977, it was converted into a pedestrian and bus mall, and it became a busy shopping district for Black and Caribbean Brooklynites, known for its sneaker stores, hip-hop fashion, and music.
It was celebrated in early hip-hop culture.
Since the 2000s, it has gentrified, with national chains, new office buildings, and high-rise apartments.
Look for the Dime Savings Bank of Brooklyn building, on DeKalb Avenue, near Fulton Street, with its massive dome and columns, modeled on the Pantheon in Rome, completed in 1908.
Look for the dimes incorporated into its decoration.
Its banking hall has been preserved as part of a new residential tower, which became one of the tallest buildings in Brooklyn.
Finally, at the corner of Flatbush and DeKalb Avenues, look for Junior's, a restaurant that has been serving its famous cheesecake since 1950.
It was founded by Harry Rosen, who named it after his two sons.
Its cheesecake, rich and creamy, made with cream cheese, became famous across the country.
Junior's survived a fire in 1981, rebuilt, and remains a Brooklyn icon.
A slice of cheesecake at Junior's is a fitting way to end a walk through Brooklyn's downtown.
Williamsburg and Greenpoint, along the East River in North Brooklyn, were once among the most intensely industrial places in America.
In the second half of the nineteenth century, this waterfront was lined with sugar refineries, oil refineries, breweries, shipyards, ironworks, glass and porcelain factories, and pencil makers.
Greenpoint was famous for what were called the five black arts: printing, pottery, gas, glass, and iron, all industries that involved fire and smoke.
Some of the most powerful companies in American history had major operations here.
The sugar refinery of the Havemeyer family became the heart of the Sugar Trust, which controlled almost all of the sugar refining in the country.
Charles Pratt's Astral Oil Works became part of John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil.
Brewers made Williamsburg and neighboring Bushwick one of the beer capitals of America.
And in Greenpoint, the shipyards built the USS Monitor, the ironclad warship that changed naval warfare.
Williamsburg was a separate city until 1855, when it merged with Brooklyn.
The opening of the Williamsburg Bridge in 1903 brought a flood of new residents from the crowded Lower East Side, especially Jewish families.
After World War Two, Hasidic Jews, many of them Holocaust survivors from Hungary and Romania, settled in South Williamsburg, which remains one of the largest Hasidic communities in the world.
Puerto Rican and Dominican families settled in the area known as Los Sures, on the South Side.
Greenpoint became the heart of the Polish community in New York, often called Little Poland.
As factories closed in the second half of the twentieth century, the waterfront emptied.
In the 1990s, artists, musicians, and young people priced out of Manhattan discovered the cheap lofts of Williamsburg, a stop or two from Manhattan on the L train.
By the 2000s, Williamsburg had become a global symbol of hipster culture, of indie rock, artisanal food, and fixed-gear bicycles.
In 2005, the city rezoned the waterfront, and luxury towers rose where factories had stood.
Today, the neighborhood is one of the most expensive in Brooklyn, and the transformation has been a subject of fierce debate.
This tour runs south to north, from the Domino Sugar refinery to Newtown Creek, the border between Brooklyn and Queens.
You're at Domino Park, on the waterfront at Kent Avenue and South 3rd Street.
Look at the massive brick building along the water, with the giant illuminated sign that reads Domino Sugar.
This is the old Domino Sugar refinery.
The story starts with the Havemeyer family, German immigrants who began refining sugar in Manhattan in the early nineteenth century.
In 1856, they built a refinery here in Williamsburg, on the waterfront, where ships could unload raw sugar from the Caribbean.
After a fire, the main building was rebuilt in 1882, and it was then one of the largest sugar refineries in the world.
By the late nineteenth century, the Williamsburg refineries were producing more than half of the sugar consumed in the United States.
Henry Osborne Havemeyer was the driving force behind one of the most powerful monopolies of the Gilded Age.
In 1887, he organized the Sugar Refineries Company, combining most of the major refiners into a trust, which was later reorganized as the American Sugar Refining Company.
By the early 1890s, it controlled the vast majority of the country's sugar refining.

When the federal government sued, in a case known as United States versus E. C. Knight Company, the Supreme Court ruled in 1895 that the Sherman Antitrust Act didn't apply, because refining was manufacturing, not interstate commerce.
The decision greatly weakened antitrust enforcement for years, until later cases, including the breakup of Standard Oil, restored it.
In 1900, the company introduced the Domino brand, and it eventually renamed itself Domino Sugar.
The work inside was grueling and dangerous: workers labored in intense heat, and many were immigrants, first German and Irish, later Polish, Puerto Rican, and others.
The refinery closed in 2004.

In 2014, before redevelopment began, the artist Kara Walker filled the building's vast, sticky interior with a giant sculpture made of sugar: a sphinx-like woman with the features of a stereotypical mammy figure, called A Subtlety, or the Marvelous Sugar Baby.
It confronted the history of slavery in the Caribbean sugar plantations that produced the raw sugar refined here.
More than a hundred thousand people came to see it.
The site has since been redeveloped by Two Trees Management, the same company that redeveloped DUMBO.
The waterfront became Domino Park, which opened in 2018, designed by James Corner Field Operations, the firm behind the High Line.
Look for the old cranes, gantries, and syrup tanks that were incorporated into the park's design, and for the walkway built from salvaged industrial pieces.
Walk to Broadway and Driggs Avenue, near the foot of the Williamsburg Bridge.
Look for a plain brick building with a sign reading Peter Luger Steak House.
Peter Luger has been serving steaks here since 1887.
It was founded as Carl Luger's Café, Billiards and Bowling Alley, in what was then a German neighborhood, near the ferry to Manhattan.
Peter Luger was the owner; his nephew Carl was the chef.
After Peter Luger's death, the restaurant declined.
In 1950, it was bought at auction by Sol Forman, a businessman whose metalware factory was across the street, and who had eaten lunch there for years.
His wife, Marsha, learned to select beef, and the family turned it into the most famous steakhouse in New York.
Its porterhouse steak, dry-aged on the premises and served sizzling, is legendary.
For many years it accepted only cash or its own house card.
Look up at the Williamsburg Bridge.
As you may have heard on the Lower East Side tour, when it opened in 1903 it was the longest suspension bridge in the world.
It transformed Williamsburg from a German neighborhood into a crowded, largely Jewish and Eastern European neighborhood almost overnight.
South of Broadway is South Williamsburg, home of a large Hasidic Jewish community, centered on the Satmar sect.
The Satmar Hasidim came from the town of Satu Mare, in present-day Romania.
