Their leader, Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, survived the Holocaust and arrived in New York in 1946.
He built a community here that has grown into tens of thousands of people.
The community is very traditional, speaking Yiddish as its primary language, with distinctive dress: men in black coats and hats, with sidelocks, and women in modest dresses with head coverings.
Walk along Lee Avenue, the main commercial street, and you'll see kosher shops, Yiddish signs, and bustling families.
The area to the east, along Broadway and the South Side, known as Los Sures, has been the heart of the Puerto Rican and Dominican community in Williamsburg since the 1950s.
Community organizations here fought for affordable housing in the 1970s and 80s, when many buildings were abandoned.
Walk north to North 11th Street, near Wythe Avenue, to the Brooklyn Brewery.
In the late nineteenth century, Brooklyn was one of the largest beer-producing places in America.
German immigrants brought lager brewing with them, and by the 1890s, Brooklyn had several dozen breweries, concentrated in Williamsburg and Bushwick, in an area nicknamed Brewers' Row.
Brands like Schaefer, Rheingold, Piels, and Trommer's were brewed here.
The Schaefer brewery, on the Williamsburg waterfront along Kent Avenue, was one of the largest in the country.
Its slogan, Schaefer is the one beer to have when you're having more than one, was famous in the mid-twentieth century.
Prohibition, from 1920 to 1933, closed many breweries.

Those that survived faced competition after World War Two from national brewers like Anheuser-Busch, which could produce beer more cheaply in giant, modern breweries and advertise on national television.
Brooklyn's breweries closed one after another.
Schaefer and Rheingold, the last big ones, closed in 1976.
For about a decade, there was no commercial brewing in Brooklyn.

Then, in 1988, two men founded the Brooklyn Brewery: Steve Hindy, a former Associated Press foreign correspondent who had learned home brewing from diplomats in the Middle East, and Tom Potter, a banker.
They hired the brewmaster Bill Moeller, whose family had brewed beer in Germany, and they hired the famous graphic designer Milton Glaser, who created the I heart NY logo, to design their logo.
The first beers were contract brewed upstate.
In 1996, they opened their own brewery here, in a former ironworks.
In 1994, they hired Garrett Oliver as brewmaster, and he became one of the most influential figures in American craft brewing.
The Brooklyn Brewery was one of the pioneers of the craft beer movement, and it helped revive Williamsburg's industrial waterfront.
It has offered tours and tastings to visitors for years, and its connection to Williamsburg defines the brand.
Look around at the old brick factory and warehouse buildings nearby.
Many of them have been converted to offices, shops, music venues, and condominiums.
Walk to Bedford Avenue and North 7th Street, at the Bedford Avenue station on the L train, the first stop in Brooklyn coming from Manhattan.
In the 1970s and 80s, this area was a struggling industrial neighborhood, with Polish, Italian, and Puerto Rican working-class families and many empty factories.
In the late 1980s and 1990s, artists began moving into the lofts, priced out of the East Village and SoHo.
The L train put them just one stop from Manhattan.
By the late 1990s, Williamsburg had a thriving underground art and music scene, with galleries, performance spaces, and illegal warehouse parties.
In the 2000s, Williamsburg became internationally famous.
Bands like Yeah Yeah Yeahs, TV on the Radio, and Vampire Weekend were associated with the Brooklyn indie rock scene.
Coffee shops, vintage clothing stores, and restaurants serving artisanal food opened along Bedford Avenue.
The word hipster became almost synonymous with Williamsburg.
Magazines and newspapers around the world wrote about it, and the neighborhood's aesthetic, beards, tattoos, flannel, craft beer, and pickles, was exported to cities everywhere.
Then the money came.
In 2005, the city rezoned the Williamsburg and Greenpoint waterfront, allowing towers of up to forty stories on land that had been zoned for manufacturing.
Glass towers rose along the river.
Rents soared.
Many of the artists who had made the neighborhood famous were priced out, moving farther east to Bushwick and beyond.
Big brands arrived: Apple, Whole Foods, and luxury hotels opened stores and locations near Bedford Avenue.
Walk toward the river, to Marsha P. Johnson State Park, formerly East River State Park, named in 2020 for the transgender activist who was a central figure in the gay liberation movement.
On weekends in warm months, it's the site of Smorgasburg, a giant outdoor food market, launched in 2011, with dozens of vendors.
From the waterfront, look across the river at the Manhattan skyline, from the Williamsburg Bridge to the Empire State Building.
Every new tower on this side of the river was built to capture this view.
Walk east to McCarren Park, at the border between Williamsburg and Greenpoint, around Bedford Avenue and Lorimer Street.
On the west side of the park, look for the large building with a grand arched entrance.

This is McCarren Park Pool, one of eleven huge public swimming pools that opened in New York City in the summer of 1936, built by Robert Moses with funding from the federal Works Progress Administration during the Great Depression.
The eleven pools were designed to bring recreation and relief to working-class neighborhoods during the heat of summer.
McCarren Pool could hold nearly sixty-eight hundred swimmers at a time.
The pool was a beloved neighborhood institution for decades, but by the 1980s, it had deteriorated, and the city closed it in 1984.
It sat empty for more than twenty years, a ruin surrounded by a fence.

In the mid-2000s, while plans for its restoration were made, the empty pool became a concert venue, hosting free summer concerts by indie rock bands, as well as dodgeball leagues and other events, part of Williamsburg's emergence as a cultural destination.
After a major restoration, the pool reopened for swimming in 2012.
In winter, part of it becomes an ice skating rink.
Just east of the park, at North 12th Street and Driggs Avenue, look for the Russian Orthodox Cathedral of the Transfiguration of Our Lord, with its five green onion domes.
It was built in the 1920s, and it's a reminder of the many Eastern European communities in North Brooklyn.
The park is named for Patrick McCarren, a state senator and Democratic political boss of Brooklyn in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
Today, it's the backyard of the neighborhood, filled with soccer games, softball, runners, and people lounging on the grass.
Walk north into Greenpoint, to the corner of Kent Street and Franklin Street, near the Greenpoint waterfront.
Look at the buildings at Greenpoint Avenue and West Street, and on Kent Street.
On the facade of one of them, look for decorative ornaments shaped like giant yellow pencils, along with stars.
These were the buildings of the Eberhard Faber Pencil Company.
Eberhard Faber came from a German family that had been making pencils in Bavaria since the eighteenth century, and he came to New York in 1848 to represent the family business.
In 1861, he opened a pencil factory in Manhattan.
After it burned down in 1872, he moved the factory here to Greenpoint, and over the following decades the company expanded into a complex of buildings.
Eberhard Faber became one of the largest pencil manufacturers in the country.
Its Mongol pencil was one of the most popular pencils in America.
The company also made erasers, rubber bands, and pens.
The factory moved to Pennsylvania in 1956, and the buildings were converted to other uses.
They're now protected as a historic district.
The pencil company was one of many factories in Greenpoint.
Along with the five black arts, Greenpoint had shipbuilding, rope making, and sugar refining.
The Union Porcelain Works, in Greenpoint, produced fine porcelain tableware in the nineteenth century, some of which is now in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum and the Brooklyn Museum.
Walk along Manhattan Avenue, Greenpoint's main shopping street, a few blocks to the east.
For more than a century, Greenpoint has been the heart of the Polish community in New York, with Polish bakeries, butcher shops selling kielbasa, delis, churches, and restaurants.
Polish immigrants came in waves, in the late nineteenth century, after World War Two, and again in the 1980s, when many fled the communist government's crackdown on the Solidarity movement.
The Polish population has declined as younger generations have moved and new residents have arrived, but you'll still hear Polish spoken on the street.

Look also at the beautiful churches of Greenpoint, including St. Anthony of Padua, on Manhattan Avenue, with its tall spire, and St. Stanislaus Kostka, the Polish Catholic parish, which Pope John Paul the Second visited as a cardinal in 1969 and again in 1976.
Walk north along Franklin Street, to Franklin and India Streets.
In the nineteenth century, Greenpoint and the shore of Newtown Creek, just to the north, became one of the largest oil-refining centers in America.
In 1867, Charles Pratt, a businessman who had made money in paint and oil, opened the Astral Oil Works on the creek.
He produced kerosene, a fuel refined from petroleum, used for lighting lamps.
Pratt's brand, Astral Oil, was known for its quality and safety, at a time when cheap kerosene often exploded.
Its advertising slogan claimed that the holy lamps of Tibet were primed with Astral Oil.
In 1874, Pratt sold his company to John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil, becoming one of its leading partners and making a vast fortune.
He used part of it to found the Pratt Institute, an art and engineering school in Clinton Hill, which opened in 1887 to train working people in practical skills.
He also built the Astral Apartments, at 184 Franklin Street, completed in 1886, as model housing for his workers, with better light, air, and sanitation than typical tenements of the time.
Look for it, a large, handsome brick building in the Queen Anne style.
The oil industry left a toxic legacy.
In 1978, a Coast Guard helicopter patrol spotted an oil slick on Newtown Creek.
Investigators discovered that over many decades, oil from refineries and storage facilities had leaked into the ground under Greenpoint.
Estimates of the total ranged from seventeen to thirty million gallons, making it one of the largest oil spills in American history, larger than the Exxon Valdez spill.
Cleanup has continued for decades, and Newtown Creek is now a federal Superfund site.
Now walk to the waterfront at the end of India Street, near the ferry pier.
Just north of here, at the Continental Iron Works on the Greenpoint shore, the USS Monitor was built.
The Monitor was a revolutionary ironclad warship, designed by the Swedish-born engineer John Ericsson, with a low, armored hull and a rotating gun turret, something no ship had used in battle before.
It was built in about one hundred days and launched on January thirtieth, 1862.
On March ninth, 1862, at the Battle of Hampton Roads, in Virginia, the Monitor fought the Confederate ironclad CSS Virginia, formerly the Merrimack, to a standoff.
It was the first battle between ironclad warships, and it signaled the end of the age of wooden warships.
In McGolrick Park, a few blocks east, look for a monument to the Monitor and its crew.
End your walk at the Newtown Creek Nature Walk, at the end of Paidge Avenue, on the shore of Newtown Creek, the waterway that separates Brooklyn from Queens.
Look at the giant, shining, egg-shaped structures rising beside the creek.
These are the digester eggs of the Newtown Creek Wastewater Treatment Plant, the largest of the city's wastewater treatment plants.
There are eight of them, each about one hundred forty feet tall, clad in stainless steel.
Inside, bacteria break down sludge from the city's sewage, producing methane gas.
The egg shape helps the sludge mix and the process run efficiently.
Completed in the 2010s, they've become an unlikely architectural landmark, and they glow blue at night.
The plant offers tours a few times a year, including at sunrise or sunset, and the view from the top of the eggs is said to be remarkable.
The Nature Walk was designed by the artist George Trakas, and opened in 2007, as part of the plant's commitment to the community.
It's a winding path along the water, with granite steps, plantings, and references to the creek's history.
It includes a timeline of the area carved into stone, and features that recall the creek's natural past, before industry transformed it.
Newtown Creek was once a tidal estuary, with marshes and wildlife.
The Lenape fished here, and Dutch and English settlers farmed nearby.
In the nineteenth century, it became one of the busiest industrial waterways in the country, lined with refineries, chemical plants, fertilizer works, and factories.
At one time, the creek carried more cargo than the Mississippi River, by some accounts.
It also became one of the most polluted waterways in the nation, absorbing oil, chemicals, and raw sewage.
Today, community groups and the federal government are working on a long, slow cleanup.
Kayakers and canoeists now paddle the creek, and scientists monitor its recovery.
It's a fitting place to end a tour of North Brooklyn: a place where industry made fortunes, left scars, and is now being slowly transformed into something new.
If you ask Brooklynites which park is better, Central Park or Prospect Park, many will tell you Prospect Park.
And they have a strong ally: Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, who designed both, reportedly considered Prospect Park their finer work.
In the 1860s, the City of Brooklyn was booming, and its leaders wanted a great park to rival Manhattan's new Central Park.
The driving force was James S. T. Stranahan, a businessman and civic leader who was also a key promoter of the Brooklyn Bridge.
An initial plan for the park would have split it in two with a major road.
Vaux, who had been consulted, argued for a different site and a unified design, and in 1865, he and Olmsted were hired.
Unlike in Manhattan, they didn't have to work around a reservoir or a rigid rectangle.
They had a chance to design a park closer to their ideal: a huge, sweeping meadow, a deep forested ravine, and a large lake, each arranged as a distinct experience, flowing into one another.
The park opened in stages starting in 1867.
It covers about five hundred twenty-six acres.
Around it, the neighborhoods developed quickly.
Park Slope, on the hill to the west, filled with grand mansions along Prospect Park West, and with block after block of brownstones on the side streets.
The neighborhood declined in the mid-twentieth century, but in the 1960s and 70s, young families, many of them professionals, discovered its brownstones, bought them cheaply, and restored them.
They called themselves brownstoners, and they helped launch the brownstone revival movement that transformed many Brooklyn neighborhoods.
Today, Park Slope is one of the most desirable and expensive neighborhoods in New York, famous for its strollers, its food co-op, and its progressive politics.
The land here also holds the story of the largest battle of the American Revolution.
On August twenty-seventh, 1776, the Battle of Brooklyn was fought across this terrain, along the ridge that now runs through Prospect Park, and down in the lowlands near the Gowanus Creek.
The Americans were routed, and only a heroic rear-guard action and a foggy night escape saved Washington's army.
This walk starts at Grand Army Plaza, explores the park, climbs into Park Slope, and ends at the Old Stone House and the Gowanus Canal.
You're at Grand Army Plaza, the great oval plaza at the northern entrance to Prospect Park, where Flatbush Avenue, Eastern Parkway, and Prospect Park West meet.
Olmsted and Vaux designed this plaza as a grand entrance, a kind of buffer between the city and the park, with an oval shape to direct traffic around it.
At its center rises the Soldiers' and Sailors' Memorial Arch, completed in 1892, honoring the Union forces in the Civil War.
It was designed by John Duncan, the architect of Grant's Tomb, and modeled on Roman triumphal arches.
The sculptures were added later.
On top is a dramatic bronze quadriga, a chariot pulled by four horses, with a figure of Columbia, representing the United States, by the sculptor Frederick MacMonnies.
On the sides are groups representing the Army and the Navy.
Inside the arch, look for bronze reliefs of Abraham Lincoln and Ulysses S. Grant on horseback, by Thomas Eakins and William O'Donovan.
The arch is sometimes open for climbing, offering a great view.
North of the arch is the Bailey Fountain, with figures representing Wisdom and Felicity and Neptune with tritons.
And on the southwest side of the plaza, there's a bust of President John F. Kennedy, the only official memorial to him in New York City.
On the east side of the plaza, look for the Central Library of the Brooklyn Public Library, completed in 1941.
Its striking Art Deco facade is shaped to follow the curve of the plaza, like the spine of an open book.
Its entrance is framed by tall bronze screens with gilded figures from American literature, including Moby Dick, Tom Sawyer, Rip Van Winkle, and characters from Edgar Allan Poe.
Brooklyn's library system is independent from the New York Public Library, a legacy of Brooklyn's days as a separate city.
On Saturdays, the plaza hosts one of the city's largest greenmarkets.

Eastern Parkway, running east from here, was designed by Olmsted and Vaux as the first parkway in the world, a broad, tree-lined boulevard for carriages, with separate lanes for local traffic and walkways.
It was meant to connect Prospect Park with the rest of the city and served as the model for parkways everywhere.
Walk east along Eastern Parkway to the Brooklyn Museum, the grand Beaux-Arts building with a columned portico.
The Brooklyn Museum was designed by McKim, Mead and White, and the first section opened in 1897.
It was planned to be the largest art museum in the world, larger even than the Louvre.
Brooklyn was then an independent city, and its leaders wanted it to have cultural institutions to rival anything in Manhattan.
But in 1898, Brooklyn merged into New York, and the political will and funding for the giant museum faded.
Only about one-sixth of the planned building was ever completed.
The museum is still one of the largest in the United States.
Look up at the attic of the building, the top of the facade.
You'll see a row of statues representing great figures and cultures of the ancient world, created by many sculptors, including Daniel Chester French.
Notice that the grand front staircase is missing: it was removed in the 1930s, a decision later regretted.
A modern glass entrance pavilion was added in 2004.

Inside, the museum is known for its Egyptian collection, one of the finest in the world, and for its American art, its African art, and its feminist art center, which houses Judy Chicago's famous installation The Dinner Party, a triangular banquet table with place settings for thirty-nine women from history.
Next to the museum is the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, founded in 1910 on the site of a former ash dump.
It covers fifty-two acres, with themed gardens, conservatories, and collections.
Its Japanese Hill-and-Pond Garden, designed by the Japanese landscape architect Takeo Shiota and completed in 1915, is among the oldest Japanese-inspired gardens in an American public garden.
In spring, the garden's cherry trees burst into bloom along the Cherry Esplanade, and the garden holds a festival to celebrate them.
Across the street, the Brooklyn Public Library's Central Library and the museum and garden together form a cultural complex that reflects Brooklyn's ambitions in its days as a great independent city.
Walk back into Prospect Park through the entrance at Grand Army Plaza, under the Endale Arch, a dark, low stone tunnel.
As you walk through it, the park opens up in front of you, and you see the Long Meadow.
This was exactly what Olmsted and Vaux intended.

They used the dark, enclosed arch as a kind of threshold, a compression, so that when you emerged, the vast open meadow would feel even more expansive, like stepping from the city into the countryside.
It's a classic technique of landscape design, and it's one of the most dramatic moments in any park in the world.
The Long Meadow stretches almost a mile, about ninety acres, making it one of the longest continuous meadows in any urban park in the United States.
Olmsted and Vaux shaped it carefully.
Notice how its edges curve, and how groups of trees are planted to hide its full length, so you never see the whole thing at once.
It invites you to keep walking to see what's around the next bend.
It's the heart of the park: on a sunny weekend, it's filled with picnics, soccer games, dogs, frisbees, and families.
Before nine in the morning and after nine at night, dogs are allowed off leash on the meadow, and it becomes one of the best dog parks in the city.
Just like Central Park's Sheep Meadow, the Long Meadow had sheep.
A flock grazed here from the park's early years, and in 1934, when Robert Moses removed the sheep from Central Park, he sent that flock here too.
Not long afterward, Prospect Park's sheep were retired as well, and the meadow's grass has been mowed by machine ever since.
Look along the western edge of the meadow, near Prospect Park West, for Litchfield Villa, an Italianate mansion completed in 1857, before the park existed.
It was built for Edwin Clark Litchfield, a railroad developer and lawyer who owned much of the land that became Park Slope.
His property was taken for the park, but the villa survived, and it now houses the offices of the Prospect Park Alliance, the nonprofit that manages the park.
Walk to the east side of the park, near Flatbush Avenue and the zoo, close to the carousel and the Lefferts Historic House.
You're in the area where the Battle of Brooklyn was fought, on August twenty-seventh, 1776.
Here's what happened.
After the British army landed on Staten Island and then in southern Brooklyn, about twenty thousand British and Hessian troops faced about ten thousand Americans defending Brooklyn.
The Americans had built fortifications on Brooklyn Heights, and they posted troops on the Heights of Guan, a forested ridge running across Brooklyn, which today passes through Prospect Park.
There were four passes through the ridge.
One of them, Flatbush Pass, also called Battle Pass, was right here, along what is now the East Drive near the zoo.
The Americans left the easternmost pass, the Jamaica Pass, almost undefended.
The British, guided by local loyalists, marched through it overnight and attacked the Americans from behind.
Meanwhile, Hessian troops attacked through the passes here.
The Americans were caught between the two forces and routed.
Many were killed or captured.
The survivors fled west, toward the Gowanus Creek and the fortifications on Brooklyn Heights.
Look for the boulder with a plaque near the zoo, marking the site of Battle Pass, and the Dongan Oak, a giant tree that the Americans felled to block the road.
Nearby, look for the Lefferts Historic House, a Dutch colonial farmhouse with a gambrel roof and a long porch.
The Lefferts family were Dutch settlers who farmed in Flatbush for generations.
Their original house was burned by the Americans during the battle, to keep it from being used by the British.
The family rebuilt it in 1783.
In 1918, the house was moved into the park from its original site on Flatbush Avenue.
It's now a museum about life on a farm in Brooklyn in the 1820s, including the history of the enslaved people who worked on the Lefferts farm, since slavery was common in Dutch Brooklyn.
Nearby is the Prospect Park Carousel, built in 1912 by the master carver Charles Carmel, with horses, a lion, a giraffe, and a deer.
Walk to the Boathouse, the white terracotta building with arched openings on the shore of the Lullwater, a narrow arm of Prospect Lake.
The Boathouse was completed in 1905, designed by the architects Helmle and Huberty in a Beaux-Arts style inspired by the Library of St. Mark's in Venice.
It was built to serve boaters on the lake, and it's one of the most photographed spots in the park, reflected in the still water of the Lullwater.
In the 1960s, the Parks Department planned to demolish it.
A public campaign saved it, and in 1968 it became one of the early buildings designated as a landmark by the city.
It's now the Audubon Center, the first urban Audubon center in the country, which offers nature exhibits, programs, and electric boat tours.
The Lullwater flows into Prospect Lake, about sixty acres, Brooklyn's only freshwater lake.
In winter in the nineteenth century, the lake was crowded with skaters.
Today, people fish, boat, and watch the birds on the lake, including swans, herons, and cormorants.
West of the Boathouse, across a bridge, is the Ravine, the wooded valley at the heart of the park.
It's the only forest in Brooklyn, though it's as man-made as the rest of the park.
Olmsted and Vaux designed a stream, the Ambergill, which flows through a rocky gorge, with waterfalls and pools, designed to evoke the Adirondack Mountains.
When you're in the Ravine, you can't see the city at all, and the sound of water hides the noise.
In the 1990s, the Prospect Park Alliance launched a long restoration of the Ravine's woodlands, which had been degraded by erosion and invasive plants.
Look also for the Cleft Ridge Span, a bridge near the lake, built in 1872.
It's one of the earliest structures in the United States built of concrete, cast in blocks, with intricate decorative patterns molded into its arch.
It was an experiment in a new building material that would later transform architecture.
Walk west out of the park and into Park Slope, to Seventh Avenue and Sterling Place.
Park Slope rises up the hill from the Gowanus Canal to the edge of Prospect Park, which is why it's called Park Slope.
It was developed mostly from the 1870s to the early 1900s, after the park opened, with rows of brownstones and brick houses for the growing middle class.
Along Prospect Park West, wealthy families built mansions, and the area became known as Brooklyn's Gold Coast.

Walk along the side streets between Seventh and Eighth Avenues, like Carroll Street, Montgomery Place, and Berkeley Place, to see some of the finest rows of nineteenth-century townhouses in America, in Romanesque, Queen Anne, and Renaissance Revival styles.
Montgomery Place, a single block, has a remarkable collection of houses designed by the architect C. P. H. Gilbert.

At the corner of Eighth Avenue and Lincoln Place, look for the Montauk Club, a private club housed in a building modeled on the Ca' d'Oro, a Gothic palace on the Grand Canal in Venice, completed in 1891.
Look closely at the facade: the friezes depict scenes from the life of the Montaukett, a Native American people of Long Island, after whom the club is named.
This intersection also has a tragic history.
On December sixteenth, 1960, two passenger planes collided in the sky over Staten Island.
One crashed there; the other, United Airlines Flight 826, crashed here, at Seventh Avenue and Sterling Place.
All the people on both planes were killed, along with several people on the ground, including people in a church and in shops.
In total, one hundred thirty-four people died.
It was, at the time, the deadliest aviation disaster in history.
An eleven-year-old boy on the United flight survived the crash, and he was found in a snowbank, but he died the next day.
A memorial to the victims is in Green-Wood Cemetery.
A few blocks away, on Union Street, is the Park Slope Food Coop, founded in 1973, one of the oldest and largest member-owned food cooperatives in the country.
Members must work a shift every few weeks in exchange for the right to shop there, at prices well below regular grocery stores.
End your walk downhill, at J. J. Byrne Park, on Fifth Avenue and Third Street, at the Old Stone House, a small two-story stone farmhouse.
The original house was built in 1699 by a Dutch farmer named Klaes Arents Vechte.
On August twenty-seventh, 1776, during the Battle of Brooklyn, this house was at the center of one of the most heroic moments of the Revolution.

As the American army fled toward the Gowanus Creek and the safety of Brooklyn Heights, a regiment of about four hundred Maryland soldiers, under Lord Stirling, turned to face the British, who had occupied the house.
The Marylanders charged the British again and again, holding them off long enough for most of the American army to escape across the creek.
Most of the Maryland soldiers were killed or captured.
Watching from a nearby hill, George Washington reportedly exclaimed, Good God, what brave fellows I must this day lose.
The soldiers are remembered as the Maryland Four Hundred.
The original house was buried in the 1890s, and the building you see is a reconstruction from the 1930s, using some of the original stones.
There's also a twist: in the 1880s, the house served as the clubhouse for the baseball team that later became the Brooklyn Dodgers, which played at a ballpark nearby called Washington Park.
Walk a few blocks west to the Gowanus Canal.
In the colonial era, Gowanus Creek was a tidal marsh, famous for its oysters.
In the 1860s, it was turned into a canal, to serve the growing industrial waterfront.
Factories, coal yards, gas plants, chemical works, tanneries, and cement plants lined its banks.
It became one of the most polluted waterways in America, filled with industrial waste and raw sewage.
Locals nicknamed it Lavender Lake, for its strange color.
In 1911, the city built a flushing tunnel to pump in water from Buttermilk Channel, to flush the canal.
It helped, but not enough.
In 2010, the canal was designated a federal Superfund site, and a massive cleanup is underway.
In 2021, the city rezoned the neighborhood, allowing thousands of new apartments to be built along the canal.
It's a remarkable transformation for a waterway that was once a symbol of industrial filth.
From the battlefield to the factories to the brownstones and the condos, this corner of Brooklyn has seen the whole history of the city.
